`docs/decisions/0001-repo-layout.md`:

```md
# 0001 — Repo layout and keeping game data out

<!-- decision
state: accepted
date: 2026-10-14
replaces: none
code: .gitignore, config.example.toml, tools/yw4/config.py
-->

Date: 2026-10-14
Status: accepted

## Decision

- `tools/` — Python analysis and input-pipeline scripts (Phase 0). Python because these are one-shot binary-parsing jobs where iteration speed matters more than speed of execution. Stdlib only for now (`tomllib` needs Python 3.11+).
- `runtime/`, `recomp/` — C/C++ built with CMake. Empty until Phases 1–2.
- `docs/` — recon reports, baseline numbers, and these decision records.
- `work/`, `build/` — all generated output. Gitignored.
- `config.local.toml` — the only place paths to user-supplied files live. Gitignored. `config.example.toml` is the committed template.

## Why

- Rule 1 (no game data) is enforced by `.gitignore`, not by memory. It blocks dump/container formats, NSO/ELF, the extensionless ExeFS module names (`main`, `rtld`, `sdk`, `subsdk*`), keys, firmware, and Ghidra/IDA databases. Reverse-engineering databases are on the list because they embed the game's code.
- The ExeFS names are ignored everywhere, not just in `exefs/`. Cost: a source folder can't be called `sdk` or `main` without a `!` exception. That is cheaper than one accidental commit of `main`.
- `**/generated/` and `work/` cover recompiler output, which is derived from the game's code.
- In-source CMake builds are refused so build output can't mix with tracked files.

## Known risk

The repo path is under `OneDrive\Desktop`, but OneDrive sync is turned off on the owner's machine (confirmed 2026-10-14), so nothing is uploaded. If sync is ever turned back on, `work/` (decompressed ELF, RomFS extracts, generated C) would be uploaded. `tools/yw4/config.py` prints a warning when `work_dir` is under a cloud-folder path as a reminder; it can't tell whether sync is actually on.

```

`docs/decisions/0002-nso-pipeline-and-version-lock.md`:

```md
# 0002 — NSO input pipeline and version lock

<!-- decision
state: accepted
date: 2026-10-20
replaces: none
code: tools/yw4/nso.py, tools/yw4/lz4_block.py, target.toml
-->

Date: 2026-10-20
Status: accepted

## Decision

- Decompress NSO modules with our own code (`tools/yw4/nso.py`, `tools/yw4/lz4_block.py`), not nx2elf or the `lz4` package.
- Output is a **flat memory image** per module (`work/exefs/<module>.bin`): text, ro, and data placed at their memory offsets, gaps zero-filled, .bss left out. Plus `modules.json` with segment layout, build ID, and `.dynstr`/`.dynsym` locations.
- The build is identified by **SHA-256 of `main`'s flat image**, pinned in the committed `target.toml`. The build ID is recorded next to it for humans and IPS-patch tooling.
- `ingest` verifies `main` first and refuses to write anything on a mismatch. With nothing pinned yet, it prints the hash and needs `--pin` to record it. After that, changing the target means editing `target.toml` by hand.

## Why

- **Own decoder:** LZ4 block format is ~40 lines. Writing it keeps Phase 0 stdlib-only (no new dependency) and makes the pipeline fully explainable. Speed is fine: ~2 s for 32 MB of compressed data in pure Python. The `lz4` package is used only in tests, as a reference to compare against.
- **Flat image, not ELF:** the Ghidra Switch loader reads NSO directly, so we don't need an ELF yet. A flat image is the simplest thing that later tools (string scan, RTTI survey, import parsing) can index by virtual address. If we need an ELF later, it can be built from the image plus `modules.json`.
- **Hash the image, not the file:** the same game code can be stored compressed or uncompressed (some tools rewrite NSOs). The image hash only changes if the code or data changes. Each segment's SHA-256 in the NSO header is also checked during decompression, which catches corrupt dumps before hashing.
- **Hash + build ID:** the hash is what we enforce. The build ID is what the modding community uses to name patches, so it's useful to have both.

## Not done here

- Other modules (`rtld`, `sdk`, `subsdk*`) are decompressed and their hashes recorded in `modules.json`, but not pinned. If `main` matches, they come from the same update.

```

`docs/decisions/0003-nsp-extraction-with-hactool.md`:

```md
# 0003 — Extracting ExeFS/RomFS from NSPs with hactool

<!-- decision
state: accepted
date: 2026-10-20
replaces: none
code: tools/yw4/extract.py, tools/yw4/pfs0.py
-->

Date: 2026-10-20
Status: accepted

## Decision

- `tools/yw4/extract.py` turns the user's own base + update NSPs into the `exefs_dir` / `romfs_dir` that `ingest` reads, with the update applied.
- We read the NSP container (PFS0) ourselves (`tools/yw4/pfs0.py`) and call **hactool 1.4.0** (SciresM, ISC license) for NCA decryption and update patching. hactool is a user-supplied tool, set by `[tools] hactool_exe`. It is not vendored.
- Keys are given to hactool through a temporary home folder (`.switch/prod.keys` + `.switch/title.keys`) that is deleted afterwards. The temporary `title.keys` holds only the rights IDs found in the two NSPs' tickets.

## Why

- **hactool, not hactoolnet:** the LibHac repo (hactoolnet) returned 404 on GitHub on 2026-10-20. hactool's official repo is still up. We only run it, never copy its code, and its license is ISC anyway, so the GPL question (CLAUDE.md rule 5) does not come up.
- **Old build is fine:** hactool 1.4.0 (2020) reads master keys from `prod.keys`. This game uses key generation 7 (firmware 7.0.0–8.0.1), so it is well within range.
- **Temporary home folder:** base and update have different rights IDs, so they need different title keys, but `--titlekey` takes only one. hactool also loads `~/.switch/title.keys` on its own and matches keys per NCA. Pointing `USERPROFILE`/`HOME` at a temp folder uses that without touching the user's real home. Writing only the two needed keys also gets around hactool 1.4 aborting on duplicate entries, which real `title.keys` dumps can contain.
- **Doing PFS0 ourselves:** it is a 20-line format, and it lets us find tickets (rights IDs) and skip `.cnmt.nca` without parsing hactool's text output.
- **Update applied via `--basenca`:** the update's RomFS is a patch (BKTR) on the base RomFS and can't be read alone.

## Consequences

- The unpacked NCAs in `work/nca/` (~9 GB) are deleted after a successful run unless `--keep-nca` is passed.
- If hactool disappears too, the same flow works with any tool that accepts a base NCA and a patch NCA; only `run_hactool` and `find_program_nca` would change.

```

`docs/decisions/0004-pi5-as-arm64-reference.md`:

```md
# 0004 — Raspberry Pi 5 as the ARM64 test reference; x86-64 is the first target

<!-- decision
state: accepted
date: 2026-10-20
replaces: none
code: none
-->

Date: 2026-10-20
Status: accepted

## Decision

- The recompiled game targets **x86-64 (Windows, then Linux) first**. The generated C stays portable, but nothing is tuned for ARM hosts yet.
- Correctness of the instruction translation is checked against **real ARM64 hardware**: the owner's Raspberry Pi 5 (Cortex-A76, 8 GB, GCC 14.2). A small harness on the Pi runs instruction sequences with chosen inputs and records the resulting registers, flags, and memory as golden test files. The x86 test suite runs the recompiled C on the same inputs and compares.
- We do **not** use Unicorn (or any other CPU emulator) as the reference.

## Why

- **Real silicon beats an emulator as the reference.** A reference emulator has its own bugs; the Pi doesn't.
- **No GPL.** Unicorn is GPL-2. Using it only in tests would probably not affect the project's license, but avoiding it removes the question (CLAUDE.md rule 5).
- **Close enough to the Switch.** The Switch's Cortex-A57 is ARMv8.0; the A76 is ARMv8.2 and runs every v8.0 instruction the same way. The A76 also has newer instructions (LSE `atomics`, `lrcpc`, dot product, fp16) that the Switch lacks, so the harness only tests encodings that appear in `main` (or synthetic v8.0 encodings), never "everything the Pi supports".
- **Golden files make day-to-day work Pi-free.** Results are generated in batches; the normal test run happens on the PC.

## Data handling

- Golden files built from synthetic encodings can be committed.
- Golden files built from instructions taken from `main` are game-derived and stay in `work/` (CLAUDE.md rule 1).

## Access

The Pi is reached over SSH with a project-only key (`~/.ssh/yw4_pi`), installed by the owner. The host and user will come from `config.local.toml`, never hardcoded.

```

`docs/decisions/0005-phase1-runtime-strategy.md`:

```md
# 0005 — Phase 1 runtime strategy

<!-- decision
state: accepted
date: 2026-10-20
replaces: none
code: none
-->

Date: 2026-10-20
Status: **accepted** (2026-10-20, owner). CLAUDE.md's phase plan updated to match.

## Recommendation in one paragraph

Recompile **only `main`** to C. Write our own small native runtime that implements the **578 `sdk` imports** directly on the host (threads, files, input, audio, window). Handle graphics at the **NVN API level**: implement the **177 NVN functions the game actually uses** on top of Vulkan, and translate shaders ahead of time from the NVIDIA assembly shipped with every shader. Don't link any emulator code. Use an emulator only as an **external reference**: run the original game in it to get screenshots, frame captures, and timings to compare against.

## What the measurements say (docs/recon.md)

| Fact | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| `main` makes **0 syscalls**; everything goes through **578 `sdk` imports** | We can cut at the `sdk` boundary and never emulate the Switch kernel |
| The imports are high-level APIs: `nn::os` threads/mutex/event, `nn::fs` open/read/write, `nn::hid` controller state, `nn::audio` PCM output, `nn::vi` window | Each maps cleanly to host APIs (OS threads, files, SDL3 or similar for input/audio/window) |
| ~140 imports are online/peripheral (socket, ssl, ldn, nfc, ...) | Can start as stubs |
| CRI, PhysX, Lua, NEX/Pia are statically linked in `main` | They get recompiled with the game, so nothing extra to implement |
| NVN is reached through one import; **177 of 513** NVN functions are used | An NVN→Vulkan layer is a bounded job, not "all of NVN" |
| Every shader ships with **NV_gpu_program5 assembly** | Shader translation works from documented text, not GPU machine code |
| The NVN *driver* lives inside `sdk` | The emulator-GPU fallback would mean recompiling `sdk` too and emulating the kernel's GPU interface. That is the expensive path this proposal avoids |

## Options considered

### A. Hybrid with an emulator (the plan in CLAUDE.md before this decision)
Recompile `main` **and** `sdk`. Link an emulator (Eden/Citron/Ryubing-family) for kernel services, system services, and its Maxwell GPU emulation.

Why `sdk` has to come along: emulators don't implement NVN or `nn::fs`. They run the game's own `sdk` code and step in one level lower, at the kernel's system calls and service messages. Their GPU layer reads the raw Maxwell command stream that the NVN driver in `sdk` writes. So reusing any of it means running `sdk` and providing the kernel interface it talks to.

- For: rendering would be correct early; lots of existing behaviour comes for free.
- Against: we'd have to recompile `sdk` too (5.4 MB more code, including the NVN driver and the syscall layer), and adapt emulator code that expects to own guest CPU emulation, guest memory, and guest threads. Untangling that is a large, open-ended job. And everything that works only works through a GPU *emulator*: exactly the layer the project wants to replace.
- License: the yuzu-derived emulators are GPL, so linking them makes the project GPL. That is acceptable for a fan project if chosen on purpose; it was not the deciding factor. (Ryujinx/Ryubing is reportedly MIT, but it is C#. Verify its license file before relying on that.)

### B. Custom runtime, HLE at the `sdk` boundary, NVN→Vulkan (recommended)
- For: small and fully ours; no GPL; native x86-64 threads and memory; the NVN layer is already the start of the "own renderer" goal. It stays fast because nothing is emulated.
- Against: no free correctness reference for rendering. NVN details (memory pools, texture layouts, command buffers backed by app memory, sync) must be implemented carefully. The first time anything appears on screen is later than in A.

### C. B plus an emulator used only as an external reference (recommended, = B in practice)
Same as B. Separately, run the original game in an emulator to capture reference screenshots, RenderDoc frames, and timings. No emulator code in this repo, so no GPL. This keeps the "screenshot diff" check that CLAUDE.md wants for Phase 4c.

## Performance compared with A (expected, not yet measured)

- **CPU:** same. Both recompile `main` the same way; C runs less code because `sdk` is replaced by direct host calls.
- **GPU:** expected faster. C skips the work A does every frame: running the NVN driver, decoding the Maxwell command stream back into meaning, and the emulator's texture cache (guessing what memory holds textures and keeping copies in sync).
- **No shader stutter:** all shaders are translated ahead of time, while emulators compile shaders the first time an effect appears. The baseline benchmark should show that stutter; the port shouldn't have it.
- **Where C can be worse:** visual bugs early on (no years of emulator fixes), a naive first NVN layer that is slow in spots (over-cautious syncs, extra copies), and any CPU readback of GPU results, which emulators already handle. Check early how much the game reads back.

## Other design points this enables

- **Same addresses on host and guest.** The Switch is 64-bit little-endian like x86-64. We can map `main` at a fixed host address and let guest pointers *be* host pointers, with no address translation in generated code. (N64Recomp has to translate 32-bit addresses; we don't.) Risk to check: whether the game assumes addresses fit in the Switch's 39-bit space or tags pointers. That seems unlikely; verify early.
- **Function list:** `.eh_frame_hdr` starts (39,094) plus address-taken targets, cross-checked by Ghidra (docs/ghidra.md). Indirect calls go through a lookup table built from that list, with a loud "unknown target" trap instead of a JIT. If the trap ever fires in practice, we add an interpreter fallback then.
- **Atomics:** exclusive pairs become compare-and-swap on the host. x86's stronger memory model covers ordinary loads and stores.
- **Testing:** instruction-level golden tests generated on the Pi 5 (decision 0004).

## What changes in CLAUDE.md if accepted

- Phase 1: "Hybrid is the expected start" → custom runtime (option C).
- Phase 3: unchanged in spirit (implement only what the import list needs), now with no emulator code underneath.
- Phase 4a: "keep the emulator's GPU layer" → our NVN→Vulkan layer for the 177 used functions is the fallback, with AOT-translated shaders. The external emulator run is the correctness reference. The 4b/4c plan (trace the frame, replace passes one at a time) stays the same.
- The line "deliberately skipping a full NVN → Vulkan reimplementation" stays true in spirit: it's not *full*, only the 177 used functions.

## Risks to watch

1. **NVN semantics without a reference implementation.** Mitigation: emulator captures to compare against. The NVN headers' documented behaviour; small test scenes first (menus are 2D).
2. **Something in `main` depends on `sdk` internals** beyond the import list (shared structs, callbacks into `sdk`). The import list shows the surface, but data layouts passed across it still have to be right.
3. **Compile size:** 4.3 M instructions of generated C. Plan for splitting into many files and a parallel build from day one.

## First milestone if accepted

`main` recompiled, linked against a runtime where every import logs and returns a safe default, running from the entry point until it needs something real. That run produces the ordered to-do list for Phase 3.

`docs/decisions/0006-recompiler-design.md`:

```md
# 0006 — Recompiler design (first version)

<!-- decision
state: accepted
date: 2026-10-20
replaces: 0001 (part)
code: recomp/golden.py, recomp/check.py, recomp/pi
-->

Date: 2026-10-20
Status: accepted (revisit after the first full compile of `main`)

## Decision

**Language.** The recompiler (ARM64 → C translator) is written in **Python**, in `recomp/`. It shares the readers in `tools/yw4/` (NSO, relocations, symbols). The *generated* code is C, compiled with any C11 compiler (GCC 13 today; Clang later for the full build). This replaces the "C/C++ in `recomp/`" note in decision 0001.

**Guest CPU state.** One struct holds the ARM64 registers:

```c
typedef struct {
    uint64_t x[31];   // x0..x30 (x30 = link register)
    uint64_t sp;
    uint64_t nzcv;    // flags in bits 31..28, same layout as the NZCV system register
    v128 v[32];       // SIMD/FP registers (later)
    uint32_t fpcr, fpsr;
    uint64_t tpidr;   // thread pointer (later)
} CPUState;
```

**Functions.** Each guest function becomes one C function `void f_<offset>(CPUState *ctx)`:
- branches inside the function become `goto` labels per instruction address
- `bl` becomes a direct C call
- `ret` becomes `return`
- `br`/`blr` go through a lookup table from guest address to C function; an unknown target traps loudly
- a `b` to another function's start is a tail call: call it, then return

**Pointers.** Guest addresses are host addresses (decision 0005), so loads and stores are plain memory accesses at the register value. Nothing is translated.

**Instruction semantics** follow the Arm Architecture Reference Manual pseudocode (DDI 0487), restricted to ARMv8.0 (what the Switch's Cortex-A57 implements).

## Testing

Every supported instruction form is tested against real hardware (decision 0004):

1. `recomp/golden.py` makes test cases: random encodings within an instruction form (no PC-relative or branch forms yet), plus register values that mix edge cases (0, 1, -1, signed min/max, sign-boundary values) with random ones. Each encoding also gets *pair states*: every even register holds one value of a known-dangerous pair and every odd register the other (e.g. INT64_MIN and -1), because random states almost never produce such exact combinations.
2. It copies `recomp/pi/` to the Pi 5 over SSH, builds the harness with the Pi's GCC, and runs the cases. The harness copies each instruction into an executable page between code that loads and stores the full register file (x0–x30, SP) and flags, then runs it.
3. The results come back as golden files in `tests/golden/` (xz-compressed, about 7 MB).
4. `recomp/check.py` translates each test encoding to C, compiles one test program with the host GCC (`-O2 -Wall -Werror` by default; `--opt=-O0` and `--ubsan` for other builds), runs it on the same inputs, and reports every mismatch with the instruction, inputs, expected, and actual.

**Loads and stores** (added 2026-10-20). Both machines keep a 128 KiB scratch buffer with the same byte pattern (`recomp/pi/testcase.h`). The generator decodes each test encoding with the lifter's own decoder (`MemAccess`) and sets the base register to an *offset* into the buffer so the access lands inside it. Each case line says which registers hold offsets; each side adds its own buffer address before running and subtracts it after. Results therefore don't depend on where each machine's buffer is. The output lists every changed buffer byte, so stores are checked byte by byte. Cases the scheme can't express are skipped: storing the base register itself (it would store a machine-specific address) and register-offset forms whose offset register is the base. SP-based accesses keep SP 16-byte aligned, because Linux faults on misaligned SP use.

The golden files are synthetic (random encodings, not taken from the game), so they are committed (changed 2026-10-20, after review): anyone can re-run `recomp.check` without the Pi, and a lifter change can't silently pass because the old results were lost.

## Open risk: single-copy atomicity

Loads and stores are emitted as `memcpy` into a local, which compilers turn into one host load/store. ARMv8 guarantees that aligned accesses up to 64 bits are not torn, and multithreaded game code may rely on that for plain (non-exclusive) shared variables. x86-64 gives the same guarantee for aligned accesses, but C does not promise the compiler keeps one access as one instruction. If torn or merged accesses ever show up, switch the helpers to `__atomic_load_n`/`__atomic_store_n` with relaxed order (same code on x86, but guaranteed).

## Why

- **Python:** the recompiler runs once per build, not at game time, so speed barely matters (4.3 M instructions is minutes at worst). Iteration speed and readability matter more for a learning project. If it becomes the bottleneck, the decoder can move to C++ later behind the same tests.
- **Registers in a struct first:** simplest correct translation, easy to test and debug. Keeping registers in C locals inside a function (much faster) is an optimisation for later, guarded by the same tests.
- **Test against hardware per instruction form:** recompiler bugs are silent wrong results. Catching them per instruction is far cheaper than debugging a crashed game.

```

`docs/decisions/0007-whole-function-translation.md`:

```md
# 0007 — Whole-function translation

<!-- decision
state: accepted
date: 2026-10-20
replaces: none
code: recomp/function.py, runtime/src/dispatch.c, tests/functest
-->

Date: 2026-10-20
Status: accepted (revisit when the runtime first runs recompiled code)

Builds on 0006 (one C function per guest function, `CPUState`) and 0005 (guest addresses = host addresses).

## Decision

**Entry points** = `.eh_frame_hdr` starts ∪ address-taken targets ∪ Ghidra's entries ∪ every `BL` target. That gives 40,228 functions in `main`.

**Function bodies are found by following control flow** from each entry (`recomp/function.py`, `discover`). We don't use Ghidra's sizes, because they are sometimes wrong. Measured: ~230 branches landed "in the middle of another function" by Ghidra's boundaries, and the examples checked were Ghidra cutting a function short (e.g. a function's size ending 4 bytes before its own tail code). Following flow stops at `ret`, at traps, at a branch to another entry, and when code falls through into another entry. Code reachable from two entries is translated into both; only 162 instructions in `main` are duplicated this way.

**Control flow:**

| Guest | C |
|---|---|
| `b`/`b.cond`/`cbz`/`tbz` inside the function | `goto L_<offset>` |
| branch (or fall-through) to another entry | tail call: `TAILCALL(f_x)` |
| `bl` | `x30 = yw4_image_base + return offset; f_x(ctx);` |
| `blr` | the same through `yw4_resolve(target)` |
| `br` with a recognised jump table | `switch (target - yw4_image_base) { case …: goto …; default: indirect tail call }` |
| other `br` | indirect tail call (`TAILCALL_INDIRECT`) |
| `ret` | `return` |
| `adr`/`adrp`/`ldr` (literal) | `yw4_image_base + constant` |

- **Tail calls** use Clang's `musttail`, which guarantees no host stack growth. That matters if some loop goes through tail calls. GCC usually turns them into jumps at -O2 but doesn't promise it, so the full build uses Clang. Since 2026-10-21 that is llvm-mingw 20261006 (Clang 23.1.3, UCRT), set as `[tools] cc`. All of `main` compiles with it warning-free (about 4 min on 16 threads at -O1) and links; GCC still works for the tests.
- **Jump tables** are matched against the one pattern Clang emits in `main`: `cmp #N; b.hi; adrp/add (often hoisted, sometimes copied with mov); ldrsw [T, idx, lsl #2]; add; br`. The table gives the targets and lets discovery reach the case code. The switch is on the *target address*, not the index, so every instruction before the `br` still runs exactly as on hardware. A target we didn't predict goes to `yw4_resolve` and traps loudly instead of jumping somewhere wrong. In `main`: 1,344 tables recognised, 12 `br`s that look like tables are not (their table register is set somewhere the backwards scan can't follow), and 2,252 `br`s are real indirect tail calls (vtables, PLT stubs).
- **Indirect calls** look up the target in `yw4_funcs[]`, a generated table sorted by offset (binary search, `runtime/src/dispatch.c`). An unknown target aborts with the address.
- **Imports** need nothing special in the translator. PLT stubs are ordinary functions ending in `br x17` through the GOT. The runtime's loader will fill each GOT slot with an address `yw4_resolve` maps to the native implementation (Phase 3).
- **Image base** must be 4 KiB aligned, because `adrp` results are computed at translation time as page offsets.
- **Untranslated instructions** compile to `yw4_unimplemented(ctx, pc, enc)`, which aborts with the address. Today that is 11% of `main`, almost all SIMD/FP.

Output goes to `work/recomp/` (`python -m recomp.translate`): 81 files of 500 functions each, plus `funcs.h` and `func_table.c`. All of it compiles warning-free with GCC 13 and with Clang 23 (`-O1 -Wall`) and links.

## Testing

`python -m recomp.functest`: our own test functions (`tests/functest/`: loops, recursion, mutual recursion, indirect calls, tail calls, stack arguments, rodata via ADRP, structs, and two jump tables written by hand in Clang's shape) are compiled on the Pi as ARMv8.0 without SIMD and linked into a flat image like `main`. The Pi runs them natively; the same image is translated, compiled on the host, and run on the same inputs. Return values and every changed byte of the scratch buffer must match. All 17 match. Planted translator bugs (inverted CBZ, wrong TBZ bit, wrong B.cond condition, ADRP off by a page, wrong jump-table targets, jump tables not recognised) are all caught.

## Open risks

- **`ret` ignores x30.** Correct for normal code. It's wrong for code that returns somewhere other than its caller. `main` imports **`setjmp`/`longjmp`** (Lua 5.2's error handling uses them), so this is real. Plan: the translator treats a call to the `setjmp` import specially, using host `setjmp` inside the calling C function so that the HLE `longjmp` can return there. Must be solved before Lua runs.
- **C++ exceptions.** `__cxa_begin_catch`, `_Unwind_Resume` and `__gxx_personality_v0` are imported, but `__cxa_throw` is not, so `main` may never throw. Check before relying on that.
- **False entry points** (e.g. Ghidra-only entries that are really labels) turn a `goto` into a tail call. That's still correct, but slower, and without `musttail` it uses host stack.
- **12 unrecognised jump tables** trap at run time if reached. Fix them when the trap fires, or improve the matcher.

## Why

- **Flow-following instead of trusting boundaries:** a wrong boundary silently drops code. Following flow can only add code, and every path still ends at a defined exit.
- **Switch on the address, with a trapping default:** an imperfect jump-table matcher can only make the result slower or louder, never wrong.
- **Testing on real compiled code:** single-instruction tests can't check branches, calls, the stack or jump tables. Compiling real C on the Pi gives those cases for free and checks the whole chain (discovery, labels, calls, dispatch).

```

`docs/decisions/0008-floating-point-semantics.md`:

```md
# 0008 — Floating-point and SIMD semantics

<!-- decision
state: accepted
date: 2026-10-21
replaces: none
code: runtime/include/yw4fp.h
-->

Date: 2026-10-20
Status: accepted (FPCR = 0 verified 2026-10-21)

## Decision

**FP mode.** Generated code implements ARM floating point with FPCR = 0: round to nearest even, no flush-to-zero, no default-NaN mode.

**Verified (2026-10-21) that every game thread runs with FPCR = 0:**
- **`main`** contains no `MRS`/`MSR` of any system register (its only system instructions are 1,189 `clrex`, 505 `nop`, 16 `dmb`). It does import `fegetenv`, `fesetenv` and `fesetround`, but calls them from exactly two tiny functions:
  - `0x10048c0`: `fegetenv(saved)`, then `fesetenv(FE_DFL_ENV)` and `fesetround(0)`;
  - `0x10048e0`: `fesetenv(saved)`.

  That is a save / set-default / restore guard (typical of physics code), so the only mode the game itself sets is the default.
- **`sdk`** writes FPCR in three places:
  - `nn::os::detail::UserExceptionHandler` saves and restores FPCR around a callback;
  - `__fesetround` (reached only from `fesetround`);
  - `fesetenv`, which writes FPCR = 0 for `FE_DFL_ENV` (reached from `main`'s guard and from `feupdateenv`).

  The only internal callers of `fesetround` are in `fmal`, which saves the rounding mode, uses nearest, and restores it. `rtld` never touches FPCR.
- **Kernel** (Atmosphère's reimplementation, read as a reference: `KThreadContext::Initialize` and `svc::CreateThread`): a thread's context starts with FPCR = 0. `CreateThread` then copies the *creating* thread's FPCR into the new thread. So the first thread starts at 0, and since nothing above leaves FPCR non-zero, every later thread inherits 0 as well.

**For the runtime (Phase 3):** `fegetenv`/`fesetenv`/`fesetround` can be implemented as storing and returning the environment value. If one is ever called with a non-default mode, it must trap loudly, because generated code only implements FPCR = 0.

**FPSR** (cumulative exception flags) is not modelled. `main` never reads it.

**Arithmetic** goes through helpers in `runtime/include/yw4fp.h` that take and return raw bit patterns:
- For non-NaN inputs and results, x86-64 SSE rounds exactly like ARM, so the helpers use the plain C operation.
- **NaNs differ.** ARM returns the first signalling NaN (quietened), else the first quiet NaN, else the positive default NaN. x86 returns a *negative* NaN for invalid operations, and picks NaN operands by instruction-operand order, which the compiler may swap. So every helper handles NaN inputs first and replaces a NaN result with ARM's default NaN.
- ARM-specific rules are written out: `max(+0, -0) = +0`, `FMAXNM` ignoring one quiet NaN, saturating float→integer conversion with NaN → 0, `FCMP` flags, and NaN payloads in `FCVT`.
- `FRECPS`/`FRSQRTS` are fused (one rounding). Single precision computes in double. A float × float product is exact in double, but adding 2 or 3 to it is not, and rounding that sum first to double and then to float can go wrong. The Pi tests found such a case: the 3 is far below the product's last bit, the double sum drops it, and the float rounding becomes a false tie. The first version assumed the usual double-rounding argument covers this; it doesn't, because the product has 48 bits, not 24. The fix rounds the double sum *to odd* (TwoSum gives the exact error, and a nonzero error forces the last bit to 1), which makes the final rounding to float exact. Double precision uses FMA.
- Fixed-point `SCVTF`/`UCVTF` (4 uses) divide by 2^fbits after converting; this is exact except for results in the subnormal range.
- `FRECPE`/`FRSQRTE` implement the Arm ARM estimate tables bit for bit.

**No libm.** The Pi tests found that MinGW's math library is not exact:
- double `sqrt` and `fma` are off by one unit in the last place on hard inputs;
- `round(0.49999997) = 1`.

The helpers therefore use the CPU instructions instead: SSE2 `sqrtsd`/`sqrtss`, FMA3 `vfmadd`, and hand-written exact rounding. Consequences:
- **Hosts need FMA3** (every x86-64 CPU since 2013: Intel Haswell, AMD Piledriver), but only for double-precision `FRECPS`/`FRSQRTS`. Recheck if older CPUs ever matter.
- **Generated code must be built with `-ffp-contract=off`** and without `-ffast-math`, so the compiler doesn't fuse or reorder float operations itself.

**Vectors** are emitted as loops over lanes of a local copy (sources may alias the destination), using the same scalar helpers. Q=0 forms zero the upper 64 bits.

**Not implemented** (they would trap): `FMLA`/`FMLS` (unused in `main`) and half-precision arithmetic (ARMv8.2, not on the A57). Every SIMD/FP instruction in `main` is implemented.

## Testing

Golden tests as in 0006. On top of that, the vector registers get float edge cases (signed zeros, infinities, quiet/signalling NaNs with payloads, denormals, conversion limits, rounding ties) and *pair states* (e.g. +inf/−inf, two different NaNs, products near 2 and 3 for the reciprocal steps).

Every helper was checked by planting bugs: 23 planted FP/SIMD bugs are all caught, plus the missing round-to-odd (with curated operand pairs for exactly that case). One planted change was not caught, and it is provably equivalent: the `<`/`<=` in the reciprocal-sqrt table loop can't differ for any reachable input.

Golden files store registers an instruction can't read as `*`: a deterministic filler, `recomp.check.filler`. Output lines store only the registers that changed. This keeps 42 forms at 9 MB.

## Why

- **Bit patterns instead of `float` parameters:** NaN payloads and signs can't be lost or normalised by the compiler or the calling convention.
- **The ARM rules are written out instead of trusting the host:** ARM and x86 really do differ on NaNs, and only ARM's results are correct for this game. Writing the rules out costs one predictable branch per operation (NaN inputs are rare).
- **No libm:** "correctly rounded" isn't guaranteed by C for `sqrt`/`fma`/`round` in practice, and the tests proved it. CPU instructions are exact by definition.

```

`docs/decisions/0009-atomics.md`:

```md
# 0009 — Atomics: exclusives, acquire/release

<!-- decision
state: accepted
date: 2026-10-21
replaces: none
code: tests/functest/atomics.S, tests/test_kernel.py
-->

Date: 2026-10-20
Status: accepted

## What main uses (measured)

| Instruction | Count |
|---|---|
| `ldarb` / `ldar` (32-bit) | 7,177 / 1,119 |
| `stlr` (32-bit) / `stlrb` | 373 / 83 |
| `ldaxr` + `stlxr` (32-bit) | 2,581 + 2,580 |
| byte exclusives (`ldaxrb`/`stlxrb`/`stxrb`) | 90 |
| 64-bit exclusives (`ldxr`/`stxr`) | 10 |
| `clrex` | 1,189 |
| `dmb` | 16 |

There are no exclusive pairs (`ldxp`/`stxp`) and no ARMv8.1 atomics (the A57 has none).

## Decision

Guest threads will be host threads on shared memory (decision 0005), so these become real host atomics (`__atomic` builtins on the guest address):

- **`ldxr`/`ldaxr`** do an atomic load (relaxed / acquire) and record a reservation in `CPUState`: address, size, and the value seen.
- **`stxr`/`stlxr`** succeed only if there is a reservation for the same address and size *and* a host compare-and-swap from the recorded value to the new one succeeds. Status 0 = stored, 1 = failed. The reservation is always cleared, as on hardware.
- **`clrex`** clears the reservation.
- **`ldar`** is an acquire load.
- **`stlr` is a sequentially consistent store, not just a release.** On ARM, `stlr` followed by `ldar` can't be reordered (RCsc). On x86 a release store followed by an acquire load can be reordered (store buffering); a seq_cst store (`xchg`) prevents it.
- **`dmb`** becomes a full fence.

## Known difference: ABA

A hardware exclusive store fails if *any* write hit the location since the `ldxr`. The CAS only checks that the value is the same, so it succeeds if another thread changed the value and changed it back. This doesn't matter for the loops compilers emit for counters, flags, locks and plain compare-and-swap: they only care about the value. It would matter for hand-written lock-free stacks that rely on LL/SC to avoid ABA. If such code turns up, the fix is a per-address version counter in a side table.

## Testing

- Single instructions (golden tests): `ldxr`/`ldaxr` (value loaded) and `ldar`/`stlr`, with naturally aligned addresses: ARMv8.0 faults on unaligned exclusive/acquire/release accesses.
- A lone `stxr` is not golden-tested, because its result after the harness's own code is IMPLEMENTATION DEFINED.
- Whole loops (`tests/functest/atomics.S`): atomic add, compare-and-swap with `clrex` on the failure path, `stxr` without a reservation, byte and 64-bit exclusives, and acquire/release. All match the Pi. Planted bugs ("store ignores the reservation", "clrex does nothing") are caught.
- Between threads (2026-10-21, decision 0015): `tests/test_kernel.py` runs 8 host threads × 100,000 increments through the recompiler's own `ldaxr`/`stlxr` output; all 800,000 land. With `stlxr` planted as a plain store, 167,482 did.

```

`docs/decisions/0010-loader-and-import-stubs.md`:

```md
# 0010 — Loader and import stubs (Phase 3 skeleton)

<!-- decision
state: accepted
date: 2026-10-21
replaces: none
code: recomp/translate.py, recomp/build.py, runtime/src/sha256.c, runtime/src/hle.c
-->

Date: 2026-10-21
Status: accepted

## Decision

`python -m recomp.translate` also writes `work/recomp/image_info.c`: the tables the loader needs, all generated by the tested Python readers in `tools/yw4/`. `python -m recomp.build` compiles everything into `work/build/yw4.exe`, which takes the path to `main.bin` on the command line.

**Image bytes are never built in.** The executable reads `work/exefs/main.bin` at start-up and refuses it unless both the size and the SHA-256 match the build it was recompiled from. That is the version lock again (CLAUDE.md rule 3), enforced by the runtime itself (`runtime/src/sha256.c`, tested against `hashlib`).

**Memory.** One block holds the image and its `.bss`: 0x6AE9000 bytes, about 112 MB, 90 MB of it `.bss`. It is placed at **`0x7100000000`, main's address on the Switch**, and falls back to anywhere if that range is taken. Guest stacks go to `0x7000000000`. Reasons:
- Everything stays inside the 39-bit address space a Switch game may assume (CLAUDE.md, Phase 1 note). The first run without this put the stack at `0x288…` (41 bits).
- Logged addresses equal Ghidra's addresses, which makes debugging easier.

**Relocations** (measured in `main`):

| Type | Count | Applied as |
|---|---|---|
| RELATIVE | 56,775 | image base + addend |
| ABS64 | 4,253 | import address + addend |
| JUMP_SLOT | 551 | import address |
| GLOB_DAT | 19 | import address |

**Imports** (578, all referenced):
- **554 functions.** Each gets a unique address in a stub region. `yw4_resolve` maps that address, through a lookup hook, to a generated `imp_<i>`, which calls `yw4_import_call(ctx, i)`. That runs a native implementation found by mangled name, or stops with the import's name and the guest address of the call. Function pointers to imports (e.g. in vtables) work the same way, because every indirect call goes through `yw4_resolve`.
- **20 data objects** (C++ type-info vtables, the fundamental type infos, `stdin`/`stdout`/`stderr`). Each gets a zeroed 4 KiB block until their implementations fill them.
- **4 weak symbols that nobody exports** (`__rel_dyn_start` and similar linker markers) resolve to 0.

**Start-up order**, as in the Nintendo SDK:
1. `nninitStartup`: the game's memory set-up hook, called before static constructors;
2. `DT_INIT` (`main+0x30`), which calls `__nnmusl_init_dso` and then runs the 830 `.init_array` constructors;
3. `nnMain`.

## Result (2026-10-21)

```
yw4: main loaded at 0000007100000000 (its Switch address), 61598 relocations, 578 imports (20 data)
yw4: running nninitStartup (main+0x94eb50)
yw4: unimplemented import #157 _ZN2nn2os15QueryMemoryInfoEPNS0_10MemoryInfoE
     called from main+0x94eb6c with x0=0x70007fff98 x1=0 x2=0
```

Recompiled code runs natively until its first `sdk` call. That call sits exactly where the disassembly says it does.

The imports each stage calls directly (static scan):
- `nninitStartup`: `nn::os::QueryMemoryInfo`, `SetMemoryHeapSize`, `AllocateMemoryBlock`, plus `nn::diag` logging/asserts;
- `DT_INIT`: `__nnmusl_init_dso`;
- `nnMain`: `GetHostArgc`/`GetHostArgv`, `GetSystemTick`, `__cxa_guard_acquire`/`release`, `SleepThread`.

## Open

- Implementations go in `runtime/src/hle.c`'s table for now; split by `nn::` namespace once there are more than a handful.
- The 20 data imports need real contents before RTTI, `dynamic_cast` or stdio are used.
- Guest stack size is a fixed 8 MB; take it from the NPDM later.
- Threads: one guest thread only (`nn::os::CreateThread` will need per-thread `CPUState` and stacks, plus TLS).
- Build speed: a full Clang `-O1` build of the 88 files takes about 4 minutes. A change to a runtime header recompiles everything, because generated code includes `yw4rt.h`.

```

`docs/decisions/0011-first-hle-memory-and-diag.md`:

```md
# 0011 — First HLE: memory start-up, diag logging, StandardAllocator

<!-- decision
state: accepted
date: 2026-10-21
replaces: none
code: runtime/src/hle.h, runtime/src/hle.c, runtime/src/hle_os.c, runtime/src/hle_diag.c, runtime/src/hle_mem.c, runtime/src/heap.c
-->

Date: 2026-10-21
Status: accepted

## What nninitStartup does (read from the disassembly, main+0x94eb50)

1. `nn::os::QueryMemoryInfo`, then heap = (available − used) rounded down to 2 MiB.
2. Asserts heap > **0xB9C00000** (~2.9 GiB): the size the game wants for malloc.
3. Logs `Remain Memory Size %lluMiB (%llubyte)` (heap − malloc size, rounded to 2 MiB).
4. `SetMemoryHeapSize(heap)`, `AllocateMemoryBlock(0xB9C00000)`, and hands that block to an `nn::mem::StandardAllocator` (main+0xc5a8d0: constructor + `Initialize(addr, size, false)`).
5. `AllocateMemoryBlock(remainder)`, kept at main+0x5864cb0 for later.

`malloc` is not an import: the game defines its own on top of that StandardAllocator. So the allocator below is the game's whole C/C++ heap.

## Decisions

**Files.** `runtime/src/hle.h` (private to the runtime, so editing it doesn't rebuild the 88 generated files; `recomp/build.py` now tracks `runtime/src/*.h` for runtime objects only), `hle_os.c`, `hle_diag.c`, `hle_mem.c`, `heap.c`. `hle.c` keeps the name → function table.

**Memory numbers.** `QueryMemoryInfo` reports what a retail 4 GiB Switch gives an application: 0xCD500000 bytes available (the application pool of the 4 GiB memory arrangement; from the kernel's table, not measured on hardware). Used = main's image + bss + the 8 MiB main stack. The game then logs 198 MiB remaining. If the real value ever matters, it can be checked on the owner's console.

**Heap address.** The heap is reserved at `0x7200000000`, just above main, inside the 39-bit space. `AllocateMemoryBlock` hands out blocks bottom-up. `FreeMemoryBlock` isn't imported, so nothing more is needed. Only one `SetMemoryHeapSize` call is supported; a second, different size stops with a message.

**Host memory.** The whole ~3.2 GB heap is committed up front (`yw4_reserve`). On Windows that counts against the commit limit (RAM + page file) but uses no RAM until touched; Linux overcommits anyway. If this becomes a problem, reserve the heap and commit per block.

**StandardAllocator = TLSF over the game's own region** (`heap.c`). Reasons:
- Returned pointers must lie inside the block the game passed in: they stay within the 39-bit space, and `GetTotalFreeSize`/`GetAllocatableSize` mean the same as on the Switch. Host `malloc` gives neither.
- TLSF is O(1) for allocate/free, merges neighbours immediately (low fragmentation in a long session), and handles alignment. It is ~250 lines of plain C, so no new dependency.
- Block headers live in the guest region (16 bytes, payloads 16-aligned like AArch64 malloc). Only the free-list index lives in host memory. The guest object keeps a pointer to it in its first 8 bytes.
- `Free`/`Reallocate` check that the pointer is a live block (header + both neighbours agree). A double free or a stray pointer stops the program instead of corrupting the heap.
- Not thread-safe yet; a lock comes with threads.
- Unverified sdk behaviour is not guessed: `Reallocate(p, 0)` stops.

Tested in `tests/test_runtime.py` (300,000 random allocate/aligned allocate/free/realloc operations). Checked: alignment, no overlaps, contents preserved, double free/stray pointers refused, everything merges back into one block, and the largest free block can be allocated whole. Two injected bugs (no backward merge; no minimum gap for aligned allocations) both fail the test.

**diag.** `LogImpl` is variadic. Guest varargs can't go to the host `vprintf`, so `yw4_guest_format` reads each argument where AAPCS64 puts it: x-registers then stack for integers, v-registers then stack for doubles. It formats one conversion at a time with `snprintf`. `%Lf` (128-bit long double) is refused. Log lines are printed as `[game <function>] <message>`. `OnAssertionFailure` and `AbortImpl` stop with whatever strings the release build kept, plus the call address. `nndetailDiagAbortFormatImpl` is a C symbol with no signature, so it prints raw registers instead of guessing.

## Result

```
yw4: running nninitStartup (main+0x94eb50)
[game Startup] Remain Memory Size 198MiB (207618048byte)
yw4: nninitStartup returned, x0=0
yw4: running DT_INIT (static constructors) (main+0x30)
yw4: unimplemented import #1 __nnmusl_init_dso
```

## Next

`__nnmusl_init_dso` gets 18 pointers (x0 = image base, 7 more in registers, 10 on the stack). They look like the module's section bounds for musl's TLS and unwinder registration. If it returns 1, DT_INIT skips the constructors. Implementing it means deciding on TLS and C++ exception unwinding first.

# 0012 — musl start-up, TLS, C++ exceptions, first C library functions

<!-- decision
state: accepted
date: 2026-10-21
replaces: none
code: runtime/src/hle_string.c
-->

Date: 2026-10-21
Status: accepted (except the open question at the end)

## `__nnmusl_init_dso`: return "run the constructors", nothing else

main's DT_INIT (main+0x30) calls `__nnmusl_init_dso` with main's base and section bounds: dynamic section, relocation tables, hash table, GOT, init/fini arrays, and what look like TLS bounds (0x150d650/0x150d651, base+1). It saves the result in a flag (main+0x150e0d0):
- result **1**: skip the constructors. On the next DT_INIT call the flag is non-zero and DT_INIT jumps straight to the constructor loop. So 1 means "not now".
- any other result: run the 830 `.init_array` constructors now.

The sdk's own version (read in the owner's `sdk.bin`, ~775 instructions) returns only 1 or 2. Its real work is registering the module and giving it a TLS block in the calling thread (`nnosAllocateMemoryForThreadLocal` + `memset`). A search of all of `sdk` for an init-array call loop found only the sdk's own `_init`, so nothing else ever runs main's constructors.

**Decision:** return 2 after checking that the base is main's. `__nnmusl_fini_dso` does nothing (main's `.fini_array` is empty).

## TLS: main has none to set up

main contains no `MRS` at all (decision 0008), so it never reads the thread pointer and can't reach a TLS block. Its per-thread values go through `nn::os` TLS slots (`AllocateTlsSlot`, `GetTlsValue`, `SetTlsValue`...), which are ordinary imports. They come with threads.

## C++ exceptions: not supported, because nothing throws

`main` neither imports nor defines `__cxa_throw`, `__cxa_allocate_exception` or `__cxa_rethrow`. It imports `_Unwind_Resume`, `__cxa_begin_catch` and `__gxx_personality_v0` (landing pads compiled into the code), but those run only while an exception unwinds, and none can start. They stay unimplemented: if one is ever reached, the import stub stops with its name. No unwinder is needed.

## `__cxa_guard_acquire` / `__cxa_guard_release`

Function-local statics. The game's inline fast path is `ldarb` + `tbz #0` on the guard's first byte (main+0x5c64), the Itanium C++ ABI layout. So byte 0 bit 0 = initialized (stored with release order), and byte 1 = initialization in progress (a second acquire then stops as recursion). With threads, acquire must instead wait for the other thread.

## C library: only what is exact

The host computes a libc function only if its result is fully defined by the inputs: memory and string functions, character classes, integer parsing (`hle_string.c`, 37 functions). Where C leaves the value open, musl's choice is reproduced:
- `memcmp`/`strcmp`/`strncmp`/`strcasecmp` return the difference of the first differing bytes (as unsigned chars), not just −1/0/1. Game code may store the value.
- Character classes are musl's "C" locale: ASCII only, nothing above 127.
- Guest `long` is 64-bit and the Windows host's is 32-bit, so `strtol`/`strtoul` go through `strtoll`/`strtoull`.
- `errno` is one guest-visible int for now (per thread later).

## Open: functions whose results depend on the implementation

`sin`/`cos`/`pow`/`exp`/... (28 math imports), `qsort` (the order of equal elements depends on the algorithm; musl uses smoothsort), the `printf` family's float output, `strtod`, `strerror` text. The host's versions can differ from musl's (decision 0008 found MinGW's libm off by one unit in the last place). Matching the Switch exactly means using musl's own source for these. musl is MIT-licensed, so it's compatible, but it's a new third-party dependency (CLAUDE.md rule 6). **Not decided yet**; until then these imports stay unimplemented and stop the program when reached.

## Result

```
yw4: running DT_INIT (static constructors) (main+0x30)
yw4: unimplemented import #94 _ZN2nn7account12AsyncContextC1Ev
     called from main+0x3a9a8
```

`docs/decisions/0013-libm-from-musl-checked-against-the-sdk.md`:

```md
# 0013 — libm from musl 1.1.19, checked against the sdk's own code

<!-- decision
state: accepted
date: 2026-10-21
replaces: none
code: runtime/src/hle_math.c, third_party/musl, tools/yw4/sdkref.py, tools/yw4/pi/sdkrun.c
-->

Date: 2026-10-21
Status: accepted (owner chose "use musl's source" over the host's libm)

## Problem

main imports 40 math functions (`sin`, `pow`, `expf`...). Their last bit depends on the implementation, and the host's libm is not the Switch's (decision 0008 found MinGW's off by one unit in the last place). Different last bits can make physics or battle results drift from the real game.

## Decision

1. **The reference is the sdk itself.** `python -m tools.yw4.sdkref` copies the owner's `sdk.bin` to the ARM64 reference machine (decision 0004), applies its relocations there and calls each function directly (`tools/yw4/pi/sdkrun.c`). That is Nintendo's compiled code running on a real ARM CPU with FPCR = 0, as on the Switch. 20,000 inputs per function: half random (edge values, random bit patterns), half where each function is hard (trig near multiples of π/4 and at huge arguments, exp near overflow, log near 1, integer/half-integer powers). Results go to `work/sdkref/` (derived from the sdk, so not committed). The sdk is now version-locked too: `[sdk]` in `target.toml`.
2. **The runtime uses musl 1.1.19's C** (`third_party/musl`, MIT). Measured, not guessed: 1.2.5 matches 29/40 functions, 1.1.24 31/40, 1.1.19 39/40. The sdk's math contains no fused multiply-add instructions, so compiling the C with `-ffp-contract=off` on x86 can reproduce it exactly.
3. **One patch:** `acosf` returns correctly rounded π/2 and π on two paths (the sdk has them as constants). All `acosf` mismatches were these two values.
4. **`ceil`/`floor`/`sqrt`/`fabs`** (and `f` versions) are single instructions in musl's aarch64 build, so they use the recompiler's exact instruction models (`yw4fp.h`). That covers musl's internal calls to `sqrt`/`floor` too. musl's portable C differs on signalling NaNs (it returns them unquieted).
5. **NaN results are made ARM's** after each call. Measured on the reference data: where musl returns a NaN argument without arithmetic, both machines agree, because it's the same C. They differ only where decision 0008 says: a NaN made from non-NaN inputs (x86's default NaN is negative, ARM's is `0x7ff8...`), and two NaN arguments (ARM prefers the signalling one). `hle_math.c` fixes exactly those two cases.

`python -m tools.yw4.sdkref --check` compiles the runtime's real `hle_math.c` + musl with the build's flags and drives it through a `CPUState`, as the game calls it. **Result: 40 of 40 functions match the sdk bit for bit on all 800,000 inputs.** Planted bugs are caught: undoing the `acosf` patch (1,150 mismatches) and turning off the NaN fix (thousands in `log`, `pow`).

## Why not the alternatives

- **Host libm:** not exact (decision 0008), and its errors can't be fixed afterwards.
- **Recompiling the sdk's math functions like main:** exact by construction, but it reverses decision 0005 (recompile only main) for a small set of functions. musl's C plus a bit-exact check gives the same result with readable code.
- **musl 1.2.x, the current release:** measured to differ from the Switch.

## Still open (same approach later)

`qsort` (smoothsort, order of equal elements), the `printf` family's float output, `strtod`, `strerror` text. The reference tool needs a way to pass buffers and callbacks for these.

# 0014 — Recompile the sdk too; native code at the kernel and service level

<!-- decision
state: accepted
date: 2026-10-21
replaces: 0005 (part), 0010 (part)
code: runtime/src/kernel.c, runtime/src/ipc.c, runtime/src/romfs.c, runtime/src/crypto.c, recomp/function.py, tools/yw4/sdkref.py
-->

Date: 2026-10-21
Status: accepted (owner, 2026-10-21). Replaces the "recompile only main, implement the 578 sdk imports natively" part of decision 0005. 0005's graphics plan (NVN at the API level on Vulkan) stands.

## Why change

Implementing sdk functions natively means proving each one matches the Switch. Decision 0013 did that for libm and needed an old musl version, a patch and an ARM NaN rule. Doing it ~480 more times (`nn::account`, `nn::fs`, `nn::os` threads, sockets, `printf`, `qsort`...) is most of the remaining work, and every one is a chance to differ from the real game.

Measured 2026-10-21 by translating the owner's `sdk.bin` with the current recompiler, in memory:
- 33,616 functions found (96% of `.text`); **33,366 (99.3%) translate completely already**.
- 2,245 instructions out of 1.3 M are missing: AES/SHA/PMULL crypto (~1,400, `nn::crypto`), SIMD integer (~600: `addv`, `smlal`, `sqadd`, `sqrshrn`... in audio DSP and string code), CRC32 (14), cache maintenance, `MRS`/`MSR` of the thread pointers, counters and FPCR/FPSR.
- 60 different `SVC` numbers: the sdk's whole interface to the kernel.

LAS Recomp (github.com/peiikai/LASRecomp, MIT), a working static recompilation of Link's Awakening for Switch, uses this model: main + sdk recompiled, a small Horizon kernel and the system services implemented natively, NVN and a few functions overridden by symbol.

## Decision

- **Recompile `main` and `sdk`.** `rtld` is not needed: the loader does its job (load, relocate, resolve symbols between the two modules).
- **Native code sits at the kernel boundary:** `SVC` calls (memory, threads, synchronisation, handles, IPC), the thread-local region (`TPIDRRO_EL0`), and the system services the game opens through IPC (`fs`, `hid`, `acc`, `time`, `audio`, `vi`...). Like unimplemented imports today, an unimplemented SVC or service command stops with its name and caller.
- **Overrides by symbol stay possible**, for NVN (graphics, decision 0005) and for any function where native code is clearly better. Each override is listed and justified.
- **Start-up as LAS Recomp does it:** call the sdk's `nn::init::Start(thread handle, argument region, init, fini)` on the main guest thread. It calls back to run the sdk's DT_INIT after `nnosInitialize` and main's DT_INIT after `nninitStartup`, then `nnMain`.
- **Memory:** main stays at `0x7100000000`; sdk follows it; everything stays inside the 39-bit space.

## What happens to the native sdk functions written so far

They become unnecessary once the recompiled sdk runs: heap (0011), diag, string and libc (0012), libm (0013). They stay in the tree until the recompiled sdk passes the same tests: `tools/yw4/sdkref.py --check` then checks the *recompiled* sdk functions against the sdk running on the Pi. After that they are removed, `third_party/musl` included, unless one is kept deliberately as an override.

## Plan

1. **Recompiler:** the missing instruction groups, each with Pi golden tests like the existing 51 forms; `SVC` and `MRS`/`MSR` become calls into the runtime.
2. **Translate both modules:** per-module function names and one address-sorted dispatch table.
3. **Loader:** load main + sdk, relocate both, resolve imports in both directions.
4. **Kernel, minimal:** the main thread, its thread-local region, memory SVCs, `GetInfo`. Grow it as the start-up path reaches more.
5. **Services** as the game opens them.

Each step lands as its own commit, with the README progress log updated.

## Progress

- **Step 1 done (2026-10-21).** New and extended forms, all checked against the Pi: CRC32/CRC32C (`dp2`); `sqadd`, `sqsub`, `smax`, `mla`, `mul` (three same); `cnt`, `neg`, `rev16`, `rev32`, `shll`, `fcvtl`, `fcvtn`, `frintm` (two-register misc); `smlal`, `uaddw`, `pmull` incl. 64-bit (three different); `shrn`, `sqshrn`, fixed-point `fcvtzs` (shift by immediate); `fmla`, `mul`, `smlal` by element; new forms `simd_across` (`addv`, `smaxv`, `uaddlv`), `simd_scalar_addp`, `simd_scalar_shift_imm`, `crypto_aes`, `crypto_sha3`, `crypto_sha2`, `fp_dp3` (`fmadd` family). 13 forms, 120,000 cases, all match. Planted bugs caught: double-rounded single-precision FMA, AES row shift reversed, wrong CRC32C polynomial.
  - Fused multiply-add (`f32_muladd`/`f64_muladd` in `yw4fp.h`), which decision 0008 skipped because main had none: the Arm ARM's `FPMulAdd` NaN order, single precision via the existing round-to-odd add.
  - AES/SHA in `runtime/src/crypto.c`, written from the pseudocode; the AES S-box is computed, not typed.
  - System instructions (`function.py`): `MRS` of `TPIDRRO_EL0`, `TPIDR_EL0`, `CNTPCT_EL0` (19.2 MHz), `CTR_EL0` (the A57's value), `FPCR`, `FPSR`; `MSR` of `TPIDR_EL0`, `FPCR` (non-zero stops, 0008), `FPSR`; `DC CVAU/CVAC/CIVAC` and `IC IVAU` are no-ops; `SVC` calls `yw4_svc` (`runtime/src/kernel.c`, which stops on every call for now).
  - Result: every instruction the sdk's 33,616 functions reach translates, except one word that is not an instruction (data between functions; it traps if executed). main: still 0 traps, same run as before.
- **Steps 2 and 3 done (2026-10-21).**
  - `recomp.translate` translates both modules (main `f_<off>` with base `yw4_image_base`, sdk `s_<off>` with base `yw4_sdk_base`): 40,228 + 33,616 functions. One function table per module (`yw4_code[]`); `yw4_resolve` finds the module containing an address, so calls between modules (through the PLT, `BR x17`) just work.
  - Symbols are resolved at translation time, in load order (main, then sdk), as rtld does: main's 574 imports go to the sdk, the sdk's 8 imports to main, and the 9 symbols both define resolve to main's copy inside the sdk too. 5 weak symbols nobody defines (linker markers, `nnosGetDefaultUserExceptionStackForApplication`) are 0. The import stubs of decision 0010 are gone.
  - Memory: main at `0x7100000000`, sdk right after it at `0x7106c00000` (2 MiB aligned), main thread stack and priority from the NPDM (1 MiB, 44), thread-local region at `0x7040000000`, host callbacks at `0x7080000000`.
  - Start-up: `nn::init::Start(0x101, 0, run sdk DT_INIT, run main DT_INIT)` on the main thread. The thread handle is a placeholder until the kernel owns handles.
  - Result: Nintendo's start-up code runs natively until its first system call, `SVC 0x29` (`GetInfo`, info type 11: random entropy). Next: step 4, the kernel.
- **Step 4 started (2026-10-21), `runtime/src/kernel.c`.** Implemented as reached, with LAS Recomp's kernel as the reference for argument layouts and result codes:
  - Address space (`yw4load.h`): stacks `0x7000000000` (1 GiB), thread-local regions `0x7040000000`, host callbacks `0x7080000000`, modules `0x7100000000`, heap `0x7200000000` (6 GiB reserved, committed as `SetHeapSize` grows it, decommitted when it shrinks), alias `0x7400000000` (4 GiB); ASLR region `0x7000000000`-`0x7800000000`.
  - `GetInfo` (core/priority masks, all regions, total memory 0xCD500000 as on a 4 GiB Switch, used memory, program ID, random entropy: fixed for now so runs are reproducible), `SetHeapSize`, `QueryMemory` (a sorted region list: modules, main stack, thread-local region, heap), thread properties (`Get/SetThreadPriority`, `Get/SetThreadCoreMask`, `GetCurrentProcessorNumber`, `GetThreadId`), `SleepThread`, `GetSystemTick`.
  - Mutexes and condition variables (`ArbitrateLock/Unlock`, `WaitProcessWideKeyAtomic`, `SignalProcessWideKey`) with single-thread semantics: nobody to wake, so the words go back to 0; a wait that could only end through another thread stops with a message. Real blocking comes with `CreateThread`.
  - Handles: a table from `0x101`; the main thread is the first; pseudo-handle `0xFFFF8000` = current thread.
  - Build: generated code now depends only on the headers it includes (`yw4rt.h`, `yw4cpu.h`, `yw4fp.h`; `yw4load.h` for `image_info.c`), so kernel and loader changes rebuild in about a second.
  - Result: 50 system calls later, start-up calls `ConnectToNamedPort("sm:")`, the service manager: step 5 (IPC) starts there. `YW4_TRACE_SVC=1` prints every call.
- **Step 5 started (2026-10-21).** `runtime/src/ipc.c`: the HIPC/CMIF message codec (Switchbrew "IPC_Marshalling"; LAS Recomp's `ipc.c` as the cross-check), sessions as kernel objects, domains, control messages (convert to domain, clone, pointer buffer size). Services are an explicit table in `ipc.c`; handlers in `svc_*.c`. Commands with no logic are table entries (`ipc_simple.h`: succeed / return a constant / return an event nothing signals), each named after Switchbrew.
  - Unknown services and commands stop with their name and number. `YW4_IPC_STUB=1` answers them with "success, zeroed output" and logs them, for surveying; it fails as soon as a stubbed command should have returned an interface. `YW4_TRACE_IPC=1` prints every request.
  - So far: `sm:`, `appletOE` (`IApplicationProxy`; `ICommonStateGetter` with the system message queue, `ISelfController`, `IWindowController`, `IApplicationFunctions`), `apm`, `lm` (prints the game's log text), `aoc:u` (no add-on content), `pctl` and its variants (no restrictions).
  - Kernel additions: events (`CreateEvent`, `Signal/Clear/ResetSignal`, single-thread `WaitSynchronization`), `CloseHandle`, `SendSyncRequest(WithUserBuffer)`, `svcBreak` (prints the result code and a guest backtrace from the frame-pointer chain), `OutputDebugString`.
  - Found on the way: the sdk finds modules through `QueryMemory` (`nn::ro::detail::GetExceptionInfo`, used when logging), so each module is now three regions as Horizon maps an NSO: `.text` code R-X, `.rodata` code R--, `.data`+`.bss` mutable code RW-. One big region made the sdk abort.
  - Result: the sdk's start-up and the game's `nninitStartup` run on Nintendo's recompiled code (the native heap of decision 0011 is no longer involved); `main`'s constructors have started and open `time:u`.
  - `time:u`: clock interfaces and the shared clock page (steady clock from runtime start, system clocks from the host's time). Needed kernel shared memory (`MapSharedMemory`). On Windows, reservations start only at 64 KiB boundaries while the game maps at 4 KiB ones, so the kernel reserves every free part of the guest window at start-up and mappings become commits; the heap's range is reserved first.
  - `fsp-srv`: the game reads its data as one raw RomFS image. `runtime/src/romfs.c` builds that image's tables from the owner's extracted folder at start-up (4,518 files, 3,322 directories, 8.5 GiB, well under a second) and serves file-data reads from the original files: no copy. Same layout and name hash as LAS Recomp's `romfs_build.c` (MIT), which copies the data instead. Tested (`tests/test_runtime.py`): an independent Python reader finds every file of a test folder through the hash tables; a wrong hash constant is caught. The runtime now takes the RomFS folder as its second argument.
  - `MapMemory`/`UnmapMemory` by copying (the source is inaccessible while mapped, so a copy is equivalent): the game uses it for its first thread's stack.
  - Result: the constructors get to `SVC 0x8 CreateThread`. Next: real threads.
  - Threads (decision 0015): one host thread per guest thread, one kernel lock, blocking synchronisation as in mesosphere; `CreateTransferMemory`. Result: 8 threads run; the game opens `nvdrv`.
