`docs/decisions/0015-guest-threads.md`:

```md
# 0015 — Guest threads are host threads; one kernel lock

<!-- decision
state: accepted
date: 2026-10-21
replaces: none
code: runtime/src/host.c
-->

Date: 2026-10-21
Status: accepted

## Context

With the sdk recompiled (0014), the game makes its own threads through `svcCreateThread` and synchronises them through the kernel: `ArbitrateLock/Unlock` (mutexes), `WaitProcessWideKeyAtomic`/`SignalProcessWideKey` (condition variables), `WaitSynchronization` (events, thread exit), `WaitForAddress`/`SignalToAddress` (address arbiter). Until now the kernel had one thread and stand-ins that could never block. Main's start-up stopped at its first `CreateThread`.

## Decision

**One host thread per guest thread.** Each has its own `CPUState` and its own thread-local region (TLR, `TPIDRRO_EL0`). Guest code runs truly in parallel on the host's cores, with no lock held. This is what decision 0005 assumed ("guest pointers are host pointers, shared memory") and what 0009's atomics were built for. LAS Recomp does the same.

**One kernel lock (`klock`).** Every SVC runs holding it, services included (they are called from `SendSyncRequest`). A thread that has to block waits on its own host condition variable, which releases the lock meanwhile. Why one lock: kernel calls are rare next to guest code (the fast path of a mutex is pure guest code), so contention on it is not a cost worth designing for yet, and one lock makes every kernel operation trivially atomic. If profiling ever shows the lock hot, it can be split.

**Semantics follow Atmosphère's kernel (mesosphere)**, step by step:
- Mutex word: 0 = free, else the owner's handle, bit 30 = someone waits. `ArbitrateLock` waits only if the word still reads "owner | waiters"; otherwise it returns and the guest retries. `ArbitrateUnlock` hands the mutex to the best waiter (highest priority, then first come), keeping bit 30 if others still wait.
- Condition variable: `WaitProcessWideKeyAtomic` releases the mutex (as unlock does), writes 1 to the key, waits. A signalled waiter takes the mutex back if it is free, else joins the mutex's queue; the key goes back to 0 when no waiter is left. **On a timeout the kernel does not re-take the mutex**: the sdk does that itself (libnx does the same). The single-thread stand-in had this wrong.
- `WaitSynchronization`: events and threads (signalled when they exit); `CancelSynchronization` ends a wait with `ResultCancelled`, or the next one if the thread isn't waiting.
- Address arbiter: `WaitIfLessThan`, `DecrementAndWaitIfLessThan`, `WaitIfEqual`; `Signal`, `SignalAndIncrementIfEqual`. `SignalAndModifyByWaitingCount` stops with a message until something uses it and its value rule is checked.
- Words in guest memory that guest code changes at the same time are changed with host atomics (compare-and-swap loops), as mesosphere uses exclusive accesses.

**Thread life.** `CreateThread` makes the thread suspended (TLR page zeroed, `x0` = argument, `sp` = stack top); `StartThread` starts its host thread (16 MiB host stack, reserved only, for the recompiled code's C frames; the guest stack is the game's). `ExitThread` jumps back to the host thread's entry (`__builtin_setjmp/longjmp`, which skips the generated C frames without unwinding them: they hold nothing to clean up). A thread is freed once it has exited and its handle is closed.

**TLRs**: one 4 KiB page per thread slot at `0x7040000000` (256 slots, reserved at start-up). Horizon packs 0x200-byte regions eight to a page; the guest can't tell the difference.

**Deadlock detector.** The kernel counts threads that can still run (timed waits count as runnable). If every thread waits with no timeout, nothing can ever wake them, because nothing outside guest threads signals anything yet. The kernel then stops and prints each thread's wait and backtrace instead of hanging. When native services start signalling events from host threads (audio, vsync), this check has to learn about them.

**Host layer** (`runtime/src/host.c`): lock, condition variable, thread start, yield, monotonic clock, for Windows (SRW lock, condition variable, `_beginthreadex`, `QueryPerformanceCounter`) and Linux (pthreads, `CLOCK_MONOTONIC`). The system counter (`CNTPCT_EL0`) now uses the monotonic clock.

## What we don't do (known differences)

- **Priorities and core masks are recorded, not enforced.** The host schedules. On the Switch, two threads pinned to the same core never run at the same time, and a higher-priority thread on a core runs until it blocks. Code that relies on that instead of locks would race here. Emulators run the same games with host scheduling, so this is usually safe; if a race turns up, the fix is per-core run locks for threads pinned to one core.
- **Timeout resolution on Windows is 1 ms** (waits round up, never short). Frame pacing may want better later.
- **No priority inheritance** for mutex owners.
- Exclusives keep 0009's ABA difference.

## Testing

`tests/test_kernel.py` builds the kernel with a C driver (no game) whose guest threads use an nn::os-style mutex and condition variable, and checks:
- 8 threads × 20,000 increments of a plain counter under a contended mutex (the kernel path must actually run);
- a bounded queue with 4 producers and 4 consumers on two condition variables (count and sum);
- joining threads through `WaitSynchronization`, half ending by `ExitThread`, half by returning;
- timeouts (event wait, condition variable: mutex not held after a timeout, timeout 0), events, `CancelSynchronization` (while waiting and pending), the address arbiter;
- **0009's exclusives between real threads**: 8 × 100,000 increments with the recompiler's own `ldaxr`/`stlxr` output;
- the deadlock detector stops (exit code 3) instead of hanging.

Planted bugs caught: unlock drops the waiters bit, unlock hands over without waking, a signalled waiter skips taking the mutex, thread exit not signalled, a pending cancel ignored, `stlxr` as a plain store (167,482 of 800,000 increments survived). The test also found a real bug in the first version: a thread woken but not yet running again was counted as blocked, which made the deadlock detector fire falsely.

## Result

Main's start-up creates and starts 8 threads (file loading and others), which take mutexes, wait on condition variables and send IPC requests from their own threads. With transfer memory added (`svcCreateTransferMemory`: the game lends a block of its memory to a service), the game reaches its first graphics service, `nvdrv`.

```

`docs/decisions/0016-native-overrides-and-the-nvn-entry.md`:

```md
# 0016 — Native overrides by symbol; NVN starts at nvnBootstrapLoader

<!-- decision
state: accepted
date: 2026-10-21
replaces: none
code: recomp/overrides.toml, runtime/src/nvn.c
-->

Date: 2026-10-21
Status: accepted (follows 0005's graphics plan and 0014's "overrides by symbol stay possible")

## Context

With threads (0015), main's start-up reached `sm: GetServiceHandle("nvdrv")`, the GPU driver service. The backtrace (`tools/yw4/where.py` names the sdk addresses) shows who opens it: `nnMain` → game code → **`nv::InitializeGraphics(memory, 8 MiB)`**, the set-up of the NVN driver inside the sdk. That driver turns NVN calls into Maxwell GPU commands sent through `nvdrv`. Emulating that path is option A of decision 0005, which was rejected. Graphics is done at the NVN API level instead.

## Decision

**Overrides live in the translator** (`recomp/overrides.toml`: module, symbol, native function, why). The overridden function keeps its address and name (`s_<offset>`), but its body becomes one call to the native function. So every way of reaching it is covered: direct `BL` inside a module, calls through the PLT, and function pointers. A runtime-only hook in `yw4_resolve` would miss direct calls. The translator refuses an override whose symbol isn't a defined function. This is the "per-function config for stubs and patches (TOML, N64Recomp-style)" from the Phase 2 plan. Natives use the AArch64 calling convention on the `CPUState`, like the old HLE functions.

**The graphics boundary is three functions:**
- `nvnBootstrapLoader`, NVN's only entry point: it returns our native functions (`runtime/src/nvn.c`).
- `nv::InitializeGraphics` / `nv::FinalizeGraphics`: do nothing. The 8 MiB the game hands over is the driver's bookkeeping memory, and we have no driver.

`nv::SetGraphicsAllocator` and the other `nv::` setters stay recompiled: they only store pointers.

**NVN names.** The game asks for `nvnDeviceGetProcAddress`, then for each NVN function by name. Every name gets a guest address (host callbacks can now carry a data pointer, `yw4_host_function_data`, so one "missing" stub stands behind all unwritten names). Calling an unwritten function stops with its name, its caller and the first arguments. Real NVN returns NULL for unknown names; the game only asks for names it uses, so giving every name an address is the stricter choice: a NULL might be silently tolerated.

## Result

The game skips the sdk's GPU driver and stops at its first NVN call, `nvnDeviceBuilderSetDefaults` (main+0x94a778). From here on it's Phase 4a: the NVN → Vulkan layer.

```

`docs/decisions/0017-nvn-headless-first.md`:

```md
# 0017 — NVN on the host: headless first; SDL3 and Vulkan next

<!-- decision
state: accepted
date: 2026-10-21
replaces: none
code: runtime/src/nvn.c, runtime/src/nvn_objects.c, runtime/src/tegra.c, runtime/src/vi.c, runtime/src/svc_am.c, runtime/src/svc_acc.c
-->

Date: 2026-10-21
Status: accepted (owner chose all three options below, 2026-10-21)

## Owner's choices

1. **Headless first.** NVN objects hold state, command buffers record, nothing is drawn, until the game reaches its frame loop. This needs no new dependency, shows the whole set of NVN calls a frame makes before the Vulkan design is fixed, and reaches the next non-graphics blockers (input, audio, saves) sooner.
2. **SDL3** (zlib licence) for the window later, and also for input (`hid`) and audio output (`audren`).
3. **Vulkan headers vendored** (Khronos, Apache-2.0/MIT), with `vulkan-1` loaded at run time so building needs nothing installed. The owner installs the LunarG SDK only for its validation layers.

## How NVN is built (runtime/src/nvn*.c, tegra.c)

NVN's headers aren't public. Argument orders, builder field offsets, the packing of the small state objects and the device limits come from **LAS Recomp's NVN** (MIT; `third_party/lasrecomp/README.md` lists what was adapted from which file, with its licence). Each file that adapts LAS code says so. Our versions are rewritten in this project's style, and the parts we can check are checked against our game (below).

- **Only the 177 NVN functions the game uses** (`work/recon/nvn.md`). Any other one stops with its name (0016).
- **Objects** (memory pool, texture, program, window, command buffer, texture/sampler pool) keep a pointer to our host object in their first 8 bytes. **Builders and small state objects** keep their fields in guest memory, inside their ABI size, because the game copies them by value (the command buffer copies a bound blend state, for example).
- **GPU addresses are guest addresses.** A memory pool is the game's own memory, so mapping it returns that memory and flushes are no-ops.
- **Command buffers record into the game's command memory** as records holding the call's arguments and copies of what its pointers point at. A command handle is the address of a list's first record, and lists continue across memory chunks through jump records. That way the game's own command-memory management behaves as designed. This game sets no out-of-memory callback, so running out stops.
- **Headless semantics:** work is finished the moment it is submitted, so every sync is signalled and `SyncWait` returns "already signalled". Submitting walks the lists (a broken list stops) and counts draws. `ReportCounter` writes a zero value and the current GPU timestamp. Presenting counts frames and logs the first three and every 300th.
- **Texture storage sizes** follow the Tegra X1 block-linear layout (`tegra.c`): GOBs of 64 bytes × 8 rows, the block height the driver picks, mip levels shrinking it, layers aligned to blocks. Multisampled textures are stored as a wider/taller surface (2× as 2×1, 4× as 2×2, 8× as 4×2). The game sizes its memory from these numbers, so `tests/test_nvn.py` checks them against sizes worked out by hand and checks the swizzle against an independent model of the layout. A planted sector-order bug is caught.

## nn::vi: overridden, like the GPU driver

On the Switch, NVN's window presents through a vi layer and an Android-style binder buffer queue. Our NVN presents itself, so the game's 8 `nn::vi` imports are overrides (`recomp/overrides.toml`, `runtime/src/vi.c`). The display, layer and native window are objects to hand back. The vsync event is real: a host thread signals it at 60 Hz.

Two small mechanisms came with it:
- **Guest symbols for native code** (`[[guest_symbol]]` in `overrides.toml`, `yw4_guest_symbol(name)`): the vsync override attaches its event handle with the sdk's own `nn::os::AttachReadableHandleToSystemEvent`, because the layout of `SystemEventType` is the sdk's business.
- **Host-signalled events** (`KEvent.host_signalled`, `yw4_event_signal_from_host`): a wait on one isn't "blocked forever", so the deadlock detector (0015) still works with vsync running.

## Services reached on the way (svc_am.c, svc_acc.c)

Operation mode is docked, so the game makes a 1920×1080 layer. `apm` performance settings are accepted and ignored. One local user account (fixed id, which keys the save data later) is passed as the preselected-user launch parameter. Desired language is `ja`: the game is Japanese only. Small output buffers can arrive as C (pointer) buffers instead of B buffers; `ipc_out_buffer()` takes either.

## Not verified yet

- `nvnQueueBuilderGetQueueMemorySize` returns 0x10000. That is a guess at what the game must allocate, and our NVN uses none of it.
- Storage alignment 512 bytes (32 for linear) is from LAS. Real compressible render targets may want more. Harmless headless; it matters once Vulkan textures alias game memory.
- The MSAA storage layout is from the Maxwell sample arrangement, not measured.

## Result

NVN device, window (2 textures) and display set-up all pass. The game reaches input: `hid` (`nn::hid::InitializeNpad`).

```

`docs/decisions/0018-setjmp-longjmp.md`:

```md
# 0018 — setjmp and longjmp in recompiled code

<!-- decision
state: accepted
date: 2026-10-21
replaces: 0015 (part)
code: runtime/src/setjmp.c, recomp/translate.py, recomp/function.py
-->

Date: 2026-10-21
Status: accepted

## Problem

The game's Lua (5.2) handles script errors with `setjmp`/`longjmp` (`luaD_rawrunprotected` in main, through the PLT to the sdk's musl `_setjmp`). The guest `setjmp` saves x19-x30, sp and d8-d15; `longjmp` restores them and ends with `br x30`, a jump to the return address of the `setjmp` call. In recompiled code that address is the middle of a C function, not a function, so the jump stopped with "indirect call to main+0xd2ce38: no translated function there".

Measured: one `setjmp` call site in main, four in the sdk. There is no `sigsetjmp` and no other `longjmp` user.

## Decision

- **The translator** (`recomp/translate.py`, `function.py`) finds the setjmp functions: the sdk's `_setjmp`/`setjmp`/`__setjmp` (one address), and in each module the PLT stubs whose GOT slot resolves to it. At each call to one, it emits a host `setjmp` in the calling function's own C frame, with the `jmp_buf` declared at the function's top level so it lives as long as the frame. On the first return, it registers the point and calls the guest `setjmp` as before.
- **The runtime** (`runtime/src/setjmp.c`) keeps the registered points per thread, keyed by (return address, guest sp), ordered outermost first. A new point drops the deeper ones, whose frames must have returned. When `yw4_resolve` misses, it asks `yw4_setjmp_resume`. A matching point is jumped to with the host `longjmp`, which lands in that frame right after the call. The guest registers are already the restored ones, and x0 is the longjmp value.
- **The C library's `setjmp`/`longjmp`, not `__builtin_setjmp`.** The first version used the GCC/Clang builtins, which are cheaper and don't unwind. On Windows x64 they broke. In a frame over 128 bytes Clang sets `rbp = rsp + 0x80` and addresses locals through `rbp`, but `__builtin_setjmp` saves the canonical frame address, so after the jump `rbp` was 0x80 too low and `ctx` was read from the wrong slot (an access violation in `f_d2cde0`, seen in the disassembly). The CRT's `longjmp` unwinds properly; on Windows that's `RtlUnwind` over the unwind data Clang emits for every x64 function. Lua errors are rare, so the cost doesn't matter. The kernel's `ExitThread` jump (0015) moved to the CRT pair as well: it only worked before because `thread_main`'s frame is small.

## Also in this step: a crash handler

A host crash (access violation, segmentation fault) now prints the host address, the offset in `yw4.exe` (look it up with `llvm-nm -n`), and the guest thread's backtrace (`host_install_crash_handler`, `yw4_stop`). An indirect call to nowhere prints the backtrace too.

## Testing

`tests/test_kernel.py` repeats what generated code does three times: a caller with a 320-byte frame does `setjmp` and registers, a "guest longjmp" six calls deeper restores sp and branches to the return address, and the caller checks x0, sp and its locals. A planted wrong jump fails the test.

## Result

The game passes its first Lua error and stays in its frame loop: 8,400 frames in 13 minutes without a stop. That is about 11 frames per second, not 60, still to be explained. Every frame shows the same 27 draws, so it is probably waiting on one screen.

```

```md
# 0019 — The window: SDL3 and Vulkan; CPU clears as the first pixels

<!-- decision
state: accepted
date: 2026-10-21
replaces: none
code: runtime/src/window.c, recomp/build.py, tools/yw4/deps.py, runtime/src/nvn_cmdbuf.c, third_party/vulkan
-->

Date: 2026-10-21
Status: accepted (follows the owner's choices in 0017: SDL3, vendored Vulkan headers)

## Dependencies

- **SDL3 3.4.18** (zlib licence), the official MinGW development release, fetched by `python -m tools.yw4.deps` into `<work_dir>/deps/` (pinned by version and SHA-256; `recomp/build.py` calls it). No binary is committed. Linux uses the system's SDL3 through `pkg-config`. `SDL3.dll` is copied next to `yw4.exe`.
- **Vulkan headers** `vulkan-sdk-1.4.357.0` (Apache-2.0 or MIT), committed in `third_party/vulkan/`. Vulkan itself is loaded at run time through `SDL_Vulkan_GetVkGetInstanceProcAddr`; no Vulkan library is linked. `YW4_VULKAN_VALIDATION=1` enables the Khronos validation layer once the owner has installed the LunarG SDK.

## Threads

The process's main thread owns the window and pumps its events. The main guest thread moved to its own host thread (64 MiB host stack, reserved only), and `yw4_kernel_init` runs there, because the kernel binds the main guest thread to the calling host thread. Closing the window ends the process. `YW4_HEADLESS=1` (or no usable window) runs everything as before, without a window.

## What is shown, for now

Nothing draws yet: draws need the game's shaders translated (Phase 4a proper). So that the window shows the game's real state from the start:
- **Colour clears run on the CPU** (`nvn_cmdbuf.c`): `SetRenderTargets` and `ClearColor` write the clear colour into the texture's storage in the game's memory. If every texel is equal and the texel size divides 16, the layout doesn't matter and the whole level is filled. Clear colours are encoded per format in `pixels.c` (8-bit unorm and sRGB, BGRA, half and single floats, RGB10A2, R11G11B10F). Other formats, and partial channel masks, are reported once and skipped.
- **Present reads the window texture back** from the game's memory (`tegra_read_region`, 16-byte runs where possible), converts it to RGBA8 and gives it to the window. Vulkan copies it into an image and scales it into the swapchain, letterboxed to keep its shape. FIFO presentation; the game already paces itself to 30 frames per second (0017).
- **Screenshots:** F12, or `YW4_SCREENSHOTS=<frame>,<frame>,...`, as BMP files in `YW4_SCREENSHOT_DIR` (`build.py --run`: `<work_dir>/screenshots/`, never committed: they are pictures of the game).

## What the first frames show

The window is black, and that is correct for now. Logging the clears shows how the game renders. It clears a **1600×900 set of render targets** every frame (RGBA8 to (0,0,1,0), R11G11B10F to grey 0.298, RGBA8 to black, RG16F): a deferred renderer's G-buffer at 900p. It also clears 533×300 targets (a third of 1600×900: bloom or blur buffers). The very first frame used 1920×1080 targets, so the internal resolution changes at run time. The 1920×1080 window texture is never cleared: the final picture is *drawn* into it, and drawing doesn't exist yet. These numbers are the first real input for the renderer design (Phase 4b).

## Testing

`tests/test_nvn.py` adds region round trips: writing a whole level equals the swizzle, and reading whole and partial regions back (aligned and unaligned starts; 1-, 4-, 8- and 16-byte texels) returns the source. With the window open the game still runs at 30.0 frames per second.
```

`docs/decisions/0020-shaders-from-the-assembly.md`:

```md
# 0020 — Shaders: translate the shipped assembly, not the GPU code

<!-- decision
state: accepted
date: 2026-10-21
replaces: none
code: tools/yw4/shaders.py, recomp/shader.py
-->

Date: 2026-10-21
Status: accepted (owner: "which is best, not accounting for complexity")

## The choice

Every shader file carries two forms of the same program: Maxwell GPU machine code, and the NV_gpu_program5 assembly it was compiled from (recon section 6). The shaders are translated from the **assembly**, ahead of time, to GLSL and then SPIR-V. LAS Recomp's Maxwell translator (MIT, `runtime/nvn/maxwell/translate.c`) is a reference for the Vulkan side only: descriptor layout, constant buffers, texture handles.

Why the assembly, even ignoring effort:
- **It is the source.** The machine code is compiled from it and has lost what matters for a good translation: structured control flow, named and typed declarations, no register allocation or scheduling. The game's shaders were written in HLSL, converted by `hlslcc` (names like `hlslcc_mtx4x4matScale`), and compiled by NVIDIA's GLSL compiler to this assembly.
- **Better Vulkan shaders.** Structured input gives structured SPIR-V that the PC driver optimises well. Lifted machine code becomes jump-driven state machines.
- **Phase 4c edits shaders** (resolution, shadows, AA). That needs readable output.
- Against it: the machine code is exactly what the Switch ran, rounding included. Screenshot diffs against the emulator reference catch differences, and the machine code stays in the files as a cross-check.

## What the shaders use (all 1,891 programs measured)

- 1,022 vertex (`.vsb`, and `.esb`, also `!!NVvp5.0`), 842 fragment, 13 geometry, 14 compute. **1,349 distinct texts.**
- **58 opcodes.** Control flow is only `IF/ELSE/ENDIF`, `REP/ENDREP` (one with a fixed count), `BRK`: structured, no `CAL`/`BRA`. Conditions test the condition code with `NE` or `EQ` only; besides `IF`/`BRK`/`KIL` they also guard writes (`MOV R0.z (EQ.x), ...`, 296 uses).
- Textures: `TEX` 2D (4,077) and `SHADOWARRAY2D` (3,123, shadow cascades), `TXL` 2D/CUBE/3D, `SHADOW2D`, `ARRAY2D`, `TXF`, `TXQ`; one compute image store (`STOREIM`).
- Every program has `NV_bindless_texture`, but **every texture handle is loaded from constant buffer 14 at a constant offset** (`LDC.U64 D0.x, buf14[k]; TEX ... handle(D0.x)`, none computed). Buffer 14 is where NVN puts bound textures' handles, so `buf14[k]` is texture binding k/8. Ordinary Vulkan descriptors are enough; no bindless emulation.
- Other constant buffers are slots 0–13; storage buffers, shared memory, barriers and a few atomics in compute; local arrays (`TEMP lmem0[N]`) in 184 programs.
- Integer vertex inputs exist (bone indices and packed data read with `.U`/`.S` instructions).

## The container (HBH1)

Documented in `tools/yw4/shaders.py`: six (offset, size) sections: vertex inputs (name, location), resources (name, kind, slot), constant-buffer members (name, offset), one not yet understood, `NXGL`, strings. `NXGL` holds the GPU code and the **control section**, which is what the game passes to `nvnProgramSetShaders` as `control` and which contains the assembly text.

## Identifying shaders at run time

Key = FNV-1a 64 of the assembly text, `!!NV` through `END`. `python -m tools.yw4.shaders` extracts each distinct text once to `<work_dir>/shaders/asm/<key>.<stage>.asm` with `index.json`. The runtime finds the text in the control section it is given and computes the same key. No file names, load order or GPU addresses are involved, and an unknown key is a loud stop.

## The translator (`recomp/shader.py`)

`python -m recomp.shader [--check]` writes `<work_dir>/shaders/glsl/<key>.<stage>` (GLSL 4.60) and `<key>.json` (what it binds). `--check` compiles them to SPIR-V with `glslangValidator` from the Vulkan SDK (owner installs it; it also brings the validation layer). Choices, all written down in the module docstring:

- **Registers are raw bits** (`uvec4`), reinterpreted per instruction, because the assembly's registers have no type: `.F`/`.S`/`.U` says how an instruction reads them. A plain `MOV` copies bits. This is exact where a float model would not be (integers stored in float registers would be denormals and could be flushed).
- **One GLSL statement per instruction**, preceded by the instruction as a comment. The GPU driver's compiler removes the redundancy; readability is what matters for Phase 4.
- `MAD` → `fma()` (Maxwell fuses it). `ROUND` → `roundEven`. `TRUNC.U` clamps negatives to 0 (Maxwell's conversion saturates; GLSL's is undefined). `RSQ` takes the absolute value (spec).
- `H` registers (fp16 on the Switch) are fp32 here. Precision can differ; screenshot diffs will show if it matters.
- Bindings: descriptor set = stage; constant buffer n → binding n, texture/image slot k → 16 + k, storage buffer n → 64 + n (texture slots reach 32); inputs/varyings/colour outputs by location. Vertex inputs are `vec4` or `uvec4` by how they are read (two passes); varyings are `vec4` carrying bits, `flat` when read as integers.
- Depth: NVN's default clip space has z in [-w, w]; a push-constant bit maps it to Vulkan's [0, w] in the last stage before rasterisation. Y orientation is left to the viewport.
- `vertex.instance` excludes the base instance (as on Maxwell): `gl_InstanceIndex - gl_BaseInstance`.

Result: **all 1,349 programs translate and compile to SPIR-V** (`--check`, glslang 16.6.0, Vulkan 1.2 target, 47 s in parallel); the translator stops loudly on anything it does not know. Not yet verified: that they render correctly (needs the draw path; checked by screenshot diffs against the emulator reference).

The SDK installer needs administrator rights, so `[tools] glslang` can instead point at a standalone Khronos glslang release (no install; the owner's copy is in the tools folder outside the repo). The SDK is still wanted for the validation layer.

## Next

The Vulkan draw path: pipelines from NVN state, vertex input, descriptors from bound buffers and textures, draws, first real pixels.

```

`docs/decisions/0021-draw-path.md`:

```md
# 0021 — The draw path: NVN command lists on Vulkan

<!-- decision
state: accepted
date: 2026-10-21
replaces: 0019 (part)
code: runtime/src/gpu.c, runtime/src/vk.h, runtime/src/gpu_draw.c
-->

Date: 2026-10-21
Status: accepted (owner: "go for it" on the proposal; this file is the proposal)

## The question

NVN commands are recorded (0017) and the shaders are translated (0020). To draw, the game's memory has to reach the GPU: vertex, index and uniform buffers, textures, render targets. How?

## Measured (YW4_NVN_STATS, title menu)

- **Six memory pools, all 4 KiB-aligned**, 1.4 GB in total:

  | Flags | Meaning (NVN memory pool flags) | Size | Probable use |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | `0xa1` | CPU no access, GPU cached, compressible | 298 MiB | render targets |
  | `0x24` ×2 | CPU cached, GPU cached | 900 + 32 MiB | textures, meshes |
  | `0x22` | CPU uncached, GPU cached | 64 MiB | |
  | `0x12` | CPU uncached, GPU uncached | 64 MiB | per-frame data (uniforms) |
  | `0x64` | CPU cached, GPU cached, shader code | 32 MiB | shaders |

- Texture data: 42 MB through `WriteTexels` at start-up, then none (the menu).
- Per frame: 25 draws (none indexed), 2 compute dispatches, 16 programs, 33 shaders loaded so far, all of them translated.
- The GPU (RTX 4070 Laptop, Vulkan 1.4) has `VK_EXT_external_memory_host`, dynamic rendering, extended dynamic state 3, vertex input dynamic state, custom border colours.

## Decision

1. **Buffers: game memory used in place.** Each memory pool the CPU can reach is imported into Vulkan with `VK_EXT_external_memory_host` (guest pointers are host pointers, pools are page-aligned). A buffer is (pool, offset): vertex, index, uniform, storage and indirect buffers need no copies and no change tracking, and what the GPU writes (compute, counters) lands where the game reads it.
2. **Textures: Vulkan images, uploaded when their data changes.** One `VkImage` per NVN texture, created at first use. Images in the CPU-no-access pool are **render targets and never uploaded or read back**: the CPU cannot see them on the Switch either. Other textures are uploaded (de-swizzled with `tegra.c`) at first use and after `WriteTexels`/copies into them. Change detection for textures the CPU writes directly is added only if a measurement shows the game doing it.
3. **Execution at submit.** `QueueSubmitCommands` walks the recorded list and records a Vulkan command buffer: dynamic rendering, pipelines built on demand from (program, state, target formats) and cached, descriptors from the bound buffers and textures. A timeline semaphore numbers submissions; NVN syncs wait on those numbers. Simple global barriers between passes first (correct, maybe slow); finer later if profiling says so.
4. **Present on the GPU.** The window texture is an image; present blits it to the swapchain. The CPU clears and read-back of 0019 go.
5. **Shaders** are loaded as SPIR-V from `work/shaders/glsl` (`YW4_SHADER_DIR`) for now; embedding comes with packaging.

Requirements: Vulkan 1.3 and `VK_EXT_external_memory_host` (NVIDIA, AMD, Intel on Windows; Mesa RADV/ANV on Linux). No new library (no VMA): the few allocations are done by hand.

## Alternatives

- **Copy buffers to GPU memory with change tracking** (what LAS Recomp does for most data). Faster GPU reads, but needs write tracking for 1.4 GB of game memory and gets stale data wrong silently. Imported memory is read over PCIe, slower for big meshes; that is a performance question for later (Phase 4c owns the renderer anyway), and copying hot buffers can be added then.
- **Adapt LAS Recomp's Vulkan backend** (MIT, ~300 KB). Built for another game and mirrors its Metal backend; too big to own line by line. It stays a reference.
- **Keep rendering on the CPU.** No.

## Steps

1. **Done:** Vulkan 1.3 device with the features the shaders need, all six pools imported (1.4 GB, no copies), an image per texture, clears and present on the GPU, NVN syncs on a timeline semaphore (`runtime/src/gpu.c`, `vk.h`). The game runs at 30 frames/s on it; the window is still black (nothing draws yet), and screenshots now come from the GPU image. Headless (`YW4_HEADLESS=1`) keeps the CPU path.
2. **Done:** pipelines and draws (`runtime/src/gpu_draw.c`). The translated SPIR-V and a small interface file per shader (`<key>.iface`) are loaded on first use; descriptor sets per stage from bound uniform buffers, storage buffers and textures (texture handle = id | sampler id << 20 in the bound pools); pipelines cached per program on formats, blending, channel masks, polygon mode, topology and vertex input, everything else dynamic. Textures in CPU-visible pools are uploaded at first use and after `WriteTexels`. Quads (the 2D passes use them) become triangles through a fixed index buffer. Measured: the game sets the **upper-left window origin and near-at-0 depth** (Direct3D conventions), so the viewport is flipped and no depth fix-up is needed. Present honours **`nvnWindowSetCrop`**: the game renders at 1600×900 into the 1920×1080 window texture and crops (dynamic resolution). Result: the LEVEL-5 logo and the autosave notice, at 30 frames/s. `YW4_GPU_TRACE=<n>` describes the first n draws (programs, targets, viewport, textures).
3. Compute dispatches, the rest of the state, then scenes beyond the menu.

```

```md
# 0022 — From the title menu into a new game

<!-- decision
state: accepted
date: 2026-10-22
replaces: none
code: runtime/src/swkbd.c, recomp/function.py, runtime/src/svc_time.c, runtime/src/svc_am.c, runtime/src/gpu_draw.c
-->

Date: 2026-10-22
Status: accepted (small steps, each forced by the next stop of the running game)

## What stopped the game, and what we did

| Stop | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `ShowKeyboard` -> `CreateLibraryApplet` (name entry) | The Switch's keyboard is a library applet; there is none here | `nn::swkbd::ShowKeyboard` is a native override (`runtime/src/swkbd.c`). It answers at once with `YW4_PLAYER_NAME` (default "Nate"). The out string is `{char16_t *buffer; size_t size}`, measured from the game's caller. Typing a real name (SDL text input) is a later step |
| Indirect call to `main+0x9a6c78` | A `br` through a switch table that the recompiler did not recognise: the compiler had put ~40 vector instructions between the bound check (`cmp`/`b.hi`) and the table load | `recomp/function.py`: the search for the bound compare reaches 8x further back |
| Indirect call to `main+0xa3e014` | Same, but the table's base register is loaded by an `adrp` laid out *after* the branch | `recomp/function.py`: if the backward scan finds no constant, take an `adrp`/`add` into that register within 32 KiB of the branch whose table has only code addresses within 64 KiB of the branch. A wrong guess still fails loudly for targets outside the table, as before. 3 more tables in `main`, 21 in `sdk` |
| `time:u` 400, 500; `IApplicationFunctions` 50 | Clock snapshots, snapshot difference, pseudo device id | `svc_time.c` (ClockSnapshot, 0xD0 bytes, layout from Switchbrew), `svc_am.c` (fixed id) |
| Vertex input 1 of shader `97a2b1f006a064b9`: `R32_UINT` read "as float" | A plain `MOV.U` copies bits and says nothing about the type, so the translator calls the input a float. 32-bit integers have no scaled format in Vulkan | `gpu_draw.c`: 32-bit integer formats are fetched as the float of the same width (bits unchanged); the shader copies them to a flat varying |

## Result

The game gets through the name entry, the new-game flow and into the opening scene: a 3D room with Whisper, Nate and Jibanyan, and the first line of dialogue (`docs/screenshots/06-opening-scene.jpg`).
```

`docs/decisions/0023-custom-renderer-plan.md`:

```md
# 0023 — Plan for the custom renderer (Phase 4b/4c)

<!-- decision
state: accepted
date: 2026-10-22
replaces: none
code: none
-->

Date: 2026-10-22
Status: accepted (owner: replace the 3D world; "UI and menu can stay on the old renderer" for now)

## The question

The NVN → Vulkan layer (0021, Phase 4a) now draws the house, town, battles and cutscenes like Eden. The project's
main goal is our own renderer, for two reasons the owner gave:

1. **Performance:** beat Eden on CPU and stutter. Ours already uses about half Eden's CPU (docs/baseline.md), but in
   busy scenes the frame is set by the main thread plus one render thread, and ~70% of that render thread is the
   game's own code building NVN command buffers.
2. **Enhancements:** higher resolution, widescreen, better shadows, 60 fps.

What do we replace, in what order, and where do we hook it?

## Measured: what one town frame draws

From an F11 log (work/logs/yw4_20261022_115926.log, street, daytime; the log stops at 450 draws, so the last
passes are cut off). Passes = consecutive draws with the same render targets:

| # | Target | Draws | What it probably is |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 240×135, depth only, 36-vertex boxes | ~45 | occlusion-query boxes |
| 2 | 1024×1024 depth, 3 times | 54 / 20 / 80 | shadow cascades |
| 3 | 128×128, 1 colour | 3 | ambient cube map update (see a9c98f1) |
| 4 | 1600×900, 3 colour + depth | 64 | G-buffer (opaque geometry) |
| 5 | 800×450 and 533×300 | ~10 | half-res: screen-space shadow mask, SSAO-like, lamp light buffer |
| 6 | 1600×900, 1 colour + depth | 70 | lighting resolve + forward/transparent geometry |
| 7 | 1600×900 / 800×450 / 533×300 mix | ~30 | effects, fog, particles |
| 8 | 400×225 → 200×112 → 120×67 | 6 | bloom chain |
| 9 | 1600×900 no depth, 340×304, 516×460 | ~45 | UI, minimap |
| 10 | 1920×1080 | 1 | final copy into the window texture (cropped from 1600×900 = dynamic resolution) |

A classic deferred renderer: ~600-1500 draws a frame, about 40 passes, most of them full-screen quads. The heavy
CPU and GPU work is in passes 2, 4 and 6 (meshes).

## Decision

1. **Scope: the 3D world.** We replace shadows, the G-buffer, lighting, forward geometry and post-processing with
   our own Vulkan code that reads the engine's data (camera, meshes, materials, lights) instead of the game's NVN
   commands. **UI, menus, minimap, movies and particle effects stay on the NVN → Vulkan layer** for now: little
   to gain, many shaders. This can be revisited later.
2. **Hook at the engine level, one pass at a time.** For each pass: find the engine function that records it, call
   our renderer there instead, skip the game's command building. Our passes and the old path share one Vulkan
   device and draw into the same images within a frame.
3. **Every replaced pass must match the old output** (screenshot diff, `YW4_CAPTURE_FS`) and can be switched back
   to the old path with an env var. The goal of the replacement is the same picture, faster.
5. **Enhancements come last, as mods** (owner: "we will look at improvements at the end with mods"): better
   shadows, AA, resolution, widescreen and 60 fps are not part of replacing passes. Once the 3D world is ours, they
   are added as optional mods on top.
4. **No separate clean-up of the NVN layer.** Its resolution-scaling and occlusion-query gaps go away with the passes
   that replace them. The one piece we need is **image tracking** (who writes which image, the right barriers and
   layouts between our passes and the old path); it is built when the first replaced pass needs it.

## Order

1. **Map the frame** (Phase 4b), shadows first: name each pass by the engine function that records it (call stacks
   from the draw wrappers in work/recon/nvn.md; yw::CMainComponent slots 11/12; lives::CDeviceUnitNX), and find
   the data it reads. Output: `docs/frame.md`. No game code changes.
2. **Replace the shadow cascades** (pass 2), plus image tracking.
3. **Replace the G-buffer and forward geometry** (passes 4 and 6), with lighting (5, 6). Biggest CPU win, biggest job
   (materials, skinning, many mesh shaders).
4. **Replace post-processing** (passes 8, 10).
5. **Mods, at the end:** better shadows, AA, render resolution, widescreen (projection aspect + UI layout width),
   60 fps (game logic step, not only rendering).

## Alternatives

- **Clean up the NVN layer first** (barriers, pipeline cache, resolution scaling, occlusion queries). Gives quick
  wins, but most of it is thrown away once the 3D passes are ours. Rejected by the owner.
- **Replace the whole renderer at once.** Nothing to compare against until it all works. Rejected: one pass at a
  time keeps the game playable and checkable.
- **Also replace UI and menus.** Little speed or visual gain for hundreds of shaders. Left for later.

```

`docs/decisions/0024-shadow-pass.md`:

```md
# 0024 — The first replaced pass: shadow casters

<!-- decision
state: accepted
date: 2026-10-22
replaces: none
code: runtime/src/shadow.c, runtime/src/gpu_shadow.c, runtime/shaders/shadow_static.vert, recomp/overrides.toml, recomp/build.py
-->

Date: 2026-10-22
Status: accepted (owner: "write it up, do what you think is best")

## The question

Decision 0023 replaces the 3D world pass by pass, shadows first. [frame.md](../frame.md) now maps the shadow pass:
where the cascades come from, which objects are drawn, their geometry, matrices, bones and instance transforms, and
the five shader programs. How exactly do we take it over?

## What the game does today (per frame, render thread A)

For each of 3 cascades: a few setup jobs (target layer, viewport, matrices into the render state), occlusion-query
boxes for 154 objects, then the model renderer `f_a45890` on a **layer of kind 1**. `f_a45890` walks the shared
draw list, keeps the shadow casters, sorts them, and for each submesh sets state (program, buffers, textures,
uniforms built on the CPU) and draws through the engine's NVN wrapper layer. Our runtime records those NVN calls
and turns them into Vulkan at submit. The expensive part is `f_a45890` plus the two layers below it.

## Decision

1. **Hook the model renderer for shadow layers only.** A new kind of recompiler entry, a *hook*: listed `main`
   functions start with `if (native(ctx)) return;`, so native code runs first and can hand back to the
   recompiled body. `f_a45890` gets one. The hook takes over when the layer item's kind is 1 and
   `YW4_SHADOWS=native` (the default stays `game` until the pass matches). Everything around it (the cascade
   setup jobs, target binding, clears, the occlusion boxes) stays the game's for now: cheap, and it keeps the
   depth target, layer and viewport exactly as the game sets them.

   Why here and not higher up: the game's setup jobs already put the right cascade layer and matrices in place,
   so the hook only has to draw casters; and when it declines (see 5) the game's code runs unchanged.

2. **Gather on the render thread, draw at submit.** In the hook (render thread, the same moment the game reads the
   list) we walk the draw list with `f_a45890`'s own filters (layer key range and mask, visible `+0x1c8`, casts a
   shadow `+0x1d1`, not `+0x1b0`), and copy what the GPU needs into a **native pass record**: per submesh the
   vertex and index addresses (game memory, already imported into Vulkan), counts, stride, vertex layout, index
   type, the world matrix, and bones / instance transforms when used. The record goes into the thread's NVN
   command buffer (`[device+0x10d0] + 0xd8`) as a new command, `CMD_NATIVE`. Copies, because the game rewrites
   this data for the next frame before our submit runs (the same reason recorded NVN commands keep copies).

3. **The executor calls our pass at that point in the stream.** `gpu_execute` meets `CMD_NATIVE` between the game's
   own commands, so ordering with the rest of the frame and the shared depth image come for free: the target is
   already bound by the game's preceding commands. Our pass binds its own pipelines and per-draw data (a
   per-frame uniform ring of our own; push constants for small things) and draws.

4. **Our own shaders, mirroring the game's math.** Hand-written GLSL, one vertex shader per caster kind: static
   (`proj·view·world·v`), instanced (`proj·view·instance·world·v`), skinned (up to 4 bones). Depth-only fragment
   stage, plus an alpha cut-out variant. The cascade matrix comes from the renderer object (`main+0x56ab1b0`
   `+0x80 + i·0x40`); the cascade index from the render state set by the game's job `f_7ee9a0`. Same operations in
   the same order as the game's shaders, so depth should match to the last bits or close to it.

5. **Decline instead of guess.** If a layer contains anything the hook does not handle yet (a custom draw callback,
   an unknown vertex format or program, a cut-out material whose texture we cannot find), the hook returns 0 for
   that layer and the game draws it as before. A log line says why, once per reason. So the switch can be flipped
   early and coverage grows while the game stays correct.

6. **How it is checked.** Same frame, `YW4_SHADOWS=game` vs `native`: the three cascade layers dumped as raw depth
   (`YW4_DUMP_IMAGE` `.depthf`) and compared (max difference, count of differing texels), plus screenshots of the
   scene. Then CPU: per-thread busy time of render thread A before and after (perf log), and frame time in the
   busy street (`docs/baseline.md`).

## Alternatives

- **Replace the whole shadow block (`f_7ed570`'s jobs).** Saves the setup jobs and the occlusion boxes too, but we
  would also own target/layer binding and clears from day one, with nothing of the game's left to compare against
  inside the pass. Later step, once the casters match.
- **Keep `f_a45890` and only replace the layers below it (NVN wrapper, our translation).** Smaller win (about 60%
  of the thread's busy time is in those layers, but the walk and the CPU-built uniforms stay), and it changes code
  every pass shares. Not now.
- **Draw from our own copy of the scene, independent of the draw list.** Needs our own culling and sorting;
  nothing to gain until the pass matches.

## Open, to be found while building

- Where a material keeps its textures (for cut-out casters). `f_974cd0` binds them from the context object
  `[device+0x10d0]`, slots at `+0x780 + slot·16`; a write watch on such a slot will show who fills it. Until then
  cut-out casters make the hook decline.
- The vertex formats `0x22`, `0x12`, `0x2f`, `0x2c` in Vulkan terms (the existing `vertex_format` table) and the
  index type bit in the submesh record.
- How the game selects the program per submesh (static / instanced / skinned / cut-out), so the hook picks the
  matching shader.

## Steps

1. **Done:** recompiler hooks (`[[hook]]` in `recomp/overrides.toml`, by `main` offset) and a `CMD_NATIVE` command; a
   hook on `f_a45890` (`runtime/src/shadow.c`) that only counts kind-1 layers and declines. Measured: 3 shadow
   layers per frame (one per cascade), each walking the whole draw list (~185 nodes); game unchanged, tests pass.
2. **Done:** gather (`shadow.c`), from Ghidra's decompile of `f_a45890`: node, object, geometry and submesh filters,
   plus our own culling of each object's box against the cascade (side planes only: casters in front of the
   cascade still cast into it). `YW4_SHADOWS=check` compares with the game's draws: 0 missed. Instanced objects are
   not culled yet (identity world matrix, each copy placed by its own transform), so we select about 2.5× the
   game's submeshes: same image, more GPU work, to fix with per-copy culling.
3. **Working, being validated:** static casters drawn by our pass (`runtime/src/gpu_shadow.c`, shader
   `runtime/shaders/shadow_static.vert`, compiled by `recomp/build.py`). Built **hybrid** rather than as
   planned in 1-3 above: the engine binds and clears each cascade layer lazily inside `f_a45890` (2 clears per
   layer), so instead of skipping it, the hook hides the nodes we draw (their kind-1 bit at node `+0x20`), the
   game draws the rest and binds/clears the layer, and our pass is queued after it from a hook on the cascade's
   end job `f_7ed350`; the executor checks the bound target is the cascade's layer. Which submeshes are ours is
   **learned from the game's own draws**: drawn with the static programs (`b320bd` + `6ead6a`), our vertex and
   index addresses equal to the game's, our matrix equal to the one in cbuf 2 (verified per draw), and its
   culling recorded. Nodes go back to the game one frame in 32 to re-check. In the street: about 15 static
   submeshes per cascade layer drawn by us, the game the other ~70; 0 wrong vertex or index addresses over
   51,000 compared draws. Depth images against the game's: differences at the level of run-to-run noise
   (moving characters, cars), checked per run against a second run of the game's own shadows.
   Open: a few submeshes (about one per cascade layer, objects not identified yet) are drawn by the game with an
   extra per-submesh offset on top of the object's world matrix (a node transform, location unknown): their
   matrix doesn't match ours, so they stay with the game until node transforms are applied.
4. **Instanced casters: done** (vertex program `a74842` + `6ead6a`). The model renderer gets an instanced model's
   copies from the model's callback `main+0x5f9420` (model `+0xe0`): it culls the copies against the view (the
   object's box, which is one copy's, through each copy's transform; then an occlusion test) and writes the kept
   ones into a new buffer every frame, bound as vertex cbuf 11. We read all copies instead: `model+0x214` sets
   (0 = 1) of `[model+0xd0]` (0x38 bytes: first copy `+0x30`, count `+0x32`), transforms at `[model+0x168]`
   (3×4, 48 bytes), a byte per copy at `[model+0x170]` (with `model+0x218` set, the callback adds byte × 100 to
   a copy's first value when it is below 100; we do the same). Each copy is its own draw with
   projection × view × copy × world, culled by the side planes only (looser than the game's). Learned like the
   static ones; the check also needs every copy the game drew to be one of ours. Street, `YW4_SHADOWS=check`:
   0 of ~75,000 instanced draws with a copy we don't have, 0 drawn copies that our culling drops; the
   screenshot against the game's shadows differs only by run-to-run noise (animation timing). Not handled
   (the game keeps them): split copies (`model+0x216`), more than 8 sets.
   **Instanced cut-out casters: done** (`744205` + `dceb89`, the biggest remaining share): the same copies and
   matrices, plus the texture coordinates (attribute 1, from the same vertex buffer), the texture (fragment slot 0,
   by its handle) and the material's alpha threshold (vertex cbuf 3 byte 12), all learned from the game's draw;
   our `shadow_cutout.vert/.frag` drop texels below the threshold as `dceb89` does. Textures are made and uploaded
   before our pass begins rendering. Street: screenshots against the game's shadows differ less than two runs of
   the game differ from each other. The game now draws about 30% of the shadow submeshes (was 85%); CPU unchanged
   so far (the game's model renderer still runs for these layers).
   Then static cut-out (`4cbb8e`) and skinned casters (`71faac`; palettes in frame.md; with the fade program only
   while the fade is 1). Not ours yet: instanced casters with per-copy fade (`9904c2` + `b7cd6e`) and the
   wind-swayed plants (`fa9033`, `61ebac`: textures read in the vertex stage).

   **Changed 2026-10-23: replace the game's draws instead of choosing our own casters.** Hiding nodes and
   drawing what our gather selected went wrong in the owner's playtest: flickering streaks of shadow. Check mode
   showed why: about 40 submeshes per layer that we would draw and the game does not (it chooses per cascade and
   per frame by rules not decoded yet; an object 150 m away was in our list for the 20 m cascade). Learning a
   submesh once and then drawing it every frame anywhere can't match that. Now the game keeps its whole selection
   (walk, culling, sort) and the submesh-draw hook (`f_a75e90`) skips the game's draw of a submesh we can draw and
   adds ours to the pass: its state flush, NVN calls and their translation are what we save. The first draw of
   each layer stays with the game (its flush binds and clears the cascade's layer); each object goes back to the
   game one frame in 32 to be checked again. Owner's field save, every frame for 160 frames: the streaks are gone
   and the character shadows match the game's; 72% of the game's shadow draws are replaced.
   The full takeover (our own selection, no `f_a45890` at all) needs the game's selection rules first.

   **Changed 2026-10-23: instanced casters (repeated props) back to the game, for now.** With them ours, the owner
   saw bands of shadow for a frame or a few while the camera moved (never standing still, never with the game's
   shadows). Found by elimination, each a playtest with env switches: everything but instanced clean; instanced
   flash. Ours now take exactly the copies the game's callback kept (vertex cbuf 11 and the count at
   `device+0x45cc`, read at the submesh-draw hook) instead of our own culling of all copies. Measured and not
   the cause: those copies and the count against the game's draw (0 different of 40,000+, live play); each copy's
   final matrix, ours against cbuf 1 byte 128 × cbuf 11 copy × cbuf 2 byte 0 at the game's draw (0 of 40,000+,
   live, with the game also drawing); cull and front face (0 different); submesh draws with no GPU draw (0 of
   450,000); two layers sharing a pass buffer (one layer open at a time); copy count (2–4 copies flash, only the
   first copy drawn still flashes); a depth bias on our instanced draws only (still flashes, so not float rounding).
   With the game also drawing (`YW4_SHADOWS_BOTH=1`) it still flashes, so the bands come from our draws, while
   every value they take matches. Also equal (2026-10-24, check mode, 96,000 instanced draws): index count, base
   vertex (always 0), vertex stride, primitive (triangles) and index type. Nothing left to compare on the CPU
   side: the fault is in how our draws run on the GPU. Next: capture a flashing frame (RenderDoc) and find the
   draw that makes the band.
   `YW4_SHADOWS_NO_SKINNED` / `_NO_CUTOUT` / `_NO_INSTANCED` leave those kinds to the game for elimination.

   **Fixed 2026-10-24: the bands were nudged copies; instanced casters are ours again.** RenderDoc can't run the
   draw path (no `VK_EXT_external_memory_host` under it). Instead, a temporary detector (with
   `YW4_SHADOWS_BOTH=1`, so our draws only repeat the game's): the layer copied on the GPU before and after our
   pass, and after each draw in small passes, compared a few frames later. Our draws should change nothing; with
   instanced ours about 100 passes per walk replay changed 1,000+ texels, 0 without. Per draw, each band was one
   instanced draw writing far outside its own box, with copy matrices whose first value was ±100 or more: copies
   the callback nudged (`model+0x218`, flag × 100: fading). In check mode the game never draws a nudged copy with
   the instanced programs we mirror (0 of ~86,000 draws), while our learning, which sees the game's draw only one
   frame in 32, kept the submesh as ours. The per-copy fade program `9904c2` is the one that decodes a nudged
   value (scale `fract(|x|) × 100`, fade `floor(|x|) / 255`); which program, if any, the game uses for nudged
   copies in the shadow layers is not pinned down yet (none showed in the walk replay's check). Ours now leave
   any draw with a nudged pending copy to the game, every frame. Detector after the fix: 0 passes with 1,000+ changed texels (100–999: as few as with no
   instanced draws, edge and rounding noise). Owner's playtest: no flashes. Why the earlier checks missed it: they
   compared only draws the game made with the mirrored programs, which never carry nudged copies.

   **Fixed 2026-10-24: character shadows animated choppier than the characters.** Our skinned draws copied the
   palette from the submesh's own buffer (`palette_of`), which the animation is writing the next pose into: exactly
   the palette of the game's draw in only 45% of 70,000 check-mode draws. The snapshot the model renderer binds to
   vs cbuf 4 before the submesh draw (read at the hook like the copies in slot 11) was exactly the game's in all
   70,000; ours now copy that. Owner's playtest: smooth. (The frame-rate note above was this, not speed: on the
   walk replay our pass costs about the same CPU and GPU as the game's shadows.)
   **Changed 2026-10-24: instanced casters drawn instanced; fading copies ours.** Measured on a quiet machine (walk
   replay, 3 runs each, alternating), our pass with one draw per copy cost more than the game's shadows: game
   work +0.4 ms, GPU +1.1 ms a frame (about 207,000 of our draws where the game made 115,000; and every draw
   compared each pending copy with all the model's, up to 64 × 64). Now an instanced submesh is one draw, as the
   game's: each copy's projection × view × copy × world (the matrices verified before) and its fade go into a
   copies ring (`gpu_shadow_copies`, a storage buffer; `shadow_instanced.vert` / `_cutout.vert` read
   `copy[gl_InstanceIndex]`, the draw's first instance being its first copy), and only the first and last copy are
   checked to be the model's own. The fading programs are ours too (`9904c2` + `b7cd6e`, cut-out `f8951f` +
   `d5f536`: half of what the game still drew): a draw with any nudged copy decodes all of them as `9904c2` does,
   in the same float operations, and drops fragments below the 16×16 dither (fs slot 18; one texture, its handle's
   sampler part changes) in `shadow_fade.frag` / `_cutout.frag`; learned only while the material's own fade (fs cbuf
   3 byte 28) is 1. Texture handles are now traced for slots 0–19. Same measurement after: game work −0.6 ms (avg
   10.9 → 10.3, every pair), p95 −1.2 ms, GPU −0.3 ms; the game draws about 30,000 of its shadow draws per report
   window instead of 73,000. The before/after detector with the game also drawing: 0 passes with 1,000+ changed
   texels, 2 of ~7,000 with 100–999. Screenshots from the same save, game's against ours: differences only from
   animation timing.
   **Changed 2026-10-24: wind-swayed casters ours.** `fa9033` (instanced) and `61ebac` (not), both with the cut-out
   fragment program: the largest share the game still drew. The vertex program moves each vertex in world space
   (after copy x world) by a wind map (vs texture 12, placed by cbuf 6 row 47) giving a height band and bend, and
   two lookups of a wind noise (vs texture 11) scrolled by cbuf 6 row 36 (direction, strength, time), scaled by the
   material (cbuf 7 rows 0, 3) and the vertex's weights (attribute 1); texture coordinates are attribute 2.
   `shadow_wind.vert` does the same operations in the game's order. The constants are read at the submesh-draw
   hook from the bound slots, as the copies (slot 11) and palettes (slot 4): equal to the game's draw in all of
   50,000 checked; the two textures had one id each throughout (handles: the latest learned). A draw is one
   header entry (the four constant rows) plus its copies' copy x world rows in the copies ring. Before/after
   check with the game also drawing: passes with wind draws changed no more texels than the others (0 with
   1,000+, 5 with 100-999 of ~3,700); Vulkan validation clean. The game's remaining shadow draws per report
   window: about 18,500-26,000 (from ~30,000). Walk replay, 3 runs each: game work 9.5 ms against the game's
   shadows' 10.2 (p95 15.0 against 16.4), GPU and process CPU equal; one of the three pairs went the other way,
   so the gain is within run-to-run noise. `YW4_SHADOWS_NO_WIND=1` leaves them to the game.
   **Fixed 2026-10-24: shadows flickered in cutscenes (forest scene), never with the game's shadows.** In
   cutscenes a cascade's job list draws two shadow layers, into two shadow maps (the usual one and a second,
   bound before the second layer starts), and only then the cascade-end job. Ours ended the first layer when the
   second began and dropped its pass (the game's draws of it already skipped): about 70,000 of our draws lost per
   report window, the game's version showing only on the 1-in-32 re-check frames. Now the next layer of the same
   cascade queues the previous layer's pass; a pass draws where the game's draws in its layer went; and when the
   game has moved on to another target, the executor draws the pass into its own layer with the target and state
   (viewport, scissor, depth and polygon state) the game's first draw there used, then restores the game's.
   Restoring only the target was not enough: a few shadows stayed missing. Check mode in the cutscene: all 81,000
   draws per window equal to ours. Owner's playtests: no flicker, identical to the game's shadows.
   **Fixed 2026-11-04: the characters lit in cutscenes, dark once every 32 frames** (worked around since
   2026-11-01 by giving cutscenes back to the game's shadows). After each cascade's first layer the game copies the
   finished layer into the second map with one full-screen draw (fs `6b4575fb57b97548`), and the characters read
   that copy. Our pass for the layer was queued when the second layer started, after the copy, so the copy lacked
   our casters; on the recheck frame the game drew the cut-out caster itself, before the copy, hence the dark frame.
   Now the pass goes in when the game moves to another depth target (`shadow_before_targets`, from
   `nvnCommandBufferSetRenderTargets`). Found with the same-frame A/B (`YW4_AB_PASS=shadow`, which until then had
   compared ours with ours) and its command-order trace (`YW4_AB_TRACE`): the second map went from ~674,000 texels
   beyond rounding to the main map's own 42-204. The workaround is gone; owner watched the cutscene: looks good.
5. Switch the default to `native` once every street, house and battle layer matches; measure CPU.

```

`docs/decisions/0025-pcss-soft-shadows.md`:

```md
# 0025 — Soft contact shadows (PCSS) in the shadow mask shader

<!-- decision
state: accepted
date: 2026-10-25
replaces: none
code: recomp/shader.py
-->

Date: 2026-10-25
Status: accepted (owner picked the approach and the defaults: "put it in the shadow mask shader only"; "4096 and x2
is best")

## The question

With shadow maps at 2048 or 4096 (F8), hard objects (poles, characters) get clean edges but tree canopies turn into a
speckled field of dots; the game's 1024 blur hides that but softens everything. We want both: sharp where a shadow
touches its caster, soft where the caster is far above the ground. That is contact-hardening shadows, PCSS
(percentage-closer soft shadows): find the casters around a point, and blur by how far they are from it.

Where do we add it, and how do we keep it from costing load time?

## What we measured

**The obvious place was too expensive to compile.** The game has ~200 translated shaders that sample shadow maps,
each doing 5 lookups per cascade, up to 27 lookups in one shader. A helper at every lookup made the house take 40-67 s
to load, **even with PCSS switched off**: the driver copies the helper into every lookup and builds pipelines when a
scene first draws them. A tool that times a cold pipeline build per shader (a random string added to the SPIR-V so
the driver's cache can't answer) showed:

| One shader with 27 lookups | Cold pipeline build |
|---|---|
| The game's lookups | 73 ms |
| Helper, 16-tap blocker search + 16-tap filter | 24,600 ms |

Two causes:

1. **`textureGrad(.., 0, 0)` on an array shadow map** compiles about 10x slower on NVIDIA than `texture()`. The
   translator used it to avoid derivatives in branches; the shadow maps have one level, so `texture()` reads the
   same texels.
2. **Any real work per lookup multiplies.** Even a loop-free version (4 gathers + 4 compare taps) stayed 4-25x the
   game's build time; telling the compiler not to unroll changed little.

**Only a few of those shaders matter.** In 80 traced frames only 7 of the ~200 ever draw. One is the game's
**screen-space shadow mask**: a full-screen pass at half resolution (800x450) that shadows everything drawn into the
G-buffer. The other 6 shadow forward-drawn objects.

## Decision

1. **PCSS goes only into the shadow mask shader** (`PCSS_SHADERS` in `recomp/shader.py`, one key today). All other
   shadow shaders keep the game's own lookups and compile as before. Its lookups call `yw4_shadow`: a 16-tap blocker
   search on the raw depth, then a 16-tap filter whose radius is the average caster-to-receiver depth gap times a
   per-cascade scale, clamped between half a texel and 6 texels of a 1024 map (map coordinates, so the size is the
   same at every F8 setting). The game averages 5 lookups per cascade; the first does the work and the other 4 reuse
   it. The compare taps use `texture()` (cause 1).
2. **The raw depth is a second binding of the same image** (`d <slot>` in the shader interface, binding 96 + slot,
   nearest filtering, no compare), and the settings are a small uniform buffer (`p 0`, binding 95) written per draw.
3. **Casters are texels with a smaller depth than the receiver.** The maps are cleared to 1.0. The game samples them
   with a GREATER compare; that only means a result of 1 is "in shadow", not that depth runs the other way (reading
   it that way first made every empty texel a caster and blurred everything).
4. **The mask pipeline is built at start-up** on a background thread with the game's exact pipeline state (it is
   the same in every traced frame). It takes ~0.2-0.3 s cold, done before the first frame; the driver's disk cache
   keeps it, so the game's own build of it later is immediate. Warming it with a stand-in vertex shader did not
   work: NVIDIA's cache depends on the vertex shader and the blend state.
5. **Defaults: 4096 maps with PCSS x2**, the owner's pick after testing the bamboo forest. F8 and F7 switch while
   playing; `YW4_SHADOW_RES=1024 YW4_PCSS=0` gives the game's original shadows. The scale per cascade
   (0.01, 0.005, 0.0025) was set from measured depth gaps: the near cascade covers a thin depth range, so a character
   standing on the ground is a gap of ~0.3-0.5.

## Consequences

- Load times are unchanged; the one extra pipeline is built before the game shows anything.
- Objects the game draws forward keep the game's filter (known-issues.md). Adding PCSS to one of those 6 shaders is
  possible one at a time, each with a start-up build like the mask's.
- Any slow pipeline build is now logged (`pipeline took N ms`), so a shader that stalls a scene shows up at once.
- Cold starts still build every *other* pipeline when first used (~60-75 ms each), as before this change. Shipping a
  list of pipeline states and building them all at start-up would remove that too; not done yet.
- **Screen-space contact shadows were tried in the same shader and removed** (to do, known-issues.md): a short ray
  march toward the sun through the mask pass's depth buffer. That buffer is half resolution, so the real contact
  gaps (thinner than one of its pixels) were never found, and the mixed depths at character outlines read as
  blockers: a ring of dark dots around every character, including Whisper, who floats. A random start per pixel
  added more dots (the game has no temporal blur to hide them). Worth redoing in our own renderer, with
  full-resolution depth and an edge-aware filter.

## Cost at 4K ultrawide, and one search per pixel (2026-10-28)

Measured on the late-game save at 4K 21:9 with full-size effects (per-pass timer): the mask shader took 14.2 ms per
frame with PCSS x2, 13.5 ms with x1 and 1.0 ms off, half of the whole GPU frame. x1 and x2 cost the same, so the
time is the blocker search, not the filter size. The mask shader's lookups (`H0`, `H1`, `H2` in its code) are a
little apart with different references, so `yw4_seen` rarely matched and every lookup did its own 16-tap search.
Now the first lookup's search (its radius, or "no casters") is reused by the others in the same cascade
(`yw4_search_*`, uniform `tune.z`); each still runs its own filter. Mask 14.2 -> 7.6 ms, GPU frame 26.4 -> 19.9 ms.
Checked in one run with `YW4_PCSS_ALTERNATE` (TAA off): old against new differs on no more pixels than two frames
of the same setting do (1.9% by more than 0.05 against 1.8-2.5%), and the differences are on the moving character.
`YW4_PCSS_SEARCH=each` gives the old behaviour.

Where the remaining 7.6 ms goes (same scene): the one search ~3.8 ms, the filters ~2.8, the game's own work 1.0.
The search is slow because its 16 taps spread over 24 texels of the 4096 map with a different disk rotation per
pixel, so neighbouring pixels read different texels and the cache rarely helps (a quarter of the radius saves ~2
ms). `YW4_PCSS_BLOCK=2` shares a rotation per 2x2 pixels: 5.0 ms, 4x4: 4.3 ms, but the noise of the soft edges
gets coarser. The owner played the bamboo forest with 2 and saw no difference, so 2 is the default (mask about
5.0 ms at 4K 21:9, from 14.2 at the start of the day).

```

`docs/decisions/0026-gbuffer-pass.md`:

```md
# 0026 — The second replaced pass: the G-buffer, hybrid first

<!-- decision
state: accepted
date: 2026-10-25
replaces: none
code: runtime/src/gbuffer.c, runtime/src/gpu_ab.c, runtime/shaders/gbuffer_main.vert, runtime/shaders/gbuffer_main.frag, runtime/shaders/gbuffer_frag.glsl, recomp/shader.py
-->

Date: 2026-10-25
Status: accepted (owner: "ok go for it", after choosing a hybrid first and the complete takeover later)

## The question

[frame.md](../frame.md) now maps the main view: the scene geometry is drawn twice (a light pre-pass renderer), first
into the **G-buffer** (layer kind 2), then again with full materials (kind 0, keys 0..2), both by the model renderer
`f_a45890` and its submesh draw `f_a75e90`, the same functions the shadow pass ([0024](0024-shadow-pass.md))
hooks. Materials are mapped too: a submesh's material record, the model's texture table, temporary texture views
the engine makes each draw. Which pass do we replace first, and how far do we go at once?

## What the G-buffer is

One layer on render thread B, ~200 submesh draws in the schoolyard, into 1600×900 with three colour targets and the
scene depth:

| Target | Format | The main program writes |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 0x11 | screen-space motion (this frame's position against last frame's) and depth |
| 1 | 0x25 | zero for most materials |
| 2 | 0x25 | the surface normal (normal map turned by the vertex's tangent frame), and a lighting term in `.w` |

16 programs in that frame. One pair is half the draws: vertex `bc358b` + fragment `a93492` (97 of 195); `bc358b`
with four other fragment programs brings it to two thirds. `bc358b`'s inputs: per-object `cb2` (world in rows 0-2,
this frame's world-view-projection in rows 8-11, **last frame's** in rows 12-15), the view's `cb1`, the material's
`cb3` (UV transform, colour); `a93492` adds the material's `cb7`, the scene's `cb8` and the normal map (slot 1).

## Decision

1. **The G-buffer first, as a hybrid.** The game keeps choosing what to draw; our renderer draws the submeshes it
   can, and the game draws the rest. Each step shows a result and the game stays playable. A **complete takeover**
   (our own selection, materials decoded instead of borrowed) comes after the hybrid is proven, starting with the
   shadow pass (owner: later is preferable). Everything the hybrid builds is part of the takeover.
2. **Hook as the shadow pass does**: the model renderer hook notes a kind-2 layer; the submesh-draw hook decides per
   submesh and, when ours, skips the game's draw. Shared code moves out of `shadow.c` where both need it (the
   selection walk, the object and geometry decoding).
3. **Our draw goes exactly where the game's would** (a `CMD_NATIVE` record per submesh, at first). The G-buffer's
   targets, clears and the state around it stay the game's; our record draws into whatever is bound. Batching
   records comes once it works.
4. **Our own shaders**, one program family at a time, starting with `bc358b` + `a93492`. Written as readable GLSL
   that does what the translated program does, so they can be changed later (resolution, new effects).
5. **Data**: geometry, world matrix, bones and instance copies from the decoded objects (as for shadows). For the
   first stage, **material constants and textures come from the game's bound state** at the hook (the engine has
   resolved them by then: frame.md "Materials"); our matrices are computed by us and checked against `cb2`.
6. **Checking before it is visible**: `YW4_GBUFFER=check` compares our inputs with what the game bound, per draw
   (matrices, buffers, textures), as the shadow pass's check mode does. Then a GPU detector (copy the targets before
   and after our draw, count changed texels) and screenshot differences.
7. **Switches**: `YW4_GBUFFER=game|native|check` (default `game` until it matches), F6 toggles while playing.

## Order

1. Shared hook plumbing for kind-2 layers; check mode for `bc358b` draws (inputs only, nothing drawn).
2. Draw `bc358b` + `a93492` (static meshes); detector and screenshots must show no difference.
3. The other `bc358b` fragment programs, then the remaining static programs.
4. Skinned, instanced and cut-out programs, reusing the shadow pass's decoding.
5. Measure; then plan the takeover (selection first, in the shadow pass).

## Alternatives

- **Complete takeover now.** Needs the game's selection rules (our own selection is what made the shadow streaks in
  0024), every material field decoded and both geometry passes at once, with nothing to compare against until all of
  it works. Rejected for now, not forever: it is step 5.
- **The material pass first.** Same objects, more programs (more varied materials, reads the light buffers):
  harder, and it needs the G-buffer's output to be right anyway.
- **Reuse the game's translated programs with our own draws.** Fastest to get pixels, but it ties our pass to the
  game's constant buffer layouts and gains nothing over drawing through the game; readable shaders of our own are what
  the later improvements need.

## Progress

- **Step 1 (check):** buffers, matrices and last frame's camera match the game on every main-program draw over an
  hour of play (4.9 M draws), once the world matrix comes from the renderer's per-draw scratch record
  (`[sp+0x30]+0x40` at the submesh-draw hook) instead of the object: the object's own matrix is wrong for posed parts
  and for moving objects (the renderer draws a copy taken earlier). Index buffers: 99.88% (to identify).
- **Step 2a (our programs):** `gbuffer_main.vert/.frag` replace `bc358b` / `a93492` in the game's own draws (same
  interface, the game's state and buffers), switched by F6. Within one run, alternating frames
  (`YW4_GBUFFER_ALTERNATE`) and dumping the G-buffer targets, our output is bit-identical to the game's on every pixel
  that did not move between frames. This step went first so that any later difference comes from our data, not our
  shaders.
- **Step 2b (our draws):** `YW4_GBUFFER=native` now records our own draw in place of the game's `DrawElements` for
  every `bc358b` + `a93492` submesh (all 97 a frame in the schoolyard): vertex and index buffers from the submesh
  record, vertex constants 2 computed by us (`=programs` keeps step 2a alone). Material constants, textures, vertex
  formats and targets are still what the game bound. The constants are **bit-identical** to the game's on every draw
  checked once they are computed in the game's order, projection × (view × world), each product summed in order with
  no fused multiply-adds: (projection × view) × world, or fused sums, were off by one last bit on 2-60% of draws
  (found by dumping the inputs of mismatching draws and trying the orders offline). The model renderer spreads one
  vertex over five vertex streams bound to the same buffer, so our buffer goes into each. In one run with alternating
  frames, ours against the game's differs no more than the game's against itself. A draw whose buffers, count or
  index type are not the ones the game was about to draw stays the game's; the 0.12% index buffer mismatches of the
  hour-long check did not occur in the test saves, so check mode now logs the first ones in detail (both addresses,
  the submesh and buffer records) for when they do.
- **Step 3/4 (the other programs, skinned included):** 13 G-buffer vertex programs are ours now, 99.5-99.9% of
  the G-buffer's draws in the schoolyard, the town and the late-game forest; 1e14f9 (an extra row) and a few rare ones
  stay the game's. A table in `gbuffer.c` says where each program reads the object in vertex constants 2: world
  (3 or 4 rows), view × world, projection × view × world, at which rows. The skinned programs keep view × world
  where the others keep the world. Our draw changes only what the vertex program reads, so any fragment program
  behind these goes with it. Check mode compares each program's parts with the game's: bit-identical on all of
  400,000+ draws in the town. Found on the way:
  - The **index buffer** is the geometry's own index buffer object (+0x28), as the submesh draw reads it. It is
    usually, not always, the second object of the vertex buffer's record (+0x68 of it), which step 1 used. The
    shadow pass used the same wrong source; fixed there too (its learning had kept those draws with the game).
  - The step 1 **0.12% index buffer mismatches** were submeshes without indices: the game draws their vertices with
    `DrawArrays`. Ours does the same.
  - A sum that starts from 0 turns the game's −0 into +0; ours starts from the first product, as the game's.
  - The skinned programs' **last frame's view × world** is this frame's on most draws, but on 0.5-30% (by area) one
    of a few fixed matrices that are the same in every area, not the object's history. It is copied from the
    game's bound constants, as last frame's bones are; everything else in constants 2 is computed by us.
- **The lit material pass and the stage layers** (layer kind 0: keys 0..2, and the other key ranges) go through
  the same renderer and submesh draw, so the same hooks take their draws (`YW4_MATERIAL=0`, `YW4_STAGES=0` leave
  them to the game). Their programs joined the table; check mode bit-identical on ~1.2 million draws in three saves;
  ~98-99% of those passes' draws are ours. The A/B for the material pass captures its target at its end
  (`YW4_CAPTURE_LAYER_AT`): ours differs from the game's less than the game's frames differ among themselves.
- **Material constants decoded**: the hook finds the renderer's draw item in its stack, and the material constants
  rebuilt from it (frame.md "Materials") equal the block the game binds, on every draw checked. Not used for drawing
  yet: the game still binds them.
- **Measured** (town walk, 3 alternating pairs): no change, game work 11.07 ms both ways, GPU 12.07 vs 12.03 ms.
  The game still sets up every draw's state before ours; only skipping its submesh draw (the takeover) removes that,
  and the render threads wait most of the time anyway (frame.md: 84%), so the takeover is for what it enables, not
  for speed.
- **Our programs for the G-buffer family**: the five fragment programs behind `bc358b` are one program with
  switches (`gbuffer_frag.glsl`), and the characters' pair (`b742aa` + `b0aa5d`: up to 8 bones, last frame's bones
  for motion, the dithered fade, the rim term) is written out too (`gbuffer_skinned.vert/.frag`).
- **Same-frame A/B** (`runtime/src/gpu_ab.c`, `YW4_AB_AT`): alternating frames can't see faults on moving things,
  so the pass's commands are run twice in one frame, ours and the game's, from the same images, and compared texel
  by texel. Result: **0 texels differ** on every colour and depth target of the G-buffer (schoolyard and town) and
  of the material pass (6 frames), with all our draws and programs. The tool was checked both ways: 0 when both runs
  are the game's, hundreds of thousands when one matrix element is off by 0.01%.
- **The material pass's main programs are ours** (`material_main.vert/.frag`, the game's `046b2a` + `5eb3b2`, most of
  the lit pass): normal mapping, the box-corrected reflection, depth-aware upsampling of the half-res shadow and
  indirect light, the sun's diffuse and GGX-like specular, ambient and reflections from the cube map, fresnel,
  emissive, fog and sky scattering, and the soft-edge blend with what is behind. Same-frame A/B: 0 texels differ
```
