```md
  (schoolyard and town, 4 frames each). The one texel that differed on the first try came from leaving out a
  "times 0" lane: where two neighbours have the same depth the game's value is NaN, and NaN x 0 spreads to the
  other lane; such lanes are kept.
- Bones (constants 4 and 5), textures and the other bound state are still the game's.
- **Every program, without a table (2026-10-26).** The per-program table grew with each new area (75 entries after
  the owner's late-game walk turned up ~60 more programs). The shaders' own headers end it: each program names its
  constant buffers, and slot 2 is the engine's local matrix block (`CBUSE_UB_LOCAL_MATRIX_IDX`) in 717 of the
  game's 757 vertex programs, all with the same members: rows 0-3 `mtxLW` (world), 4-7 `mtxLV` (view × world), 8-11
  `mtxLP` (projection × view × world), 12-15 `mtxLWOld`, 16-19 `mtxLVOld` (last frame's). That is the pattern the
  table had found program by program. `recomp/shader.py` now writes the block's name and the rows each program
  reads into its `.iface`; our draw takes any program whose slot 2 is that block and reads it at fixed rows. Rows
  0-11 are ours, last frame's are copied from the game's bound block (the object's history; ours with the
  takeover). Check mode compares exactly the rows each program reads. Instanced draws come through the same path
  (the game's copies stay bound in constants 11). The shadow pass now takes the renderer's per-draw world too
  (`[sp+0x30]+0x40`): the bamboo forest's stalks are posed parts, and its shadow coverage went from 18% to 89%.

```

`docs/decisions/0027-mit-license.md`:

```md
# 0027 — The project's license: MIT

<!-- decision
state: accepted
date: 2026-10-26
replaces: none
code: LICENSE
-->

Date: 2026-10-26
Status: accepted (owner: "mit sure", after comparing MIT and GPL)

## The question

The repository had no license, so nobody could legally reuse or contribute to it. MIT or GPL?

## Decision

**MIT** (`LICENSE` at the root). It covers our code and docs only: not the game, not files from it, not anything
generated from a player's copy (recompiled C, translated shaders, builds), which never enter the repository
(CLAUDE.md rule 1).

## Why

- No emulator code is linked ([0005](0005-phase1-runtime-strategy.md)), so GPL's main advantage for this project,
  being able to reuse code from the GPL yuzu forks (Eden, Citron, Suyu), is not needed today.
- It matches N64Recomp, the model the project follows, and most recompilation projects.
- What we ship from others fits: musl is MIT, SDL3 (fetched, not committed) is zlib.

## Consequences

- **No GPL code can be copied in** from now on (the yuzu forks included) without relicensing the project, which
  needs every contributor's agreement. CLAUDE.md rule 5 already asks to flag any emulator code before copying it.
  Code under MIT-compatible licenses (MIT, BSD, zlib, Apache 2.0) can be used, with its notice kept.
- Anyone may make closed forks of our code; that was accepted as the price of the simpler license.
- Switching to GPL later stays possible; going back from GPL would not be.

## Alternative

**GPL v3**: forks would have to stay open, and code from the yuzu forks could be reused. Rejected for now: we take
none of their code, and it would rule out MIT-only reuse of ours.

```

`docs/decisions/0028-geometry-in-video-memory.md`:

```md
# 0028 — The game's geometry in video memory

<!-- decision
state: accepted
date: 2026-10-26
replaces: none
code: runtime/src/gpu.c, runtime/src/gpu_passes.c
-->

Date: 2026-10-26
Status: accepted (the owner reported towns at 20-25 frames/s; the fix is on by default, `YW4_VRAM_GEOMETRY=0` turns
it off)

## The question

Some towns in the owner's late-game save never reached 30 frames/s: 20-26, always in the same places and looking the
same way. On the Switch the game needed an overclock for a steady 30, but this is an RTX 4070 laptop GPU. Where does
the time go?

## What we measured

**The slow places were GPU-bound.** Over a 10-minute walk, the slow stretches had the CPU's work at 14-17 ms a frame
and the GPU's at 37-45 ms (a frame at 30 frames/s has 33 ms). Switching our shadow pass, PCSS or our G-buffer draws on
and off changed nothing: the cost was in what every draw goes through.

**A per-pass GPU timer** (`runtime/src/gpu_passes.c`, F5) writes a GPU timestamp at every change of render targets
and reports where each frame's GPU time goes. In the owner's evening street (`work/testsaves/save_base_lag`):

| Pass | Draws | Vertices | GPU time |
|---|---|---|---|
| Lit material pass | 714 | 1,639k | 15.6 ms |
| G-buffer | 643 | 1,603k | 15.5 ms |
| Our shadow pass | | | 5.2 ms |
| Occlusion boxes (240x135) | 283 | 28k | 0.27 ms |
| Everything else | | | about 2.5 ms |

The two main-view passes took ~10 ns per vertex, and grew with the number of draws and vertices, not with what is on
screen. Restarts of the render pass and texture uploads inside them were counted and were not it (1-2 a pass). The
occlusion boxes, small meshes, cost under 1 µs a draw.

**The cause: every vertex came from system memory.** Decision 0021 imports the game's memory pools into Vulkan as
they are (`VK_EXT_external_memory_host`): no copies, the GPU reads the game's buffers where the game wrote them. For
vertex and index data that means reads across PCIe, every frame, for every draw. Fine for small scenes; a street of
houses at 1.6 million vertices drawn twice is not.

## The decision

**Each draw's vertex and index ranges get a copy in video memory** (`runtime/src/gpu.c`, "geometry in video
memory"): one device-local arena of 1 GiB; a range is copied the first time a draw uses it and again only when the CPU
has written one of its 4 KiB pages since (the write generations the pools already keep for textures, from the
host's page write tracking). Draws, the in-place G-buffer/material/shadow draws and our shadow pass bind the copy.

- Copies are made outside rendering, so a draw that needs one ends the render pass first: once, when a model first
  appears.
- **Ranges the CPU keeps writing** (UI, effects: rewritten every frame) are copied a few times, then left in the
  pool, read from system memory as before; copying them every frame would end the render pass at every such draw.
- **When the arena is full** (many areas visited), it is emptied at the start of the next submission, after the GPU
  has finished everything submitted, and fills again from what is drawn: a one-time pause.
- Constant buffers and textures are unchanged (constants are small; textures were already copied into images).

## Result

The same evening street: G-buffer 15.5 → 1.1 ms, material pass 15.6 → 1.3 ms, our shadow pass 5.2 → 2.4 ms, the
frame's GPU time 39 → 12 ms. All four of the owner's slow places (`save_base_lag`, `lag2`, `lag3`, `lag4`) now run
at 29.9 frames/s (the game's 30 cap), 12 ms of GPU time each.

## What it means later

- The GPU has room now: higher resolution and the other enhancements have ~20 ms of headroom in these places.
- The same is likely true of any data the GPU reads repeatedly from the pools (large constant buffers, storage
  buffers): measure first with the per-pass timer.
- The arena's emptying is simple and pauses once; a finer eviction (least recently used ranges) can come if the
  pause shows.

## Addition, 2026-11-13: small ranges are also compared by content

The minimap went blank for one frame now and then while walking. The minimap watch (`runtime/src/gpu_watch.c`,
`python -m tools.dev.minimap`) showed the bad frames had the same draws, programs and textures as their neighbours,
and that in them 76 to 107 of the ~112 minimap draws took their vertices from an old copy (0, 39 and 8 in the frames
before): the image held the icon sheet drawn over the whole map.

The cause is in "copied again only when the CPU has written one of its pages since". Written pages are read once a
frame, at present, and the game writes a frame's UI quads after that. The game hands that vertex memory out as a
ring, so most addresses are new and get a first copy. When the ring comes round to an address that still has a copy,
its pages look clean for one more frame and the draw gets the quad that was there a lap ago: an icon drawn with the
map's full-size quad.

So a range of up to 1 KiB (a quad is 160 bytes) is now also compared by content: a 64-bit FNV-1a of it is kept with
the copy and checked before the copy is used (`geo_print`, `gpu.c`). A mismatch counts as a rewrite like any other,
so such a range is left in the pool after a few. Measured on the owner's late-game save: the case happened over
2000 times in 5000 frames of walking and the watch saw no blank frame (3 in a walk of the same length before);
frame times unchanged. `YW4_GEO_PRINT=0` turns the comparison off.

Larger ranges (models) still go by pages alone: the same gap exists for them in principle (a mesh loaded into
reused memory and drawn before the next present), not seen so far.

```

`docs/decisions/0029-gpu-worker-thread.md`:

```md
# 0029 — Translating command lists on a worker thread

<!-- decision
state: accepted
date: 2026-10-26
replaces: none
code: runtime/src/gpu_queue.c
-->

Date: 2026-10-26
Status: accepted (owner chose it over more small fixes and over the takeover first: "sure go A"; asked whether the
takeover would invalidate it: it doesn't, the takeover's draws go through the same worker)

## The question

After decision 0028 the busy towns were no longer GPU-bound, but the game's work per frame was still 21-23 ms in the
owner's evening street, with spikes past the 33 ms of a 30 frames/s frame. Where does the CPU time go, and what is
on the chain the frame waits for?

## What we measured

The sampling profiler (`YW4_PROFILE`), now able to sample one thread (`YW4_PROFILE_THREAD`):

- **The main thread** runs ~7 ms of game code a frame and waits for the render threads most of the rest.
- **The busiest render thread** (thread 20) waits half of its time too; of its busy time ~55% is the game's own
  per-draw work (the model renderer `f_a45890`, state setup `f_974cd0`, ...) and **~45% is ours**: translating the
  command lists to Vulkan, including the driver's time in our calls.
- Our translation ran **inside the game's `nvnQueueSubmitCommands`**, on the game's render threads, under one lock,
  before the call returned: 9-11 ms a frame across the three render threads, all of it on the chain the main thread
  waits for.

Two small fixes cut it first (dynamic state set only when it changed; textures remember their image: 11.3 → 8.9 ms),
but the frame barely moved: the cost was *where* the work ran, not only how much.

## The decision

**One worker thread of ours runs the translation** (`runtime/src/gpu_queue.c`). The game's submit puts the command
list in a queue and returns; the worker records and submits the Vulkan command buffers in the game's order.

- **Presents** go through the same queue, so a frame is shown after its work; the game's vsync pacing stays on its
  own thread.
- **Syncs.** A fence (`nvnQueueFenceSync`, a window texture's acquire sync) records a *ticket*, the number of jobs
  queued so far, not a Vulkan submission (the work may not be submitted yet). Waiting for a ticket waits for the worker
  to have run that job, then for the Vulkan submissions it had made by then. Nothing the game waits for is signalled
  before its work has been recorded and run, so the game's reuse of command memory, buffers and textures stays safe
  by the same rules as before.
- **Freeing** a memory pool, texture, program or texture/sampler pool goes through the queue, after the queued work
  that may still read it. **Re-setting a program's shaders** first waits for the queue to empty (only while loading).
- Hooks that read the game's data for our passes (shadow.c, gbuffer.c) are unchanged: they run on the game's thread
  at the draw and copy what they need into the command list.
- `YW4_GPU_THREAD=0` runs everything in the caller as before.

What could go wrong, and why it shouldn't: the worker reads the game's memory (texture uploads, constants copied for
shadow quality) a little later than before. By NVN's rules the game may not change memory the GPU will read until the
GPU is done, which our syncs only report after the worker; a game that breaks that rule would race on the Switch too.

## Result

Owner's evening street (`save_base_lag`): game work per frame 21 → 12.9 ms (p99 29 → 22.5), the busiest render thread
38% → 22% of a core, our translation on the game's threads 8.9 → 0.4 ms. Town 9.3 ms, late-game forest 7.2 ms,
schoolyard 9.1 ms, all at 30 frames/s. Same-frame A/B 0 texels differ for the G-buffer (town), the shadow maps (forest)
and the material pass (schoolyard). 45 tests pass.

Not yet checked by a run: cutscenes (replays drift and don't reach them), battles, movies, menus: the owner's playtest.

## What it means later

- The takeover's own draws are records in the game's command lists: they run on the worker too.
- One worker is now the GPU's only feeder. If it becomes the bottleneck (it does ~9 ms a frame in the busy street),
  the next step is splitting a frame's command lists over two workers recording secondary command buffers.
- 60 frames/s needs the game's timing patched as well; the CPU budget (16.7 ms) is within reach in these places now.

```

`docs/decisions/0030-takeover.md`:

```md
# 0030 — The takeover: our renderer does the per-draw work, then the selection

<!-- decision
state: accepted
date: 2026-10-26
replaces: none
code: runtime/src/gbuffer.c, runtime/src/gpu_draw.c, runtime/src/nvn_objects.c
-->

Date: 2026-10-26
Status: accepted (owner: "Take over", then "yes go" to the order below)

## The question

Decisions 0024 and 0026 replaced the game's *draws* in the shadow, G-buffer, material and stage passes: the game
still walks its draw lists, sorts them, binds every material's constants and textures and commits its state, and
only then do we draw in place of its draw call. 0026 put off the complete takeover until the hybrid was proven.
It is proven now (same-frame A/B: 0 texels differ). What do we take over first?

## What we measured

Profile of the threads that submit GPU work, owner's evening town save (`save_base_lag`), 60,000 samples:
81% waiting, ~14% game code. Of that game code, what the takeover removes:

- ~3.5% the model renderer `f_a45890` itself (walk, cull, sort; per-draw state decisions),
- ~6% the engine's per-draw state layer (`f_974cd0`, `f_97aff0`, `f_965eb0`, `f_976ab0`, `f_977e30`, ...),
- ~0.9% the prop-copy callback `f_5f9420`.

The render threads wait most of the time, so frames per second may not move much; what the takeover buys is a
renderer that owns every draw (resolution scaling and the later improvements need it) and less CPU.

## The decision

Two steps, in this order:

1. **Per-draw work first.** The game keeps choosing and sorting what to draw (its selection rules are not decoded;
   our own selection is what made the shadow streaks of 0024). Everything it does per draw becomes ours: textures
   decoded from the model's own data instead of the views the engine makes each draw, render state, which program a
   material uses, material constants (already decoded, 0026), bones. Each piece gets a check mode that compares our
   value with what the game binds, on every draw, before anything is drawn from it. When all of a draw's inputs are
   ours, the game's state work for that draw is skipped.
2. **Selection second**: our own walk, culling and sort, once every draw's data is ours.

## Progress

**Textures: decoded (`material_textures` in `gbuffer.c`, counted by `YW4_GBUFFER=check`).** A material's texture
reference (6 bytes in the draw item's `+0x28` table; byte 0 = entry of the model record's texture table `+0xf8`)
gives a texture resource (0x48 bytes) and an index. The resource's `+0x18` is a Level-5 **G4TX** texture container:
byte `+0x20` images, each with a 0x18-byte record at `hdr + 4×u16(hdr+0xa) + 4×u16(hdr+0x3e) + 0x18×index`
whose first word + 0x18 is the NVN texture the engine made for it (the engine's textures of one container sit in
one array, 0x140 bytes apart, with consecutive texture pool ids). An index past the images is a region of an
atlas: its record (`+0x42` table) starts with the image it lies in, then the region's rectangle.

**Material texture *k* goes to fragment slot *k*.** The engine binds its slot *s* to shader binding *s* (the
program's per-stage table of (slot, binding) pairs: program `[device+0x10d0]+0x2f8`, stage objects
`+0xc8/+0xd0/+0xd8`, table `+0xb8`, count `+0xc0`); the same table lists exactly the slots the shader reads, so the
check compares only those. The shader headers name the bindings: `in_tex0` 0, `in_texNrm` 1, ...; the two-layer
ground material, for example, lists colour, normal, colour 2, normal 2, height, in slots 0-4.

How it was found: first a search for the bound texture inside the resource, which failed, then a probe that only
recorded *where* each bound texture lies relative to each reference, run over four saves (schoolyard, the town walk
replay, the late-game forest, the evening town). One off-by-one in the record index had made the slot order look
scrambled; with it fixed every program followed slot = *k*.

Check mode, four saves, all four kinds of layer (G-buffer, material pass, stage layers, shadows): **all 5.7 million
texture slots read equal ours**, none wrong, none left undecoded (the engine's other table, model record `+0xf0`
when the geometry's `+0x108` is set, would show as a difference: not met).

Still open for textures: the atlas region's rectangle becomes a UV transform in the constants (decoded from the same
record; needed once we stop taking constants from the game).

**Samplers: decoded (`sampler_state`, `sampler_desc` in `gbuffer.c`).** The engine makes a new NVN sampler id for
most draws, so the id means nothing; the settings do. A first probe that looked for the settings in the reference,
texture and UV bytes found no single byte that decides them. The engine's sampler builder (`f_976ab0`, the only
caller of `nvnSamplerBuilderSetWrapMode`) showed the path instead:

- Per texture slot the engine keeps a **15-byte sampler state** (`device+0x1120 + 0xf×slot`). Each layer starts it
  from defaults (`device+0x1300 + 0x1e0×level + 0xf×slot`, level = byte `device+0x4631`).
- A texture reference's byte 1 counts `(field, value)` byte pairs, starting at its u16 `+4`, in the geometry's header
  blob at `4×(u16 +0xa + u16 +0x6e)`; each sets one byte of the slot's state (first 12 references only).
- `f_976ab0` turns the 15 bytes into NVN settings: bytes 1-3 wrap s/t/r; 4 and 5 minification and magnification
  (low 4 bits; bit 4: anisotropic; bit 5: linear between mipmaps); 6 anisotropy; 7, 8 level-of-detail clamp (/255
  ×15); 9 level-of-detail bias (signed); 0xa depth compare function (0: off); 0xb-0xe border colour (/255). The
  device's texture quality settings (`+0x4620` mode, `+0x4624` anisotropy, `+0x4625` on) can raise the filter and
  the anisotropy.

Check mode, four saves, all layer kinds: **all 6.1 million samplers** equal the engine's state byte for byte, and our
settings equal the bound sampler's field for field. The layer defaults are still read from the engine's state (set
once per layer, not per draw).

**Render state: decoded as a block (`render_state`, `effect_id`, `effect_pass`, `draw_state` in `gbuffer.c`).** The
engine keeps the draw's fixed-function state in a 33-byte block (`device+0xeb9`), one byte per field, and turns
changed fields into NVN state at the commit through a table of handlers (`main+0x14d23b0`, one per field; e.g.
`f_979a90` for fields 4-7 and 9: depth test, depth write, depth compare function, stencil). A draw's block is:

1. **The layer's block**, after the layer's own setup (the model renderer sets some fields at its start, and the
   shadow and material layers push one of their own): the newest of the engine's saved copies
   (`device+0xefb + 0x21×(level-1)`, level = byte `device+0x4630`) at the layer's first submesh.
2. **The material's pairs**: `(field, value)` bytes, material record `+4` start and `+0xb` count, in the geometry
   header blob at `4×(u16 +0xa + u16 +0x6c)`. Setting field 20 without 21 and 22 while field 0x14 is 2 also sets
   0x15 = 1 and 0x16 = 2. In G-buffer and shadow layers they count only if they leave field 5 (depth write) set,
   and then field 0x10 is cleared. The engine restores the block after each draw.
3. **The shader pass's pairs.** The material names a **shader effect** (id: per-object overrides in the model
   record's `+0xe8` table, else the model record's `+0x110` table at the submesh's byte `+0x42`). The commit
   (`f_977e30`) picks the effect's pass whose key is the layer's pass key (`device+0x45d4`) and applies that pass's
   own pairs. This is where the material pass gets depth compare "equal" for alpha-tested materials (found with a
   write watch on the field: the only other write was the layer setup). The same pass record also picks the
   programs (next).
4. **The device's settings** at the commit (`f_9759d0`): `+0x4629` flips the cull face, `+0x462a` and `+0x462b`
   clear fields 5 and 0x10, `+0x462d` raises field 0x1c.

Check mode, four saves, all layer kinds, ~4.9 million draws: **every draw's block equals the engine's**. Still from
the engine: the conversion of the block to NVN state (the handlers; we read the NVN state the game binds).

**Effect and program: decoded (`effect_of`, `pass_shaders`).** The effect manager (`main+0x58656e8`) is a set of
plain arrays, read through small virtual methods (vtable `main+0x14deba8`):

- effect by id (from 1): `[mgr+0x10] + 0x28×(id-1)`, the effect object first (`f_a9edf0`);
- the pass record (above) names the stage shader objects: u16 `+4` the vertex shader in `[mgr+0x30]` (0x20 bytes
  each), u16 `+6` the fragment shader in `[mgr+0x78]` (0x10 bytes), u16 `+8` a third in `[mgr+0xc0]`
  (`f_a9ee60`, `f_a9eec0`, `f_a9ee90`);
- a stage object's first word is its shader code, the address our runtime names its translated shader by;
- the engine joins the stages into one NVN program (`f_965880`, cached by the stages' ids); the engine's program
  object *is* that NVN program.

Check mode, four saves: on every draw (about 4.6 million) our effect is the engine's and our vertex and fragment
code are the bound program's. So a material, through its effect and the layer's pass key, names its programs,
its render state, its textures and samplers, all from the game's data.

**Bones: decoded (`bone_palette`).** A skinned submesh's record (model record `+0xc8`, 0x140 bytes) holds three
palettes, 0x38 bytes apart from `+0x70`, which the animation writes in turn; `+0x118` points at the newest, and that
is the one the engine copies into vertex constants 4. The shadow pass had always read the first one (right a third
of the time, hence its copy of the engine's bound constants). A probe first suggested a race (the game "one step
behind" in 12% of draws); it was the probe: a character standing still has the same pose in two buffers, and the
probe named the last match. Check mode, four saves: **every skinned draw** (~390,000) equals ours.

Everything one draw needs from its material is now decoded and checked in four saves, every layer kind:
constants 2 (matrices), material constants, textures, samplers, render state block, effect, programs, bones.
Still the game's: last frame's matrices and bones (motion vectors), the scene's constant buffers (camera,
lights; per layer), vertex attribute formats, the atlas regions' UV transforms. Next: skip the game's per-draw
setup for draws whose inputs are all ours.

**The block as NVN state: decoded (`nvn_state`).** At the commit the engine runs one handler per changed field
(table `main+0x14d23b0`), which writes NVN state objects in its state (`[device+0x10d0]+0x240..0x2f2`): blend
states per colour target, channel mask, colour state, depth stencil, multisample, polygon, plus the stencil reference
and mask and the depth bias as plain fields. Which bytes feed which call is listed at `nvn_state`. We build the same
objects in our own packing (`nvn_objects.c`), starting each layer from the engine's objects for what the block doesn't
drive (the other colour targets' blend states, the colour state's logic op). Check mode, four saves, all layer kinds,
~4.4 million draws: **our objects equal the engine's byte for byte on every draw**. The check was tested by switching
the conversion off: then nearly every draw differs, in every part but the two flags.

**Vertex layout: decoded (`vertex_layout`).** It belongs to the effect, not the geometry (`f_965070`): the effect's
handle in the manager's array lists vertex elements (`+0x10`, u16 `+0x22` of them, 8 bytes: semantic, offset,
stream, NVN format at `+4`), and the pass's program entry (handle `+8`, 0x22 bytes by the pass record's byte `+0xd`)
maps each semantic to the shader's attribute. Each attribute of stream 0 gets a stream of its own (the attribute's
number) over the submesh's vertices with its stride: the five streams on one buffer seen in 0026. Check mode, four
saves: attribute states and strides equal the bound ones on every draw (~4.4 million); no draw had elements on
another stream. Self-test (every offset +4): no draw matches. (A lesson from that self-test: a run that fails to
start leaves the previous log as the newest; the runs now check that a new log appeared.)

**Last frame's matrices and bones (motion vectors).** Constants 2 are now ours in every row:

- last frame's world (rows 12-15) is this frame's world on every draw checked, walking characters too (they move
  through their bones); its bottom row is copied from the record (the game has -0 there on some objects, a last-bit
  difference otherwise);
- last frame's view × world (rows 16-19) is the renderer's record `+0x240`, which **the engine writes during its
  commit**, after our hook: read before the commit it was wrong on ~2% of G-buffer draws (the skinned ones and a few
  others). Our draws read it when the draw is recorded, after the commit. A draw that skips the commit has to compute
  it, or stay with the game while its program reads rows 16-19 (open);
- last frame's bones (constants 5) are the palette before the newest, on 99.6% of skinned draws; the rest have the
  newest there too (not decoded; it only touches motion vectors).

The check counts material constants only in the stages whose shader reads their slot (the shader's `.iface`); the
other stage keeps an older block bound. Summary over four saves, every layer kind: constants 2, material constants,
textures, samplers, effect, programs, bones, render state, NVN state and vertex layout equal the game's on every
draw; last frame's bones on 99.6% of skinned draws.

**What else changes per draw.** Check mode now counts, per layer kind, the constant buffers (only slots the draw's
shaders read, and only when the contents change) and textures the engine binds for a draw beyond what ours
provides: what a draw that skips the engine's work would still miss. Schoolyard, before the model material block:

| Slot | Name (shader headers) | Changes on |
|---|---|---|
| constants 3 | `CBUSE_UB_MODEL_MATERIAL` | every draw (now decoded, below) |
| constants 11 | `CBUSE_UB_USER_DATA01` | 12-30% of draws: instance copies |
| fragment constants 12 | `CBUSE_UB_USER_DATA02` | 79% of material-pass draws |
| fragment constants 10 | `CBUSE_UB_POINT_LIGHT` | ~2% of material-pass draws |
| fragment texture 9 | `in_texCube` | 6% of material-pass draws: a reflection probe per object |

Everything else rebound per draw is the same value again (counts of ~730 per run are once per layer).

**Model material block: decoded (`model_material`).** Constants 3 (0x160 bytes, slot u16 `list+0x74`), built on the
model renderer's stack: `u_ubParam` (1, 0, submesh index + model `+0x1fe`, alpha test reference), diffuse, ambient
and specular from a 0x30-byte colour record (diffuse times the object's colour and a fade: object `+0x1bc` × the
model record's per-submesh `+0x138`, on RGB for additive-style blending else on alpha), the UV transforms and the
atlas regions' rectangles. Check mode, four saves: equal on every draw (~3.7 million); self-test (fade × 1.001):
no draw equal.

**Where the last per-draw inputs come from (measured, not yet ours).** The engine keeps per constant slot the
buffer object it means to bind (`device+0x32c8 + 0x18×slot`, data at `[B+0x40] + [B+0x58]`), set during its walk,
before our hook:

- constants 11 (instance copies): that pending object is the bound block on every draw (walk save): a draw of ours
  can bind it as is;
- constants 10 (point lights): on 87%;
- constants 12 (`USER_DATA02`): nothing pending at our hook; a fresh block is uploaded inside the commit on every
  draw, like last frame's view × world (record `+0x240`). Both come from code the skipped draw would skip; the likely
  source is the per-draw callback the commit calls after choosing the pass (`f_977e30`, `device+0x32c0`);
- texture 9 (`in_texCube`, the reflection probe): changes per object on 6% of material-pass draws, source not found
  in the object, model record or draw item.

So the first draws that can skip the engine's work are those whose shaders read none of constants 10 and 12,
texture 9 or rows 16-19 of constants 2 (most of the G-buffer and shadow layers); the material pass needs the
commit's callback decoded first.

## The first skipped draws (`YW4_TAKEOVER=1`, with `YW4_GBUFFER=native`)

G-buffer layers only, to start. At the submesh-draw hook (`gbuffer.c` `takeover`), a draw whose inputs are all
ours is recorded as one `CMD_NATIVE` (`TakeoverDraw`: buffers, constants 2, program, NVN state objects, vertex layout,
material textures by pool id with their sampler settings, and the model material, material constants and bone
blocks appended), and the hook returns 1: the engine's commit (`f_977e30`: state handlers, program, uploads, texture
views) and its NVN calls don't run for it. The executor (`gpu_draw.c` `gpu_takeover_draw`) puts our program, state,
layout and textures into its state for that one draw and back after, and binds our blocks and samplers in
`bind_stage_set`; targets, scene constants and textures, stencil reference and depth bias stay what the game bound for
the layer.

Left to the game: the first draw of each layer (its commit binds the targets and the scene's constants), draws whose
shaders read per-object data not ours yet (constants 10-12, texture 9, constants 2 rows 16-19, vertex-stage
textures), and anything not resolved (program not seen yet: the registry is learned from the game's own draws, keyed
by vertex and fragment code; texture without a pool entry; sampler state; layout).

Schoolyard: 70% of the G-buffer's draws taken (40,200 of 57,774 per 300 frames); the rest per-object data (17,274)
and first draws (300). Check: with `YW4_TAKEOVER_ALTERNATE=1` (ours on odd frames only) and the G-buffer targets
dumped for 8 frames, ours against the game's differs as much as the game against itself (2,500-10,300 texels, the
running NPC; game against game 2,700-10,000); self-test (projection × view × world nudged by 0.01 in our draws only):
561,000 texels differ, game against game unchanged.

Measured (town walk replay, 3 alternating pairs of runs, `YW4_GBUFFER=native` with and without the takeover; the
periodic summaries after loading, since runs stopped by the time limit write no whole-run summary): process CPU
75.4% → 71.0% of a core, game work 12.50 → 11.94 ms (one slow baseline run; the other two 12.05), GPU unchanged
(6.84 / 6.83 ms). By thread: one render thread (19, the one whose CPU fell: the G-buffer's) 8.0% → 5.7% of a core,
29% less; the others within a point. This is the engine's per-draw state work for ~70% of one pass's draws; the
material pass (blocked by constants 12) and the shadow layers are bigger.

**Extended (b483776): every constant block, instancing, last frame's view × world.**

- Last frame's view × world is the device's derived matrix 10 (`f_977680`, a lazily computed matrix cache at
  `[device+0xe90] + (n-7)×0x40`, dirty bits at `device+18000`; our "record" is that cache): last frame's view (the
  device's matrix 4, `+0x380`) times last frame's world (matrix 6: this frame's). Computed at the hook, bit-identical
  on every draw checked (found with a write watch on record `+0x240`: the writer was `f_976730`, the commit's builder
  of the local matrix block).
- The commit's constant uploads (`f_965eb0`) bind, per stage set (vertex 0, fragment 2) and slot 0-13, the buffer
  object the model renderer left pending (`device+13000 + 0x150×set + 0x18×slot`, size at `+8`), copying it when the
  slot's flag `+0x15` is set: the fresh address of constants 12 on every draw is that copy. The pending block equals
  the bound one by contents on every draw checked (constants 10, 11, 12). A takeover draw now copies the pending block
  of every slot its shaders read except the ones it builds.
- Two faults found with alternating-frame dumps and difference maps (red: ours against the game's; green: the game
  against itself), each class switched off in turn: the characters' rim term (fragment constants 9, the rim settings,
  bound by the commit: our draw had inherited an older block) and the instanced props (tree trunks, a wall): the
  executor drew one instance; the count the renderer leaves (`device+0x45cc`) equals the game's draw on every draw.
  Check mode with the takeover on found no fault in the game's own remaining draws (the engine's caches stay right).
- Check mode now compares constants 2 and last frame's bones as captured at the hook (what a takeover draw uses).

G-buffer draws ours: 86% (schoolyard), 89% (town walk), 91% (late-game forest), 93% (evening town); left: texture 9
or vertex-stage textures or split instances, and the first draw of each layer. Alternating frames: ours against the
game's no further apart than the game against itself.

Copying every pending block cost what skipping the engine saved (town walk, 3 pairs: 77.8% against 75.3% process
CPU). A block that is not a per-draw copy (slot flag `+0x15` clear) and is what the command buffer bound last for the
slot is already in the executor's state: skipping those leaves ~3.2 KB per record. Then: process CPU 76.0% → 72.3%,
game work 12.31 → 11.48 ms, GPU 6.93 → 6.64 ms; the G-buffer's render thread 10.3% → 7.0% of a core (−32%), the
other two render threads and the main thread lower too.

**The material pass joins (texture 9 and every other fragment texture decoded).** The reflection probe (`in_texCube`,
fragment slot 9) is chosen per object after our hook. The engine's slot holds the previous object's probe (right on
93-94% of draws); write watches on the slot led through the draw callback to the texture binder and then to
`f_966120`, which fills the engine's texture slots (`state+0x780 + 0x200×set + 0x10×slot`) from the **pending texture
records** the model renderer left (`device+0x3808 + 0x300×set + 0x18×slot`; fragment set at `+0x3e08`), the same
records material textures go through. So a fragment slot's texture is the pending record's view (its second word,
when the record's int at `+8` is 0) or else the slot's view, the view's first word + 0x18 being the NVN texture; its
sampler the slot's 15-byte state (`slot_texture`). Check mode, every fragment slot the programs read beyond the
material's own (scene textures, the probe): textures and samplers equal on every draw (~3.4 million, two saves).

The commit also loops over consecutive pass records (`u16 +6` of the chosen pass entry), one draw each; a material
with more than one stays the game's (none met so far).

With that, the takeover takes the lit material pass too (layer kind 0, keys 0..2): 85% of its draws in the
schoolyard, 89% in the town walk; the rest read vertex-stage textures or draw split instances, or have a constant
block too big for the record (0.8%). Check mode with the takeover on: every remaining game draw equal. Screenshots of
alternating frames: the difference between neighbouring frames (ours and the game's) is the same share of motion as
in a control run without the takeover (13-15%), and no object stands out as the trunks did.

**Speed, honestly.** Town walk, 3 pairs: process CPU 73.6% → 73.3%, game work 11.62 → 11.83 ms, GPU 6.81 → 7.30 ms:
no gain this time, against −3.7 points for the G-buffer alone an hour earlier; between sessions the same setting
moves 2-3 points, so single comparisons of this size are noise. The sampling profile of the threads that submit GPU
work, same walk with and without: the engine's per-draw functions halve (`f_974cd0` 0.6 → 0.3% of samples,
`f_965880`, `f_965eb0`, `f_966120`, `f_976ab0`, `f_975540`, `f_976730` down too), our hook adds 0.2%, the
renderer's walk (`f_a45890`, kept) 2.1-2.3%; game code in all 7.1% both ways. The per-draw state work the takeover
removes was ~1% of these threads' samples; the threads wait ~90% of the time and the frame follows the main thread.
So the takeover is for owning the draws (what decision 0026 said of the hybrid), and the CPU left on the render
threads is the renderer's own walk: step 2. so in the first run the shadow
and material layers' draws were skipped with nothing in their place. The per-pass counters showed it at once.

## Alternatives

- **Selection first.** Removes the walk, but needs the rules that the shadow streaks showed we don't have, and
  every draw's data still comes from the game: nothing to skip yet.
- **Leave the hybrid.** Fine for pictures, but the engine keeps doing every draw's state work and our renderer can't
  draw anything the game didn't set up (no resolution scaling of materials, no new passes).

**Owner's playtest (late-game save, night town).** With the takeover on: grey untextured characters while circling
the camera, and no glow on street lamps, lit windows and signs; F6 (the game's draws) brought both back. Causes: the
engine registers textures at rising pool ids that wrap, and a takeover draw named a texture by the id of its last
registration, which could name another texture by the time the draw ran (the draw now carries copies of its
textures' pool entries, used only while they still picture the live texture); and the stencil reference, stencil
write mask and polygon offset, set by the commit the takeover skips (`f_974cd0`), were whatever the game's previous
draw left (now from our decoded state). Second playtest (12 minutes): owner confirms everything looks right.

```

`docs/decisions/0031-resolution-scaling.md`:

```md
# 0031 — Resolution scaling of the 3D view

<!-- decision
state: accepted
date: 2026-10-27
replaces: none
code: none
-->

Date: 2026-10-27
Status: accepted (owner: resolution scaling next, before shimmer and before finishing the takeover); off by default
(`YW4_RES=900`), F4 cycles 900 → 1080 → 1440 → 2160 lines

## The question

The game renders its 3D view at 1600×900 and the window shows that picture stretched. How do we render it sharper:
1920×1080, 2560×1440, 3840×2160? And does that need the takeover (0030) at 100% first?

## What we measured (docs/frame.md, "What depends on the screen size")

- **The images.** Everything sized from the screen is a GPU-only render target: 1600×900 (G-buffer, lit pass,
  effects, and the UI, drawn into the same colour image), copies at 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 1/8, ~1/13 of it, and the
  1920×1080 window image, into whose top-left 1600×900 the last pass copies the picture by sampling; the game
  presents that crop. At start the engine makes its targets 1920×1080 first (with copies at 960×540, 639×359,
  480×270), then 1600×900 at the same addresses: it can render at either size.
- **The shaders are resolution-independent.** They read screen images in 0..1 coordinates from interpolated
  positions. The pixel position is used only to tile a 16×16 dither texture (the screen-door fade) or as depth;
  whole-pixel reads hit the same dither texture; size queries return the real size. One constant row is in pixels:
  the camera block's row 32 (1.5/1600, 1.5/900, 0.75/533, 0.75/300), tap offsets of the lit pass's upsample of the
  half-size lighting (215 shaders).
- **No copy commands.** The engine shrinks images by drawing them into smaller ones. Pixel rectangles appear only
  as viewports and scissors (clears are whole-image).

## Decision

Scale at the image level, in the runtime, the way the shadow maps are scaled (F8):

- An image's key carries a ratio (`scale_num / scale_den`; it was a whole number for the shadow maps). Screen-sized
  GPU-only 2D targets (a list of sizes, both chains) are made `height / 900` times larger, rounded to whole pixels.
  One factor for all of them, so the ratios between them (a half-size image read at half the position) hold.
- Draws into a scaled target get their viewport and scissor scaled (from the depth target, or the first colour target
  when there is none: the bloom and UI passes have no depth). Scissors are scaled outward so they cover what they did.
- The window image is scaled too, and the presented crop with it: otherwise the sharper picture is copied into a
  1600×900 corner and squeezed back down.
- Shaders that read camera row 32 get the camera block from a copy with that row times `900 / height` (the same copy
  that scales the shadow filter spread for F8).

**The takeover is not a prerequisite.** Scaling is per image, so the game's own draws scale as ours do. Finishing
the takeover matters for step 2 (our own selection), done pass by pass.

## Results (town walk, RTX 4070 laptop)

| 3D view | GPU per frame | Frames/s |
|---|---|---|
| 1600×900 (the game's) | 6.4 ms | 30 |
| 1920×1080 | 7.4 ms | 30 |
| 2560×1440 | 8.1 ms | 30 |
| 3840×2160 | 9.6 ms | 30 |

The cost grows much slower than the pixel count: the passes are dominated by vertex work (decision 0028). At 900 the
picture is the game's (the code path is the old one with a ratio of 1; screenshots differ between runs only as much
as two runs of the same build do).

## Effects resolution (added 2026-10-27)

The same rule allows what a uniform scale can't: the half-size targets (shadow mask, lamp lights, ambient
occlusion, effects) made twice as large as the rest, i.e. the 3D view's size (`YW4_EFFECTS=1`, panel). Shadow edges
lose their blocky smear. One exception found: the distance blur's two half-size images, whose blur comes mostly from
their low resolution (full size gave +60% distant detail, undoing the blur setting); they are named from the blur's
draws (fragment shaders `b8856cfd2725bc25`, `27b63a2bf65deaf0`) and keep the game's ratio. Bamboo forest, 1600×900:
GPU 6.9 → 8.6 ms; brightness unchanged.

**First playtest: the Yo-kai World's sky went dark with a ghost shape.** Bisected with `YW4_EFFECTS_KEEP`: the
effects' half-size depth. The distance blur's passes draw into its kept half-size images with that depth attached
but unused (depth test and write off), and the viewport was scaled from the depth target: the blur images were
drawn at twice their size, and the blur spread them over everything far. Now the viewport follows the colour target.
One draw does use both: the blur's first copy (`95ea1b`) also copies depth into the half-size depth; with the scales
different it is drawn without depth (logged), since the same copy into a matching target redoes it two passes later,
before it is read.

## Open

- Battles, menus and cutscenes: other screen-sized targets (GPU-only 2D targets of sizes not in the list are logged
  once). The 1920×1080 chain's bloom sizes are not known yet (its 1/8 would be 240×135, the size of the occlusion
  boxes' depth image, which stays unscaled).
- Three shaders hold odd small constants: `4f5854cdab65c4b5`, `5ef1a937fe5a9908`, the compute shader
  `ff9fe0a375532914`.
- The same-frame A/B tool (`YW4_AB_AT`) copies targets texel by texel: not tried with scaled targets.

## Alternatives

- **Emulator-style: scale every render target.** Simpler rule, but it would also scale the shadow maps' own setting,
  the occlusion boxes (culling reads them), the ambient cube and the minimap, for no gain.
- **Our own renderer at a higher resolution, pass by pass.** Needs every pass ours first; the images-level rule gets
  the whole frame now and stays compatible with passes we replace later.

```

`docs/decisions/0032-taa.md`:

```md
# 0032 — Temporal anti-aliasing from the game's own motion vectors

<!-- decision
state: accepted
date: 2026-10-27
replaces: none
code: runtime/src/gpu_aa.c, runtime/shaders/taa_resolve.frag, runtime/shaders/taa_output.frag
-->

Status: accepted, first version (2026-10-27). The owner picked TAA as the next graphics feature, ahead of steadier
shadow cascades (which turned out to need new cascades, not snapping: the game's are perspective-warped).

## Context

FXAA and SMAA (`gpu_aa.c`) smooth the edges of one frame. They can't fix shimmer: thin things (fences, the goal
net, wires, leaves, shadow edges) that fall between pixels differently every frame, so they crawl while the camera
moves. TAA does: the 3D draws are shifted by a different fraction of a pixel every frame, and each frame is blended
into a running history, so a pixel ends up averaging many sample positions.

TAA needs three things: the shift (jitter), where each pixel was last frame (motion), and a place in the frame
before the UI.

**The game already writes motion.** The G-buffer's first target (RG16F) holds each pixel's screen position this
frame minus last frame's, in 0..1 screen units (fragment program `a93492`: current position from the per-object
`mtxLP`, last frame's from the per-object last world and the camera's last view-projection in `cb1` rows 32-35;
decision 0026). The game puts this frame's world in the "last world" slot for most objects, so the motion is
mostly the camera's; moving characters get no motion of their own.

## Decision

1. **Jitter as a viewport shift, only on 3D objects.** `gpu_dynamic_state` adds the frame's shift (Halton 2,3, 8
   positions, in pixels) to the viewport of draws whose vertex program has the engine's local-matrix block in slot 2
   (`CBUSE_UB_LOCAL_MATRIX_IDX`, the 3D objects) into a target of the scene's size. Not through the projection:
   the motion then stays free of jitter (both of its positions come from unshifted matrices), and full-screen passes
   (lighting, the shadow mask, post effects) are not shifted, so they read the G-buffer at the right texels.
   Draws after this frame's TAA (the UI, 23 draws in town) are never shifted. In town ~420-450 draws per frame are.
2. **The motion is copied when the G-buffer pass ends.** The game uses the image for something else later in the
   frame (read at the composite it held other content), so `gpu_taa_targets_end` copies it into our own image at the
   first render-target change after a G-buffer draw.
3. **The resolve goes where FXAA and SMAA go**, after the bloom composite (`58b87f44`) and before the UI, in the
   same reversible perceptual curve (`taa_resolve.frag`): history fetched at the pixel's last position (Catmull-Rom,
   5 taps), clipped toward a variance box of the 3x3 neighbourhood in YCoCg (so disoccluded or self-moving things
   don't leave trails), blended with 10% of the new frame (up to 25% when moving fast). The longest motion of the
   3x3 is used, so the edges of moving things follow them. A frame without TAA in between, a size change or no
   motion this frame starts the history over.
4. **A light sharpen on output** (`taa_output.frag`, `YW4_TAA_SHARPEN`, default 0.5): each pixel pushed from its
   4 neighbours' average, clamped to their range (no rims). Blending frames softens the picture; the owner prefers
   sharp textures.
5. **One option in the existing setting**: ANTI-ALIASING gets a fourth choice, TAA (`YW4_AA=3`). Default AA stays off.

## How it was checked

- `YW4_AA_DEBUG=4` shows the motion (x red, y green, x50): turning the camera gives a smooth sideways field over the
  world, zero on the player and Whisper (they move with the camera), zero in the sky (no G-buffer there).
- Direction of the motion: `YW4_AA_DEBUG=5` shows how far the moved history is from the new frame. Mean over the
  world on a turning frame: signs (+x, -y) 18.8, (+x, +y) 21.6, (-x, ±y) 53, no motion at all 43. (+x, -y) is what
  the code picks from the window origin (upper left).
- The goal net in the schoolyard: without AA it breaks into dots and dashes; with TAA it is a continuous mesh.
- Running player during the town walk: no visible trails.

## Not done yet

- Per-object motion (characters walking on their own get the camera's motion only; the clamp hides the trail).
  The takeover draws know last frame's world for their objects (decision 0030) and could write true motion.
- The GPU cost was not measured on its own (two full-screen passes and one copy per frame).
- Effects drawn without the local-matrix block (particles, some forward-drawn effects) are not jittered: they get no
  anti-aliasing from TAA, but are not harmed either.

```

`docs/decisions/0033-widescreen.md`:

```md
# 0033 — Widescreen: a wider camera, wider screen images, the UI kept 16:9 in the middle

<!-- decision
state: accepted
date: 2026-10-27
replaces: none
code: runtime/src/gpu.c, runtime/src/gpu_draw.c
-->

Status: accepted, first version (2026-10-27). The owner asked for widescreen/ultrawide next ("go wide").

## What we found

**The camera.** The main view's projection in the render state (`device+0x280`, device `main+0x56d8060`) has a
vertical field of view of 45° and 1.358 = 2.41421 / (16/9) across. Write watches led to the engine's camera objects:

| Camera offset | Value in town | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `+0x1a4`, `+0x1a8`, `+0x1ac`, `+0x1b0` | 0.785398, 1.77778, 0.1, 4000 | working field of view, aspect, near, far |
| `+0x1c0` | 1.358, …, 2.41421, … | the projection matrix (16 floats) |
| `+0x2e4`, `+0x2e8`, `+0x2ec`, `+0x2f0` | the same | the settings |

Every frame `f_97f510` walks the engine's camera list (`[main+0x5865720]`, count `main+0x5865728`) and copies each
camera's settings into its working fields. The projection is built from the **setting** `+0x2e8`: writing only the
working `+0x1a8` changed nothing, writing `+0x2e8` changed the projection (1.358 → 1.0347 for 21:9) and the picture
widened. The game's culling follows: objects at the new edges are drawn. A float 16/9 at `main+0x11fdf28` is only a
default that `f_53b3a0` (on-screen markers, it reads camera `+0x2e8`) uses when there is no camera; writing it at
start changed nothing.

**The images.** The screen-sized targets (docs/frame.md: 1600×900 and 1920×1080 with their smaller copies) carry
everything up to the composite; the UI is drawn after the bloom composite into a 1600×900 image; the game's last
draw copies that into one of **two** window images (1920×1080) that it presents in turn.

## Decision

1. **Camera:** a hook on `f_97f510` sets `+0x2e8` of every camera whose setting is 16:9 (or one of our shapes, so
   going back restores them) to the chosen aspect before the copy. The vertical view stays; the sides grow.
2. **Images:** every screen-sized target's width is also multiplied by the shape's factor against 16:9 (`ImageKey`
   `wide_num / wide_den`: 16:10 = 9/10, 21:9 = 4/3, 32:9 = 2). Viewports and scissors across follow it, as do the
   camera block's row 32 tap offsets (x only) and the present's crop.
3. **UI stays 16:9 in the middle:** a draw is UI when, in the same command list, it comes after the bloom composite,
   does not draw into one of the recently presented images (the window copies), and does not read a screen-sized
   image (the copy of the finished 3D picture into the UI image reads one). UI draws keep the game's width and are
   moved to the middle. TAA no longer shifts anything after the composite either (the rule it used, "after this
   frame's TAA by the frame counter", broke when render threads overlap).
4. **Setting:** ASPECT RATIO in the panel: 16:9 (the game's), 16:10, 21:9, 32:9 (`YW4_ASPECT`). The window already
   fits any aspect ratio with black bars.
5. **Full-screen layers are stretched** (added 2026-10-28): a UI draw that covers the game's whole screen is drawn
   across the full width instead of in the middle, so the dimming behind a dialog and the loading screen's black
   reach the sides. The runtime finds them without running the vertex program: the shader translator writes where
   a vertex program's position comes from into its interface (`m <buffer> <rows of x y z w>` when it is one constant
   buffer's rows dotted with input 0, as all four UI programs seen do; `m in` when it is input 0 as it is, the
   full-screen pass program), and `covers_screen` (`gpu_draw.c`) computes the corners of draws with 3 to 6
   vertices. Corners at the edges of clip space (±0.99 or beyond): the whole screen. Then, by the textures it
   samples:
   - a texture of exactly 16:9 shape from the game's files, a picture made for the screen (the copyright notice
     1920×1080, movies: 1920×1080 and two 960×540 planes, the dungeon map's backdrop 960×540): kept 16:9 in the
     middle, and the sides cleared to black first (`vkCmdClearAttachments`). Stretching made the copyright
     notice's silhouettes a third wider (owner: keep pictures 16:9); without the bars the 3D world the game still
     draws behind the bamboo forest's map showed at the sides (owner: black bars);
   - a texture of 16:9 shape the game renders into (a GPU-only memory pool: the map's UI, drawn into a
     1920×1080 image first): kept 16:9 like the rest of the UI, no bars;
   - anything else is stretched; a full-screen pass program only with no texture at all (it also copies images).

   The dimming samples a part of a 2048×2304 sheet and is stretched. The town's fast-travel map needs none of
   this: its tiles are drawn by a 3D model program (local-matrix block) with its own camera, which point 1
   widens, and they come out across the full width, showing more of the town (owner checked, 2026-10-28). The vertex and index reads are checked
   against the memory pools (`gpu_buffer_at`): checking them with `host_readable` (`VirtualQuery`) stopped the
   game at the title screen in every test run, though only reads were added. The cause was not found.

   **Widened 2026-10-31 (the diary):** the save diary's background stayed 16:9 with black sides while other
   menus stretched: its base layer is four quads in one draw (24 vertices) and its bars at the top and bottom span
   the width only. `covers_screen` now takes draws of up to 24 vertices and tells the whole screen (2) from the
   whole width (1); a draw across the whole width is stretched like one over the whole screen, unless it samples a
   16:9 picture (which still gets black bars only when it fills the screen; a band of one stays 16:9 in the middle).
   Checked at 21:9: the diary fills the width with its card and text undistorted; the copyright notice, title
   screen and loading screen unchanged. In a frame whose 16:9 picture got black bars (the map's backdrop), later
   bands across the width stay 16:9 too: the map's bottom bar stuck out into the right bar otherwise. Checked: the
   in-game save diary (D-pad right in town) fills the width, the map keeps its bars with the bar inside them.

6. **The battle's zoom** (added 2026-10-28): at a battle's start the game grows the 3D view in steps of 32×18
   from 1600×900 (1632×918 … 1888×1062, with copies at ½, ⅓, ¼ and ⅛). Those sizes were not screen-sized, so
   they stayed 16:9 and the swirl before the battle stayed at the sides for a few seconds. `zoom_chain` (`gpu.c`)
   makes them screen-sized: widened, but kept at the game's resolution. Making them 4K too ran the GPU out of
   memory within a few battles (`vkAllocateMemory` -2, frames up to 450 ms before it): every step is a new size,
   so a new set of images.

## How it was checked

Schoolyard, standing still and walking: 21:9 is 2133×900 at the 900 setting with the UI centred and the right size;
32:9 3200×900; with TAA at 21:9; the settings panel at 16:9 unchanged. The owner played at 21:9 / 4K (2026-10-28): exploring, battles
and cutscenes work; screenshots in the README.

Full-screen layers (point 5), 21:9 from the Yo-kai World save, screenshots from boot to after the "time changed"
dialog: the loading screen's black and the dialog's dimming reach the sides; the copyright notice, the LEVEL-5
movie, the autosave notice and the diary stay 16:9 with black sides, as before. At 16:10 and 32:9 the loading
screen and the copyright notice behave the same (the dialog had closed by then in those runs). 16:9 is unchanged
(nothing is checked there).

**16:10, the UI fitted (2026-11-11).** 16:10 is the only shape narrower than 16:9 (factor 9/10), so a UI kept at
the game's width stuck out of the image and lost both sides (the HUD and the Yo-kai Pad cut left and right).
Now, when the factor is below 1, `gpu_dynamic_state` (gpu_draw.c) fits the UI to the image's width: across it
takes the image's factor like the 3D, down it is shrunk by the same factor and moved to the middle, with a
45 px strip left above and below at 1600×900. Scissors follow. A whole-screen layer is fitted like the rest (so
its bands stay where the content on them is) and drawn twice more into the strips, showing only its outermost
rows (the layer 8 times as tall with its edge at the image's edge): a plain colour (dimming, loading black or
white) covers the whole image. A 16:9 picture (the copyright notice) gets its black bars above and below instead
of at the sides. The wider shapes take the old branch unchanged. Checked by the owner from screenshots: the
copyright and autosave notices, loading, the town HUD and the Yo-kai Pad.

**16:10, the in-game overlay's frame (2026-11-11).** The overlay (decision 0053) fits its 1600 x 900 design to
the picture's width at 16:10 and centres it, so a strip above and below it showed the game undimmed, with the
side panel and the key hints ending short (owner). Its frame now reaches the picture's edges (`gamemenu_draw`,
gamemenu.c): the tint and the side panel cover the strips, the header and the side buttons sit at the top, Exit
game, the version and the key hints (and Preview's bar) at the bottom; the pages and popups stay centred. The
mouse's click areas move with what is drawn. Checked by the owner at 16:10; 16:9 and wider have no strips and
are unchanged.

**World markers take the full width (2026-11-11).** The owner saw the icons that float over things (the "!"
above a yo-kai, the icon on a pole) drift away from their objects at 21:9, more the further from the middle.
A traced frame showed why: they are not UI. The game draws them after the composite as small quads placed with
the camera's (wide) projection, into the scene's image with the scene's depth attached and the depth test on, so
that walls hide them. Our UI rule kept them at the game's width in the middle like the HUD, which put each one
a quarter of its distance nearer the centre at 21:9 and made the icon as much narrower. Now a draw after the
composite that tests against a bound depth target is left out of the UI rule and gets the image's full width,
like the 3D (`gpu_dynamic_state`, gpu_draw.c). The HUD, the compass and the quest text use no depth and stay
in the middle. Checked by the owner at 21:9: markers on a pole and on a yo-kai sit on their objects. Not
checked: battles, 16:10 and 32:9, and other late draws with depth (a 3D model in a menu would now take the
full width too). The trace key (Shift+F11) records 12000 draws instead of 450: a frame in the forest is over
4000 and the markers come last.

## Not done yet

- 16:10: dialog dimming and battles not checked yet; bars at a menu's edge (the Yo-kai Pad's bottom bar) end
  45 px above the image's bottom, and the strip below shows the layer's edge colour.

- Full-screen layers seen so far: the ones above; the owner checked the Yo-kai Pad and both maps at 21:9 / 4K.
  Other menus (Yo-kai Pad apps, battle results) not checked yet: one of one colour stretches, a 16:9 picture
  gets black bars.
- A 16:9 picture fading in: the bars are black at once while the middle fades.
- At 16:10 the sides are cut, not the top: the vertical field of view is kept for every shape.

```

`docs/decisions/0034-host-cpu-target.md`:

```md
# 0034 — Host CPU target: a setting, the 2003 baseline by default

<!-- decision
state: accepted
date: 2026-10-28
replaces: none
code: recomp/check.py
-->

Status: accepted (2026-10-28). The owner asked for the CPU side to be "very very optimized, or allowed to use
more resources" after battles at 21:9 were mostly limited by the game's main thread.

## Context

The build passed no `-march`, so clang compiled the game code and runtime for the first x86-64 CPUs (SSE2
only): no SSSE3 byte shuffle (`pshufb`, close to ARM's `TBL`/`EXT`), no SSE4.1 lane inserts, no AVX2.

"More resources" in the other sense was checked first and is already the case: every guest thread is its own
host thread with no affinity and no global lock (`runtime/src/kernel.c`). The limit is the game's main
thread, which is serial by design; in the owner's 21:9 battle session the whole process used 55% of one core.

## Decision

`recomp/check.py target_flags()`: `-march` from `YW4_MARCH`, default `x86-64` (every PC). The build and the
instruction checks (`recomp.check`, `recomp.functest`) use the same value, and the build recompiles
everything but musl when the flags change (`work/build/obj/flags.txt`). musl keeps its verified flags.

Results do not depend on the target: `-ffp-contract=off` keeps every multiply and add separate and nothing
reorders floating point. With `x86-64-v3` all instruction forms matched the Pi's results.

## Measured

Benchmark: the Yo-kai World replay (busy street, ~790 draws), 21:9 at 900p so the GPU is not the limit, 3
runs of 160 s; the main thread's CPU per frame from the per-thread reports.

| Build | main thread ms/frame | game work ms |
|---|---|---|
| x86-64 (before) | 7.97 | 11.25 |
| x86-64-v3 | 7.92 | 10.30 |

No gain on the main thread beyond the noise (±0.4 ms): the generated code's shape (registers in memory,
lane-by-lane vector code) leaves the compiler nothing the newer instructions would speed up. Hence the
baseline default. A release could build both and pick at start; not worth it without a gain.

```

`docs/decisions/0035-register-caching.md`:

```md
# 0035 — Guest registers in local variables: tried, off

<!-- decision
state: rejected
date: 2026-10-28
replaces: none
code: recomp/function.py
-->

Status: rejected for now (2026-10-28); the code stays in `recomp/function.py`, off unless
`YW4_CACHE_REGISTERS=1` at translation.

## Context

The skeleton functions `main+0xa77390` / `main+0xa79c00` (bone rotations to matrices, the hottest game code
on the main thread, about doubled at 21:9) are ~550 ARM instructions each and compile to ~12,800 x86 ones.
Every guest register lives in the CPUState, so nearly every translated instruction loads its registers from
memory and stores the result back, and the vector code moves lanes between vector and integer registers.
Other recompilers (N64Recomp) keep registers in locals so the host compiler can hold them in host registers.

## What was done

`cache_registers` rewrites a function's statements after emission: each register it mentions becomes a
local loaded at the entry; registers it assigns are written back to the CPUState before every call, tail
call, return and kernel call, and everything is reloaded after a call. A function with setjmp, or one that
hands the CPUState somewhere unknown, stays as it was. 40,227 of 40,228 functions in main took the new form.
All instruction checks and whole-function tests (`recomp.functest`, against the Pi) passed.

## Why it is off

- **Slower:** main thread 9.3–9.8 ms per frame against 7.97 ms (same benchmark as decision 0034). Most game
  functions call others often; the write-back and reload of every register around each call cost more than
  the locals save in the few math-heavy stretches. The code also grew (a full build took 616 s, not ~300).
- **Hangs at start-up** in 2 of 6 runs: the main thread waiting for a job, the workers waiting for work, two
  threads running with nothing advancing. Most likely a guest wait loop that reads a memory flag set by
  another thread: once the loop no longer touches the CPUState, the host compiler may read the flag once and
  loop on the old value (plain C loads may be moved out of a loop that writes nothing). Not proven.

## If it is tried again

1. A compiler barrier (`__asm__ volatile("" ::: "memory")`) at every backward jump, so a loop reads memory
   again each time round.
2. Use the calling convention: callees keep x19–x28 and the low halves of v8–v15, so those need neither the
   write-back nor the reload around a call; that roughly halves the per-call traffic.
3. Measure with the same benchmark before turning it on.

```

`docs/decisions/0036-native-bone-matrices.md`:

```md
# 0036 — Native skeleton matrices

<!-- decision
state: accepted
date: 2026-10-28
replaces: none
code: runtime/src/bones.c, recomp/overrides.toml
-->

Status: accepted, on by default (2026-10-28). Code in `runtime/src/bones.c`, hooks in `recomp/overrides.toml`.

## Context

`main+0xa77390` and `main+0xa79c00` (twins) turn a skeleton's local bone transforms (scale, rotation
quaternion, translation) into matrices: bone 0 alone, then parent matrix × local matrix for every other bone.
They are the hottest game code on the main thread (about a quarter of its busy time in busy scenes, roughly
doubled at 21:9 in battles). The recompiled versions are ~550 ARM instructions that become ~12,800 x86 ones,
because every register lives in memory (decisions 0034 and 0035: neither a newer CPU target nor caching
registers helped).

## Decision

Hand-written C versions, run by a hook before each function (the hook returns 1, so the recompiled body is
skipped). They use the same float operations, in the same order and grouping, so the results are
bit-identical, not merely close:

- x86 SSE and ARM give the same result for every add, multiply and divide when no NaN is involved (FPCR is 0:
  round to nearest, no flush-to-zero; decision 0008). Addition and multiplication are commutative in IEEE,
  so only the grouping has to match (read from the disassembly).
- NaNs: we refuse inputs with NaN up front (the game's code runs then). Without NaN inputs every NaN comes
  from an invalid operation; ARM gives the default NaN `0x7FC00000`, x86 a negative one, so ours are fixed
  up to ARM's when stored.
- The constants the functions use (a lane mask, the vector for the parent's 4th column, the "usual scale")
  live in `.bss`, filled at start-up, so we read them from memory instead of hard-coding them.
- The rare parts call the game's own recompiled code: `main+0xa77c30` (a bone whose parent has an unusual
  scale, when the caller asks for it) and `main+0xa7a530` (the second function's per-bone extra step), with
  the registers and stack the original would give them.
- Not done natively, decided before anything is written so the game's code can take over: the definition's
  second mode (flag `+0x22` bit 0: tracks non-uniform scale with a bit set and rebuilds bones from column
  lengths with `frecpe`), and parents that don't come before their child.

`YW4_BONES=check` runs the game's code, then ours from the same starting matrices, compares every float and
keeps the game's result. `YW4_BONES=game` turns ours off for A/B timing.

## Why not a recompiler change

A general fix (registers in host registers) was tried and was slower (0035). These two functions are a
known, measured hot spot; a native version costs ~200 lines and can be checked exactly in game.

## Results (2026-10-28)

- `YW4_BONES=check` on all nine test saves (`work/testsaves`: Yo-kai World, school, forest, late game, walk,
  lag 1-4), 2 minutes each: about 10 million calls, **0 mismatches**. The scaled-parent path ran ~350,000
  times and the extra step ~5 million times; the second mode never came up, nor did a NaN input.
- Benchmark (Yo-kai World street, 21:9, 900p, 3 runs each): main thread 7.60 -> 6.45 ms per frame (-15%),
  game work 10.01 -> 8.99 ms.

```

`docs/decisions/0037-bloom-pass.md`:

```md
# 0037 — Our own bloom pass (first post-processing pass)

<!-- decision
state: accepted
date: 2026-10-28
replaces: none
code: runtime/src/bloom.c, runtime/src/gpu_post.c, runtime/shaders/bloom_bright.frag, runtime/shaders/bloom_blur.frag, runtime/shaders/bloom_composite.frag
-->

Status: accepted, on by default (2026-10-28); the settings panel's BLOOM row (F1) or `YW4_BLOOM=game` switches back.

## Context

The renderer plan (0023) replaces the game's passes one by one. After the shadow maps (0024) and the G-buffer and
lit pass (0026, 0030), the owner picked post-processing next. The game's post-processing is two engine functions
(docs/frame.md "Post-processing"): the distance blur `f_8007d0` and the bloom `f_802e40`. Bloom is the smaller and
self-contained one: 8 full-screen draws, inputs and settings all in the renderer object.

## Decision

A hook on `f_802e40(device, renderer)` (runtime/src/bloom.c) reads, from the renderer object, the 9 images the
bloom uses (records 0, 11, 9, 19-24 of its 0x28-byte image table at `+0x2e28`; record `+0x10` is a view whose first
word + 0x18 is the guest NVNtexture) and its settings (`+0x7c0` blur steps, `+0x7d0..+0x7e8` composite,
`+0x7f0..+0x80f` thresholds, `+0x388d` flag), and records one CMD_NATIVE in the device's command buffer. With
`YW4_BLOOM=native` the hook then skips the engine's function: none of its CPU work or draws happen.

The executor (runtime/src/gpu_post.c) draws the same 8 passes with our own shaders (runtime/shaders/bloom*),
written from what the game's programs do, with the same operations in the same order (`fma` where the game
multiplies and adds in one step), the same quad (its corners and texture coordinates as the engine's vertex
buffer holds them, split into triangles like the runtime splits the game's quads), the same viewport (scaled and
flipped as `gpu_dynamic_state` does for the game's draws), sampler and blend (`one`, `one minus source alpha`;
alpha kept). Then anti-aliasing runs as it does after the game's composite.

Not copied: the translated game shaders (game-derived output, never committed). Ours are hand-written.

## How it is checked

`YW4_BLOOM=check`: the engine draws its bloom as usual; our pass, recorded just before, draws the same into
copies of its 7 images and of the scene. After the game's composite (before anti-aliasing) both versions of
all 8 images are copied out and compared texel by texel when the GPU is done; a `yw4: bloom: check frame N`
line per checked frame (every 300th, or `YW4_BLOOM_CHECK_AT`). It must say 0 differ on every image, on every
test save, before ours becomes the default.

## The one thing that differed

The first check matched on most frames, but on some about 20 texels of the smallest level (and a few in the
scene) were one low bit off. Inputs and constants were equal (logged). The cause was the sampler: the game's
allows mip levels (min filter 3, levels 0-15), so the runtime's texture filtering setting (`YW4_ANISO`, default
16) turns on anisotropic filtering and blending between levels for it, and our plain linear sampler didn't
have that. With `YW4_ANISO=0` both matched exactly; now our pass makes its sampler from the game's settings
through `gpu_sampler`, the way the game's draws get theirs, and matches with any setting.

## What skipping the engine's function leaves out

Most of what `f_802e40` changes is the engine's record of what is bound (texture slots, constant buffers, the
program, the render state stack, pushed and popped). It is deliberately not recreated: none of the engine's bloom
commands are sent either, so its record and the game's command stream still agree, as they were before bloom;
setting the record alone would make the engine skip bindings the GPU never got. What it changes that is not a
binding is done by the hook: the device flag `+0x45da` bit 0, the bits in `+0x45ac` for every image it reads
(0x12 or 0x10 by the record's `+0x22`/`+0x23`), and its draw statistics (`+0x4654`, `+0x4658`).

## Results

`YW4_BLOOM=check` on all nine test saves at 4K 21:9 (the owner's settings), four frames each in the scene
(1800-2700): 0 of 564 million texels differ. Native runs load and play like the game's; the game's own draws drop
by its 8 bloom draws. (A run's draw count also depends on where the replay ends up: ~165 or ~300 in the Yo-kai
World replay, either setting.)

## Open

- Then the distance blur the same way; then improvements as options (more levels at 4K, a smoother bloom).

```

`docs/decisions/0038-distance-blur-pass.md`:

```md
# 0038 — Our own distance blur pass

<!-- decision
state: accepted
date: 2026-10-28
replaces: none
code: runtime/src/dof.c, runtime/src/gpu_post.c, runtime/shaders/dof_copy.frag, runtime/shaders/dof_blur.frag, runtime/shaders/dof_composite.frag
-->

Status: accepted, on by default (2026-10-28); the settings panel's DISTANCE BLUR PASS row (F1) or
`YW4_DOF_PASS=game` switches back.

## Context

The second post-processing pass after bloom (0037). The engine's distance blur `f_8007d0(device, renderer)`
(docs/frame.md "Distance blur") shrinks the scene into a half-size image, blurs it in rounds (across, then down,
`renderer +0x868` times: 1 in town, about 10 in a battle the per-pass timer caught, ~4 ms at 4K 21:9) and blends it over the scene
by depth. Our runtime already changed it from the outside: the panel's DISTANCE BLUR (half or off) and the effects
resolution (its images keep the game's size ratio).

## Decision

The same structure as bloom. A hook on `f_8007d0` (runtime/src/dof.c) reads from the renderer object its image
records 0 (scene), 9 and 10 (the half-size pair) and 42 (the G-buffer's depth), the rounds, the blur radius and
spread, and the camera's near/far and focus settings, and computes the constants as the engine does:

- the Gaussian weights of `f_7f3620`: `expf(-k²/2r²)` for k = 0..7 over twice their sum, in float, summed left to
  right, with the same `expf` (the sdk's is musl 1.1.19's, which the runtime already uses for the game: decision
  0013), so the weights are bit-identical;
- the composite's 8 fragment constants from near, far and the focus settings, with its divide-by-zero guards.

The executor (runtime/src/gpu_post.c, shared with bloom) draws the shrink, the rounds and the composite with our
shaders (runtime/shaders/dof*), written from the game's programs' operations in their order: the 16-tap blur with
its pairwise sums, and the composite's depth to distance to amount, the 4-neighbour edge rule, and the discard. The
quad, viewport, samplers (colour: min 3 / mag 1; depth: min 2 / mag 0; both through `gpu_sampler`) and blend
(`source alpha`, `one minus source alpha`; alpha written) are the game's. The composite reads the camera's far
distance from the camera block the game has bound, as its program does. The panel's DISTANCE BLUR setting is
applied by our pass (half: the amount constant halved; off: no composite), and its images still keep the game's
size ratio.

Left to the game's function: the variant with `renderer +0x2c70` set (a depth-aware shrink with a lookup texture
and a different composite; not seen yet, logged when it is), and a depth record without its descriptor.

## How it is checked

`YW4_DOF_PASS=check`, like bloom's: ours into copies of the two half-size images and the scene, compared texel by
texel with the game's after its composite. `YW4_DOF_CHECK_AT=<frames>` picks the frames. All nine test saves at 4K 21:9 with the half setting, two frames
each in the scene: 0 of ~29 million texels differ per save (bloom's check, run alongside, still 0 too); the
school save at the game's full setting: 0. The +0x2c70 variant did not come up.

## Open

- The +0x2c70 variant, when it shows up.
- ~~Fewer, wider rounds in battles~~: done, see below.

## Addendum 2026-10-29: the battle blur, and BATTLE BLUR fast (on by default)

The blur that costs GPU time in battles is not this pass and not the shared rounds `f_7f3620` (an earlier
commit assumed so: probes in a battle showed `f_7f1bf0`, `f_7f3620` and `f_7f3900` never run there). It is a
render job of its own, `main+0x897d90(device, job)`, queued by `main+0x89ac00` from `main+0x311f40`, with its own
loop: a copy into target `job+0`, then n rounds (across into target `job+2` attachment 4, down into its attachment
2, the same Gaussian weights, radius `job+0x10`), then back. Job: u16 `+0` / `+2` targets, f32 `+4` strength,
`+8` / `+0xc` spread across / down, `+0x10` radius, i32 `+0x14` rounds at most; n = (uint)(strength x (max - 1) + 1),
each step spread x strength / the image's size. It plays as a battle starts: strength ramps from 0.06 to ~1.5 in
about a second (1 to 17 rounds, radius 2, max 12), then the pass stops.

BATTLE BLUR fast (`YW4_BLUR_FAST`, panel PERFORMANCE): the hook hands the game's job a copy with m = ceil(n / 4)
rounds, strength 1 and the spreads times strength x sqrt(n / m). Blurs add up by their widths squared, so the
total width stays the same for a quarter of the passes; the game still draws it with its own shaders. Measured
in battles: ~0.16 ms per pass either way, so at 12 rounds 24 passes (~3.8 ms) become 6 (~1.0 ms). Not identical
texel for texel (the 8-tap kernel's ends fall differently), so it was judged by eye: the owner saw no difference
at battle start, and it is on by default (`YW4_BLUR_FAST=0` for the game's rounds). The same option also gives
`f_7f3620`'s rounds (our executor, `YW4_BLUR_PASS`) a quarter of the passes when they have more than two.

```

`docs/decisions/0039-fsr-upscaling.md`:

```md
# 0039 — Upscaling with AMD FSR

<!-- decision
state: accepted
date: 2026-10-29
replaces: none
code: runtime/src/gpu_fsr.c, runtime/src/gpu.c, runtime/src/gpu_aa.c, runtime/shaders/aa_depth_upscale.frag, tools/yw4/deps.py, recomp/build.py
-->

Status: accepted, first version (2026-10-29). The owner chose FSR (option A below) for higher frame rates at 4K,
after 60 frames/s and no limit came in (the game moves by measured time, `runtime/src/framerate.c`).

## Context

At the owner's settings (5120×2160, 21:9, PCSS, effects full) the RTX 4070 laptop is 97-98% busy at ~125 W: the
GPU limits the frame rate (~59 frames/s with TAA). Most of that time scales with the pixel count of the 3D
(soft shadows 29%, the game's surfaces and lighting, full-size effects). Drawing the 3D smaller and rebuilding
a full-size picture is the largest single lever. The UI must stay full size and sharp.

The game draws the 3D at 1600×900 and the UI into the same image, then copies it 1:1 into the window image
(decision 0031): there is no stretch of its own to replace.

## Options considered

| Option | For | Against |
|---|---|---|
| **A. AMD FSR SDK 2.4.0** (signed DLLs, Vulkan) | Newest, no shader build of our own; FSR 4 on the AMD GPUs it supports; frame generation later from the same package | Windows only (DLLs); released the day before |
| B. FidelityFX SDK 1.1.4 | Mature, full source | No FSR 4; a Windows-oriented build of its own |
| C. FSR 2 from source (GLSL) | Builds everywhere like our shaders | Older quality, no frame generation |
| Our own TAA upscaler | Cheap (~1 ms), no dependency | Softer than FSR; still to do |

Licence (checked in the archive, `Kits/FidelityFX/docs/license.md`): files not listed there fall under AMD's
binary licence (no reverse engineering), but the listed ones are MIT, and the list names everything we use: the
API and upscaler headers and `amd_fidelityfx_loader_vk.dll` / `amd_fidelityfx_upscaler_vk.dll`. MIT fits the
```
