```md
project (decision 0027). Nothing of the SDK is committed: `tools/yw4/deps.py` downloads the source archive
(pinned SHA-256), extracts only those headers and DLLs into `work/deps/fsr-2.4.0/`, and `recomp/build.py` copies
the DLLs next to `yw4.exe`.

## Decision

1. **FSR as an anti-aliasing mode** (`YW4_AA=4`, panel ANTI-ALIASING: FSR), at TAA's place: after the bloom
   composite, before the UI. Same inputs as TAA (decision 0032): the 3D draws shifted per frame (FSR's own
   jitter sequence, applied as a viewport shift), the game's motion copied when the G-buffer pass ends, plus the
   scene's depth. The colour goes in through the anti-aliasing's reversible curve (perceptual, 0..1, so FSR is
   told it is non-linear) and comes back through its inverse. `runtime/src/gpu_fsr.c` loads the DLLs on first
   use, makes a context per size pair, and falls back to TAA when FSR can't run.
2. **Upscaling as two resolutions** (`YW4_UPSCALE`, panel UPSCALING: off / quality 1.5× / balanced 1.7× /
   performance 2×, greyed out unless the anti-aliasing is FSR). `gpu.c` gives the 3D's screen-sized images the
   render height (output / ratio) and two kinds the output height: the presented window images, and the scene's
   colour and depth images from the anti-aliasing point until the present. Those two are named by address: at
   the anti-aliasing point the address starts to name a second, output-sized image, so the game's UI draws and
   its final copy land at full size without knowing. All the game's shaders read screen images in 0..1, so the
   3D needs no change; the camera row of tap offsets uses the render height.
3. **The depth is stretched too** (`aa_depth_upscale.frag`): the draws after the anti-aliasing point include world
   markers (the "!" above people) that the game hides behind what stands in front. Without depth they showed
   through walls and from afar (owner, 2026-10-29).
4. **Texture bias** while upscaling: drawn smaller, the 3D would pick smaller mip levels where fine patterns (the
   schoolyard's goal net, the perforated high fence) average out to a flat colour. Mipmapped, non-comparing
   samplers of the draws before the anti-aliasing point get log2(render / output) − 1 (AMD's recommendation;
   quality −1.58, performance −2).
5. **Device features**: 16-bit floats, 16-bit storage, 8-bit ints and subgroup size control are enabled where the
   GPU has them, for FSR's fast shader variants.
6. **Version 3.1.6** (the DLL's default on NVIDIA). It also offers 2.3.4 (`YW4_FSR_VERSION=2.3.4`): ~20% cheaper,
   but it turns the high fence into wavy moiré where 3.1.6 leaves fine grain.

## Results (late-game save, bamboo forest, 5120×2160 21:9, owner's settings, one run switching modes)

| Mode | 3D drawn at | frames/s | FSR's own cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| native + TAA | 5120×2160 | ~59 | (TAA 1.4 ms) |
| FSR, no upscaling | 5120×2160 | ~46 | ~6.6 ms |
| FSR quality | 3413×1440 | ~75 | ~4.5 ms |
| FSR balanced | 3013×1271 | ~86 | ~4.0 ms |
| FSR performance | 2560×1080 | ~104 | ~3.7 ms |

FSR's cost follows the output's size, so it shrinks little with the mode. Checked with 1:1 crops: the UI is as
sharp as native in every mode; a running character stays sharp (a faint 1-2 pixel edge on a moving leg, no
trail); objects close to the camera, which the game fades with a dot pattern, become smooth transparency.
Fine high-contrast patterns below a render pixel (the perforated fence at performance) come out grainy:
ruled out as causes were history resets (1 in 900 frames), motion (FSR's debug view), the jitter's signs (all
four alike), missing jitter (320-560 draws shifted per frame) and the camera distances given to FSR. This is the
known limit of the hand-written FSR versions; machine-learned upscalers do better there.

## Not done yet

- Our own TAA upscaler (the cheap option), and DLSS for NVIDIA RTX GPUs (licence and linking to check first).
- Linux: no FSR DLLs there; TAA is used.
- Per-object motion (decision 0032's open item) would help FSR with characters that move on their own.
- The camera's real near/far and field of view for FSR (placeholders 0.1 / 1000 / 45°; no visible effect).
- Whether the fence's own draws get the per-frame shift (decode one frame's draws).
- Testing switches: `YW4_FSR_DEBUG`, `YW4_FSR_DEBUG_VIEW`, `YW4_FSR_LOG`, `YW4_FSR_TEST_RATIO`, `YW4_FSR_MV_SIGN`,
  `YW4_FSR_JITTER_SIGN`, `YW4_FSR_NEAR` / `YW4_FSR_FAR`, `YW4_FSR_SHARPNESS`, `YW4_FSR_MIP_BIAS` (docs/debugging.md).

## Fix 2026-11-10: the game's second full-size image

Upscaled pictures (FSR and DLSS alike) had looked no sharper than a plain 1.5x stretch of the native frame
(owner: "very bad graphical downgrade"). The upscalers were fine. After the anti-aliasing point the game draws a
few UI draws into the scene image, then copies the scene into a second full-size image (`0x72664e3000`), draws
most of the UI there and copies that one into the window's image. Only the scene's colour and depth were treated
as output-sized, so the second image stayed at the render size: the upscaler's 4K result was shrunk to 1440p and
stretched again by the present. Found with a synthetic hard-edged input: the upscaler's own output had 1-pixel
edges, the screenshot of the same frame 4-5-pixel ramps; a GPU trace showed the 2560x1440 target between the
3840x2160 scene and the window image.

Now every full-size screen image (the 1600x900 or 1920x1080 layout, not presented) drawn into after the composite
is output-sized too until the present (`gpu_upscale_also`, `runtime/src/gpu.c`, called from `begin_rendering` in
`runtime/src/gpu_draw.c`). Same-run sharpness at 4K 16:9 (Laplacian variance, bamboo forest): DLSS quality 21 ->
46 (native 62, plain stretch 18), FSR quality ~16 -> 97 (native 137); the UI is sharp in upscaled modes too. 21:9
with DLSS frame generation and the Vulkan validation layer: no errors. Not yet checked with upscaling: battles,
menus, cutscenes. Found by a Fable 5.2 session; the earlier mip-bias fix (per draw) was right but not the cause.

## Fix 2026-11-15: black blurred stills (issue #10)

With upscaling on, the blurred still behind the pause menu, battle transitions and results and the capsule scene
was black. The game keeps the last finished picture in a full-size image (`0x7271d7f000`, `0x72725ef000` seen) that
it draws once, after the composite, and then only reads for many frames. `gpu_upscale_also` named such images
output-sized only until the present, so from the next frame on the reads found the render-sized image under the
same address, which nothing ever draws into. A probe of reads at the render size of images once named output-sized
showed them on the frames after each still was drawn (with and without an anti-aliasing point in the frame);
keeping the names only across frames without one was not enough.

Now the named images stay output-sized (`upscaled_more`, 8 slots, the oldest replaced when full) until one is drawn
into before the composite (a 3D target: the engine reuses addresses, `0x72664e3000` was named at frame 0 and is a
3D target later; `gpu_upscale_drop`), becomes the scene's colour or depth, or upscaling is off. Cost: those images'
render-sized twins stay in video memory until the 300-frame eviction. Checked with DLSS quality at 1080p (the
reporter's settings: pause menu, a battle, no render-sized reads left) and 4K (bamboo forest, same spot: sharpness
66.3 before, 67.0 after). Not checked: FSR, other ratios, 21:9, frame generation, the capsule scene.

```

`docs/decisions/0040-dlss-upscaling.md`:

```md
# 0040 — Upscaling with NVIDIA DLSS

<!-- decision
state: accepted
date: 2026-10-29
replaces: none
code: runtime/src/gpu_dlss.c, runtime/src/msvc_shim.c, runtime/src/window.c, tools/yw4/deps.py
-->

Status: accepted, first version (2026-10-29). Added after FSR (decision 0039) because FSR turns fine patterns
smaller than a render pixel (the schoolyard's perforated fence, far goal nets) into grain at performance; a
machine-learned upscaler handles those better. The owner's GPU (RTX 4070 laptop) runs DLSS.

## Context

The upscaling plumbing from 0039 (two resolutions, the scene image named by address after the anti-aliasing
point, the depth stretch, the texture bias) takes any upscaler with FSR's inputs. DLSS takes the same: the smaller
3D picture, its depth, motion and the per-frame shift.

Two questions before building: the licence, and whether NVIDIA's library links with our compiler.

- **Licence** (NVIDIA RTX SDKs licence, `LICENSE.txt` in the SDK): proprietary. The SDK may be distributed only
  inside an application in object code, not reverse engineered, and not made subject to an open-source licence:
  so nothing of it is committed to this MIT repository; `tools/yw4/deps.py` downloads the needed files at a pinned
  tag, each checked against its SHA-256, and whoever builds accepts NVIDIA's terms. Applications using DLSS must
  credit NVIDIA (the settings panel's option text and the README do). Notifying NVIDIA is required only before a
  commercial release.
- **Linking**: the NGX library (`nvsdk_ngx_d.lib`) is built with MSVC; llvm-mingw has neither MSVC's runtime nor
  its C++ library. Linking a test showed it needs only twelve runtime pieces: `runtime/src/msvc_shim.c` supplies
  them (MSVC-named new/delete, `_fltused`, the /GS cookie and check, two GS exception filters, two STL error
  functions, thread-safe local statics); empty stand-ins satisfy its default-library requests. It throws no C++
  exceptions.

## Decision

1. **DLSS as anti-aliasing mode 5** (`YW4_AA=5`, panel ANTI-ALIASING: DLSS), next to FSR, from the same inputs
   (`runtime/src/gpu_dlss.c`). The colour goes in through the same reversible curve (DLSS told it is not HDR) and
   DLSS works out its own exposure. Jitter: Halton 2, 3 with 8 × ratio² positions, as NVIDIA suggests. Upscaling
   modes map to DLSS's: none = DLAA, quality, balanced, performance. When DLSS can't run (no NVIDIA RTX GPU, an old
   driver, a build without the SDK), FSR takes over, then TAA.
2. **Vulkan**: on NVIDIA GPUs, `window.c` enables the device extensions NGX lists (`VK_NVX_binary_import`,
   `VK_NVX_image_view_handle`, `VK_KHR_push_descriptor`; the old `VK_EXT_buffer_device_address` is left out where
   the core feature exists, because NGX allocates with the core feature's flag). Also enabled while there:
   `shaderDemoteToHelperInvocation`, which shaders compiled for Vulkan 1.3 need for `discard` (the validation
   layer flagged it).
3. **The model**: DLSS's defaults are its transformer models (K for DLAA/quality/balanced, M for performance).
   On this GPU at 5120×2160 output they cost 5.3 and 7.4 ms. The CNN model (preset E, marked deprecated in the
   SDK but working in the pinned DLL) costs 2.6 ms, less than FSR (3.7-4.5), and looks nearly as clean on the
   fine patterns. So a panel row DLSS MODEL: FAST (preset E, default) or BEST (the transformers);
   `YW4_DLSS_PRESET=<letter>` forces one for tests.
   **Changed 2026-10-31: the transformers only, the row removed.** The CNN makes shadow edges flicker: the
   character's shadow, standing still in the forest, has 4-6% of its edge pixels flickering over 16 frames with
   it and 0% with the transformers; the same in the build that brought DLSS in (02120ba), so not a regression.
   The owner saw it too and chose the clean picture over the CNN's speed. `YW4_DLSS_MODEL=0` keeps the CNN for
   tests.

## Results (bamboo forest, 5120×2160 21:9, owner's settings, one run switching modes)

| Mode | DLSS fast | DLSS best | FSR 3.1 |
|---|---|---|---|
| none (DLAA / FSR native) | ~53 | - | ~46 |
| quality | ~81 | ~66 | ~75 |
| balanced | ~93 | ~73 | ~86 |
| performance | ~112 | ~71 (M) / ~88 (K) | ~104 |

Native with TAA: ~59. Schoolyard walk, 1:1 crops: where FSR leaves the perforated fence as grain, both DLSS
models show a clean, regular pattern (not as round as native's holes); the goal net stays more structured.
No Vulkan validation errors.

## Not done yet

- Linux: NVIDIA ships `libnvidia-ngx-dlss.so`; the build fetches only the Windows files so far.
- The transformer models' cost may suit a desktop GPU better; not measured on one.
- The jitter and motion signs were taken over from FSR and look right in still and moving shots; switches to
  flip them for tests: `YW4_DLSS_JITTER_SIGN`, `YW4_DLSS_MV_SIGN`.

```

`docs/decisions/0041-frame-generation.md`:

```md
# 0041 — Frame generation

<!-- decision
state: accepted
date: 2026-10-29
replaces: none
code: runtime/src/gpu_fg.c, runtime/src/gpu_dlssg.cpp, runtime/src/gpu_aa.c, runtime/src/gpu.c, runtime/src/window.c
-->

Status: accepted, first versions with AMD FSR and NVIDIA DLSS (2026-10-29).

## Context

In busy places the game's own CPU work limits the frame rate (~70 frames/s at the owner's 4K 21:9 settings,
`docs/known-issues.md`): upscaling frees the GPU there but can't add frames. Frame generation makes a picture
between each two of the game's from their motion and depth, so about twice as many are shown. It adds about half
a frame of delay (the game's frame waits while the generated one is on screen), so it suits a game that already
runs at 60 or more.

Both vendors' kits normally replace the window's swapchain and present on their own. Ours draws our HUD and the
settings panel onto the window image at every present (`window.c`), and the game's picture is copied, scaled and
letterboxed into the window there.

## Options considered

| Option | For | Against |
|---|---|---|
| **A. FSR without its swapchain** (`FFX_FRAMEGENERATION_FLAG_NO_SWAPCHAIN_CONTEXT_NOTIFY`): FSR writes the generated frame into our image, we present and pace | Our present path stays; HUD and panel drawn sharp onto each frame; any GPU | Our own pacing (a thread) |
| B. FSR's frame-interpolation swapchain | AMD's pacing | Replaces our swapchain and present; the HUD and panel would be interpolated or need its UI hooks |
| C. DLSS frame generation first | NVIDIA's quality | RTX 40 and newer only; Streamline and Reflex to integrate first |

## Decision

1. **A, FSR first** (owner: FSR, then DLSS). The FSR package we fetch for the upscaler has the frame generation
   DLL (`amd_fidelityfx_framegeneration_vk.dll`, MIT like the rest we take).
2. **Where:** FSR's prepare pass right after the anti-aliasing (`gpu_aa.c`), with the 3D's depth, the game's
   motion and the jitter as the upscaler gets them; so frame generation needs anti-aliasing TAA, FSR or DLSS
   (only they copy the game's motion). At the present (`gpu.c`) the game's finished image is copied into one of
   two slots and FSR makes the generated frame into the same slot (`runtime/src/gpu_fg.c`).
3. **Pacing:** a host thread presents the generated frame at once and the game's frame half the game's frame time
   later (smoothed over ~10 frames). The main thread only hands the slot over, so it never waits for the half
   frame; it waits only when both slots are still to be shown. While frame generation is on, the window doesn't
   wait for the monitor (mailbox or immediate present).
4. **A HUD-less copy keeps the menus still.** The game draws them into the 3D's image, then copies that into the
   8-bit window image it presents. Without help FSR moved the menus with the 3D's motion (doubled HUD and minimap
   when the camera turned). Right after the anti-aliasing (before the menus) the 3D's picture is now blitted into
   an image in the presented format, at the place in it the window shows (the window image is larger than the
   picture: 1920×1080 around 1600×900 at the default resolution): the conversion the game's own copy makes,
   identical to the presented frame outside the menus. FSR gets it as `HUDLessColor` and keeps the menus still.
5. **sRGB:** the game presents `B8G8R8A8_SRGB`, which has no storage use. Our slot images are made in that format
   with a UNORM view too; FSR is told UNORM, so it reads and writes the encoded bytes (its sRGB transfer function)
   and the window's copy decodes them as it does the game's.

6. **DLSS frame generation** (setting 2) runs through NVIDIA Streamline 2.14.16 (`runtime/src/gpu_dlssg.cpp`, C++
   because Streamline's headers are; the build compiles `runtime/src/*.cpp` with the same clang, no exceptions or
   RTTI, so no C++ runtime library). Unlike FSR it owns the present: Streamline sits between us and Vulkan, puts
   its generated frame in at `vkQueuePresentKHR` and paces both itself, so our pacing thread is not used.
   - Started before the Vulkan instance on every PC with an NVIDIA GPU (asked through DXGI, as Vulkan can't be
     asked yet; `YW4_STREAMLINE=0`: never), so DLSS-G and Reflex switch while playing. Loaded with both off it
     cost nothing measurable (busy spot: 81.7 against 80.2 frames/s, within the noise). Every Vulkan function then
     comes from `sl.interposer.dll`'s `vkGetInstanceProcAddr` (Vulkan's own,
     Streamline's for instance and device creation, where it adds its extensions and an optical-flow queue, the
     surface, the swapchain and the present). Its manual hooking mode (only those few from it, the rest from SDL's
     loader) crashed in `sl.common` during `vkCreateDevice` on a null function pointer.
   - `sl.interposer.dll` is loaded at run time; its core functions are reached through pointers, and our
     definitions of them forward there so Streamline's inline helpers work unchanged.
   - Per frame: a frame token, Reflex's sleep and the markers (always, as NVIDIA asks). Reflex's low-latency mode
     is the REFLEX setting (off by default, on, on + boost) and at least on while DLSS-G is chosen (NVIDIA requires
     it; the panel row is greyed then). Where the CPU limits the frame rate it costs frames (busy spot: ~14%);
 after the anti-aliasing the 3D's depth and the game's motion are tagged with the camera constants;
     before the present the game's rectangle in the window image is tagged as the backbuffer subrect (black bars
     copied as they are).
   - The game's camera matrices aren't known: a projection from the 45° field of view the FSR code uses, the
     camera motion taken as part of the game's motion vectors (it is).
   - The swapchain is made again when the player switches DLSS-G on or off (NVIDIA's guidance: without it the
     frames still go through DLSS-G's off-screen copy while it's off), and its image list is read in two calls
     (count, then images): Streamline's version returned bad handles for one call with room for 8.
   - Menus and loading screens (no 3D tagged) pause DLSS-G with `eRetainResourcesWhenOff`: its memory stays and
     the swapchain isn't made again. Until 2026-11-02 each pause freed everything and made the swapchain again;
     switching back on then rebuilt DLSS-G inside the next `vkQueuePresentKHR`: a 185-230 ms hitch at every menu
     closed (owner's 10-minute session: all 9 frames over 120 ms), ~57 ms more on opening one, plus 13-43 ms per
     swapchain. Now the worst of those frames is ~50 ms (most 13-22 ms) and nothing in the session passes 80 ms.
     When the player switches it off, `slFreeResources` gives the memory back, as NVIDIA's guide asks.
   - Its HUD-less copy: DLSS-G works on the window image (the game's picture scaled into it, black bars, our HUD
     and panel on top), so the HUD-less copy is made the same way: the picture before the UI blitted into a
     window-sized image at the same rectangle with the same filter, in the present's own submission, tagged with
     the backbuffer's rectangle. Walking through town (only generated frames shown,
     `YW4_DLSSG_SHOW_GENERATED=1`, captured from the screen): the HUD, minimap and text stay sharp, and running
     characters keep clean arms and legs.
   - DLSS-G stops generating while the window isn't focused (Streamline's own rule): background test runs need
     the window brought to the front.

## Results

Busy late-game spot (`save_base_busy`), RTX 4070 laptop, unlimited frame rate: every game frame got a generated
one. At 4K 21:9 with DLSS performance ~63 game frames/s, ~126 shown (~70 game frames/s without frame generation:
FSR's frame generation takes ~7 ms of GPU time per frame at 5120×2160, so the GPU is nearly busy). Generated
frames checked in screenshots against the game's at the same spot: same brightness, no broken areas.

DLSS frame generation, same spot and settings, window focused: 2 frames shown per game frame (Streamline's
count), ~75 game frames/s, ~150 shown; our queue's GPU time 6.3 ms (DLSS-G's own queues aren't in that number).
Its generated frames can't be screenshot by us (Streamline makes them after our present).

The HUD (F3) shows the frames on screen in a SHOWN line under FPS (the game's): FSR's share of frames with a
generated one, DLSS-G's own count.

Walking through town with FSR, the generated frames sit between the game's (camera turns, the road, poles and
trees move half way); the menus stay still with the HUD-less copy. A character's arms and legs can come out
doubled while they swing: last frame's bones are right (the palette ring moves on every frame, measured), so
this is where FSR blends instead of moving the pixels.

## Not done yet

- Objects moved by their world matrix (not bones) have only the camera's motion; a history of each object's world
  is in `gbuffer.c` (`YW4_OBJECT_MOTION=1`), off until objects sharing a model get keys of their own.
- The game's real camera matrices for DLSS-G (from the G-buffer pass's constant buffers).
- Frame generation off in menus and loading screens (NVIDIA's advice).
- The FRAME RATE setting counts the game's frames; what is shown is about twice that.
- Linux: no FSR DLLs there yet.

```

`docs/decisions/0042-button-icons-and-mouse.md`:

```md
# 0042 — Button icons that follow the device, and the mouse
<!-- decision
state: accepted
date: 2026-10-30
replaces: none
code: runtime/src/bindings.c, runtime/src/window.c
-->

Status: accepted, first version (2026-10-30). Icons checked in game for all four styles; the mouse camera and
switching devices while playing still need the owner's test.

## Context

The game's text and HUD show Switch buttons. On a PC the player uses a keyboard and mouse, or an Xbox,
PlayStation or Nintendo controller, and may rebind every input (CONTROLS page, F2). The icons should show what
the player actually presses.

The game still has the PC build's pieces: five icon sheets in `data/nx/font/font.cpk` (PlayStation, Xbox,
keyboard and mouse, the game's own, Switch), all loaded at start, and a camera path for mouse movement in the
field camera (`f_846260`) that the Switch build never feeds.

## Findings

- **Icons.** Text names an icon by a Switch tag, e.g. `[$gaiji_bt02_s000]`; command tags such as `<CMD_BACK>`
  become such tags through `menu_nx_gaiji_config.cfg.bin`. Each frame `f_a8c3f0(sheet, _, requests, count)`
  draws, for one sheet, the requests whose name it finds there, if the sheet's byte `+0x1c` is set; a request is
  0x38 bytes with the CRC-32 of the icon name at `+0`. The sheets are listed at `[main+0x58654f8]`.
- **Which btNN is which button.** The config file lists its 35 entries in Sony's pad bit order (select, L3, R3,
  start, up, right, down, left, L2, R2, L1, R1, triangle, circle, cross, square): bt09, bt11, bt12, bt10, the four
  D-pad icons, bt06, bt08, bt05, bt07, bt01..bt04. The game's text agrees (`bt05` + D-pad = the L shortcuts), and
  in game the PlayStation sheet's bt06/bt08/bt07 show L2/R2/R1 where the Switch shows ZL/ZR/R.
- **Variants.** `key_all_s100` / `s200` and `lst_`/`rst_` `s100`/`s200` are the left-right and up-down forms
  (text: "switch screens with L/R or `key_all_s100`"); the PlayStation and Xbox sheets name them `key_lr`,
  `key_updwn`, `l_lr`, `l_updwn`, `r_lr`, `r_updwn`. Their sticks are `gaiji_l` / `gaiji_r`, not `lst` / `rst`.
- **Mouse camera.** At `main+0x846bac` the camera reads a movement from `+0xcc`/`+0xd0` of its pad state; if it
  is nonzero and camera input is allowed (`+0x4ba`, `+0x4bb` both 0) it turns by it, scaled by the game's mouse
  camera speed (`main+0x56b9130`), instead of by the right stick.

## Decision

1. **Swap names, not pixels.** A hook on `f_a8c3f0`, before it runs for sheet 0, switches the PlayStation or
   Xbox sheet on and replaces each Switch button's CRC with the icon of what is bound to that Switch input now:
   the first bound key that has an icon, or the bound controller button by its position, in the connected
   controller's sheet (a Nintendo controller keeps the Switch sheet and its style suffix). The game's own name is
   remembered per request address, so a request swapped once can be swapped again when the device changes even if
   the game doesn't rewrite it. Groups (a whole stick, the whole D-pad) keep the Switch icon in keyboard mode: the
   keyboard sheet has no icon for a set of keys. Keyboard icons for punctuation and numpad operators are left out
   until someone looks at the sheet (`gaiji_symbolNN` / `gaiji_num_euNN` are not named by key).
2. **Hooks inside a function.** The recompiler's hooks only ran at a function's start (0024). A `[[hook]]` with
   `at = "<offset>"` now runs the native function just before that instruction, also when a branch lands there;
   its result is ignored, and that function keeps its registers in the CPUState (no 0035 caching) so the hook sees
   them. The mouse hook writes the window's movement since the last frame there, every frame (nothing else clears
   it), and drops it while the game locks the camera.
3. **Mouse as input.** The window takes the mouse (relative mode) at start and on a click; Alt and the settings
   panel give it back. Clicks count only while the game has the mouse, and the click that gives it back is not a
   press. Mouse buttons and the wheel can be bound, but the defaults stay keys only (Enter and Escape stay A and B).
4. **Keyboard or mouse first (2026-11-13).** With keys and mouse, an input's icon is its first bound key, else its
   mouse button; in battles the mouse comes first (the owner attacks and aims with the mouse there, so the hint
   shows the mouse button, not the U and O keys bound to the same inputs).
5. **The PlayStation middle buttons (2026-11-13): two cells' pixels after all.** The game ships only a PS4 sheet;
   its select-position icon (bt09, the Switch's Minus, auto battle in battles) is the PS4 touchpad, the wrong
   button on every PlayStation pad: Create on a DualSense, Share on a DualShock 4, Select on a PS3 pad; and its
   start-position icon (bt10) says OPTIONS, which a PS3 pad calls Start. No icon in any sheet shows those, so
   swapping names can't help. `bindings_patch_sheet` rewrites the two cells in the game's memory: the pad's word
   over a pill in the style of the sheet's Options icon (the owner picked the look from mockups). Rows 0-23 are our
   drawing as BC7 blocks (`gaiji_create.h`, made by `python -m tools.yw4.gaiji_create`); rows 24-47 are the Options
   icon's own, read from the same texture, so no game pixels are in the repo. The sheet is found before its first
   upload (`gpu.c` `upload`) by a fingerprint of the touchpad cell's blocks; the hint hook rewrites the cells when
   the PlayStation model changes (SDL's pad type; `YW4_PS_MODEL` for tests) and calls `gpu_note_written`, after
   checking they still hold what it wrote. Our own screens follow the model too: the Controls page's names, and on a
   PS3 pad (no touchpad) the overlay opens with Select + Start. Nintendo pads use the Switch sheet, which is right.
6. **Xbox 360 pads (2026-11-13).** The Xbox sheet has View and Menu, right for Xbox One and Series pads; a 360
   pad's buttons there are Back and Start, marked with a left and a right triangle. For a pad SDL reports as a 360
   one, the middle 6 x 4 blocks of the two circle icons (x 12-35, y 16-31; the circle's edge stays the game's) get
   our triangles (`gaiji_create.h`), and the game's own middles, kept when the sheet is found (the View icon's
   fingerprint), go back for other pads. The Controls page then says Back / Start and the overlay hint shows the
   triangles. Known limit: many third-party pads (and Switch-style pads in X-input mode) report as a 360 pad and
   get the triangles too; `YW4_NINTENDO_LAYOUT` still gives the latter the Switch icons.
7. **The touchpad as a menu pointer (2026-11-14).** A DualSense sends finger positions over Bluetooth too (SDL
   switches it to its full reports; checked with `tools.dev.padtest`). While one of the game's menus (decision
   0057's mouse menus) or our overlay is open, the first finger moves the cursor like a laptop trackpad (from where
   it is; lift and drag again), and the touchpad click chooses: a click at the cursor in the overlay, the left
   button in a game menu. The owner's picks: trackpad, not the pad as the whole screen; click, not tap or Cross.
   The cursor really moves (`SDL_WarpMouseInWindow`), so both menu paths take it as the mouse with no new code;
   that motion still counts as the controller's, so the overlay's hints stay on the controller. Elsewhere the
   click still opens the overlay; in menus it opens and closes with Create + Options (Share + Options on a PS4
   pad), which the overlay's hint then names. `YW4_TOUCHPAD_SPEED` scales the movement (one stroke across the pad:
   55% of the window's width; 90% was too quick). While the touchpad moves it the cursor is a see-through grey disc
   with a white edge, like a console's pointer (the owner's pick from mockups), 3% of the window's height; the
   arrow comes back when the mouse moves.

## Rejected

- Copying keyboard pixels over the Switch sheet's cells at upload: works without knowing the draw code, but can't
  follow the bindings or switch between controller makers.
- Mapping mouse movement to the right stick: no game change needed, but a stick is a speed, so the camera would
  drift on after the mouse stops and feel floaty.
- Editing the generated C by hand (what the first draft of this did for the mouse hook): lost at the next
  `recomp.translate`.

```

`docs/decisions/0043-mods-layeredfs.md`:

```md
# 0043 — Mods: a mod's romfs laid over the game's (LayeredFS)
<!-- decision
state: accepted
date: 2026-10-30
replaces: none
code: runtime/src/romfs.c
-->

Status: accepted, first version (2026-10-30). The English patch runs: the copyright warning and the town's quest
marker ("Head to Mt. Wildwood!") show in English.

## Context

The English translation is a Switch mod in Atmosphère's layout:
`contents/010086c00af7c000/English Patch/romfs/...`, 2.4 GB. Atmosphère's LayeredFS merges it with the game's RomFS:
a file at the same path replaces the game's, a new path is added. Our runtime already builds the game's RomFS
image itself from the owner's extracted `romfs/` folder at start (decision 0014), so a mod can join that build.

What the patch contains (measured against the owner's 2.2.0 romfs with `tools/yw4/cpk.py`):

- 8 replaced files: 7 rebuilt `.cpk` archives (`text/text_all.cpk`, `menu/menu.cpk`, `effect/effect.cpk`, four
  `ev_item` ones) and `data/cpk_list.cfg.bin`, the list of which file lives in which archive;
- 3,085 new loose files at paths that are inside archives in the base game (2,316 text, 714 menu, 49 effect, ...).

Its `cpk_list.cfg.bin` names the same files as the game's (none added or missing) but has fewer entries: the
game reads a file listed there from its archive and any other from the folder, so the loose files are what it
reads. 487 of them differ from their copy inside the patch's own `text_all.cpk`. The patch needs no change inside
an archive: whole-file replacement is enough.

## Decision

`romfs.c` scans the game's folder into its tree as before, then lays each mod's `romfs/` folder over that tree
(a same-named file takes the mod's path and size, new files and folders are added), then builds the image as
before. Reads need no change: each file is read from wherever its path points.

- Where: `YW4_MODS=<folder>`, default `work/mods`, `none` for no mods. Inside it, Atmosphère's layout
  `contents/010086c00af7c000/<mod>/romfs` or simply `<mod>/romfs`. Several mods go in name order; a later one wins.
- The log names each mod with its count of replaced and added files.

## Rejected

- Replacing single entries inside `.cpk` archives: the patch doesn't need it, and it would mean rebuilding
  archives or answering reads from inside them.
- Copying the patch into the owner's `romfs/` folder: changes their dump, no way back without a second copy.

```

`docs/decisions/0044-shadow-mask-pass.md`:

```md
# 0044 — Our own shadow mask program
<!-- decision
state: accepted
date: 2026-10-30
replaces: none
code: runtime/shaders/shadow_mask.frag, runtime/src/shadow_mask.c, runtime/src/gpu_draw.c, runtime/src/gpu_ab.c
-->

Status: accepted, on by default (2026-10-30); the settings panel's SHADOW MASK row (F1, DEVELOPER OPTIONS) or
`YW4_SHADOW_MASK=game` switches back.

## Context

The lighting stage is the next piece of the renderer to become ours (docs/frame.md "Lighting stage"). Its most
expensive pass is the shadow mask `f_7f3e90(device, renderer)`: one half-size draw (program `98c09b`/`06d03ad7`)
that works out per pixel how much sun reaches the surface, from the cascaded shadow maps, with our soft shadows
(decision 0025) inside. Its algorithm was decoded from the NV assembly first (frame.md, six steps).

## Decision

A readable fragment program, `runtime/shaders/shadow_mask.frag`, with the translated program's interface
(bindings, input, output), swapped in for `06d03ad7` in the engine's own draw (gpu_draw.c, like the G-buffer's
programs of decision 0026). The draw, its inputs and its target stay the engine's; only the program is ours. It
has its own switch (runtime/src/shadow_mask.c), not the G-buffer's. Its pipeline is built at start-up with the
game's (no first-use stall).

The same-frame A/B (gpu_ab.c) checks it: a hook on `f_7f3e90` records the markers around the engine's function
when `YW4_AB_PASS=shadowmask`, so in the frames of `YW4_AB_AT` the pass runs with ours and then with the game's
program from the same images. `YW4_AB_SHOW=<n>` lists the differing texels.

## Not bit-exact, accepted

Every operation is the game's, in its order (fma where it fuses, the signs made from two integer compares, an if
instead of an early return). Yet at the late-game save at 4K 21:9 a frame has 2-4 of 2.8 million texels that
differ by one bit of the 11-bit result with soft shadows off, and ~130 with them on (a hair's change tips the
blocker search, so a few pixels differ more: 0.38 against 0.21 lit at one). The control (the game's program both
times) gives 0, and the soft shadows' debug views show the compare depths themselves differ by an ulp at a few
pixels while the positions match. Splicing the game's translated code into ours section by section only moved
the differences around; both are compiled by the same glslang with the same options. So the driver optimises the
two equivalent programs a little differently.

Other options were: mark the arithmetic `precise` in both programs (likely exact, at some GPU cost, and changes the
translated game program), or keep reshaping ours to the driver's choices (no end in sight). The owner judged the
differences not visible (single scattered half-size pixels, like the soft shadows' own grain) and chose to accept
them, unlike the earlier passes, which are exact.

## Cost

The same as the game's: at the late-game save the mask took 2.54 ms per frame against the game's 2.62 (300-frame
averages of `YW4_GPU_PASSES`), with the frame's GPU time 12.4 ms either way.

## Speed-ups (2026-10-30)

Two switches in the panel's SPEED-UPS rows, off by default until the owner has compared the look in game:

- SOFT SHADOW FILTER (`YW4_MASK_FILTER=once`): with soft shadows on, the game's five lookups (points less than a
  texel apart) are each a 16-tap filter; one lookup at the centre covers the same ground.
- SOFT SHADOW SEARCH: the blocker search with every other tap of its disk. Always on since 2026-11-18 (below);
  the row and `YW4_PCSS_SEARCH_TAPS` are gone.

The mask at the late-game save, 4K 21:9, soft shadows x2, 4096 maps (300-frame averages): the game's program
2.62 ms, ours as the game does it 2.54, filter once 1.48, filter once and search 8 1.23. Both depart from the
game's result, so the A/B no longer applies with them on.

Also, always on: pixels facing away from the sun (the result is 1 whatever the lookups find) and fully faded ones
(the result is 0) skip the lookups. The same result (the A/B against the game's program unchanged: 125-128
texels), ~0.1 ms less: ours 2.45 ms, with both speed-ups 1.09. Less than hoped: few pixels face away at the
late-game save, and a group of pixels the GPU runs together only saves when all of them skip.

Owner's verdict in game (2026-10-31): SOFT SHADOW FILTER FAST looks the same, so it is now on by default
(`YW4_MASK_FILTER=five` for the game's); SOFT SHADOW SEARCH 8 looked the same but put small shadow blobs on some
objects (a thin caster missed by the halved search gives a pixel a different softness), so it stays off.

Revisited 2026-11-18 (owner's call): SOFT SHADOW SEARCH 8 is now on by default (`YW4_PCSS_SEARCH_TAPS=16` for the
full search). It saved 0.70 / 0.43 / 0.33 ms of the mask at 4K in the late-game, busy and owner's-progress saves
(16 vs 8, the owner's settings, `YW4_GPU_PASSES`), and screenshots at the same frame, cropped into the shadows (leaf
shadows on paving, the characters' feet, foliage), show no blobs and no other difference. The later mask changes
(one search per pixel, explicit level 0) likely took the blobs away; which one was not checked.

Removed 2026-11-18 (owner's call, the same day): the 16-tap search and its row. The owner compared 16 and 8 at a
sunlit crosswalk in game (F12 screenshots: no difference), and the day and night A/Bs above matched. The shader
searches with 8 taps always; a `YW4_PCSS_SEARCH_TAPS=16` line left in a settings.ini is no longer read (the game
reads only settings with a row) and drops out at the next save, so players who chose 16 are on 8. The translated
game program (Shadow mask: Game) never had the option and keeps its 16.

## Next

Owning the program lets the shadow mask improve: contact shadows for small details the cascades miss (done: decision 0045),
and the mask at full size instead of half.
```
