`docs/decisions/0045-contact-shadows.md`:

```md
# 0045 — Contact shadows
<!-- decision
state: accepted
date: 2026-11-01
replaces: none
code: runtime/shaders/shadow_mask.frag
-->

Status: accepted, on by default (2026-11-01); the settings panel's SHADOWS > CONTACT SHADOWS row switches
them while playing, `YW4_CONTACT=0` at start.

## Context

The cascaded shadow maps (4096 texels, decision 0025's PCSS) can't resolve small, close detail: a tap over a sink,
the gap under a wall's cap or a balcony, the leaves inside a hedge shading each other. Owning the shadow mask
program (decision 0044) makes room for a screen-space fix in the same draw.

## Decision

In `runtime/shaders/shadow_mask.frag` (`contact_shadow`, `contact_smoothed`), for each half-size pixel that can use
it (in a cascade, facing the sun), march 12 steps over 0.3 view units (about 30 cm) from the surface toward the sun
(cb12 row 0) across the half-size depth. The march projects with the inverse of cb8 rows 20-23, which carry the
anti-aliasing's shift (`cb8_scaled_copy`), so it lines up with the shifted depth. A step that lands behind the
picture by more than a hair and less than the thickness is a hit: the mask (how much is in shadow) becomes
max(shadow map's result, 1 - t²) for the hit at ray fraction t.

Settings go to the program in the 4th vec4 of the YW4PCSS block (binding 95, now 64 bytes):
steps, length, thickness, debug.

## What it took (each found in game by the owner, then fixed)

- **Dots** (a random start per pixel): the four pixels of a 2x2 block march a quarter step apart and share their
  results through quad swaps (`subgroupQuadSwap*`), averaged with depth-aware weights: four times the steps for the
  price of one, no blur across outlines. Pixels that don't use the result (sky, past the last cascade, facing away)
  skip the march and are left out of the average: the first version marched every pixel and cost 0.77 ms.
- **A band on the ground beside posts:** filtered depth reads blended the post and the ground into a depth nothing
  has; the march reads texels (`texelFetch`). A hairline stayed: rays passing behind a post's side, whose screen
  depth says nothing about its thickness. Hits where the blocker is seen almost exactly edge-on (|n·v| < 0.15) don't
  count.
- **The line under a wall's cap faded as the view turned:** two earlier fixes for the post (skip hits beside the
  pixel; drop a hit when the ray comes out in front again) also removed the cap's line, which is a texel or two tall
  from afar and which rays leave over the cap's top. Both are gone. The thickness is 0.07 but widened by 1/|n·v|
  (at most 4x) for slanted faces, whose depth spreads over more of the view.

## Limits

Screen space only: nothing off screen or hidden casts. It is not ambient occlusion: darkness under benches and in
corners (light from the sky blocked, not the sun) needs SSAO, next on the list.

## Cost

The shadow mask pass at 4K 21:9: +0.04 ms at the late-game save (much in shade), +0.25 ms in the sunny schoolyard
(1.08 → 1.34 ms, owner's run with F5).

Measured again 2026-11-02 with full-size effects (the mask at 2560×1080, the owner's settings) in the bamboo forest:
about 0.85 ms (`YW4_MASK_BREAKDOWN=1`: the mask 3.60 ms as set, 2.76 without contact shadows), well over the
figures above, which were at half-size effects or in shade.

2026-11-18: every pixel marched, the sky and everything past the last cascade included, and threw the result away
there. Now a 2x2 block marches only when one of its pixels uses the result (`contact_smoothed`): the four swap their
`used` flag first, while all four run, so the branch is the same for the block and the swaps after it stay safe on
AMD. The result is unchanged (a skipped pixel's 0 was 0 before, its weight in the average 0). The mask at 4K with the
owner's settings, before → after: busy town 2.44 → 2.10 ms, the owner's progress save 2.44 → 2.17, bamboo forest
3.04 → 3.00 (little sky there); screenshots at the same frame show the same contact shadows.

## How it was checked

The owner played with F7 at the lamp post, a wall's cap from several angles, hedges and houses (screenshots in the
README). Comparisons within one run (`YW4_CONTACT_ALTERNATE=1`, frames N and N+1), since separate runs of a replay
don't line up even with the clock held (`YW4_CLOCK`).

```

`docs/decisions/0046-screen-passes.md`:

```md
# 0046 — Our programs in the engine's screen passes
<!-- decision
state: accepted
date: 2026-11-02
replaces: none
code: runtime/shaders, runtime/src/gpu_draw.c
-->

Status: accepted, on by default (2026-11-02); the settings panel's SCREEN PASSES row (F1, DEVELOPER OPTIONS), F7 or
`YW4_SCREEN_PASSES=game` switches back to the game's programs.

## Context

After the shadow mask (decision 0044), the rest of the lighting stage and the passes up to the UI were still the
game's: depth copies, the lighting inputs, lamp lights, an edge-aware upsample, sky and aerial perspective, tone
mapping, the game's own FXAA and a few copies and fills (docs/frame.md "Lighting stage"). Two ways were weighed:

- **The whole pass ours** (bloom's way, decisions 0037, 0038): hook the engine's function, skip it, draw in its
  place. The half-size copy `f_80d270` showed what that costs here: its target and textures come from a GPU command
  chunk the engine records once and replays (the target description at `renderer +0x3720` points into one), and
  it leaves state behind that later passes need (record 44 bound to fragment texture 13). Each pass would need its
  own decoding of those chunks and side effects: days per pass, and a new hook (a regenerated translation) each.
- **Our programs in the engine's draws** (the shadow mask's way, 0044): the engine still issues the draw; our
  readable program runs in place of the game's, with the same inputs and targets. About an hour per program, no
  hooks, no engine state to copy.

The owner chose the second for these passes (2026-11-02): all their shader code becomes ours quickly, and the
heavier way stays for passes we want to change or speed up, where owning the draw pays off.

## Decision

Readable GLSL in `runtime/shaders`, each with the translated program's interface (bindings, inputs, outputs),
swapped in for the game's fragment program by `gpu_draw.c` (the `replacements` table, as for 0026 and 0044). The
screen passes have one switch of their own (`screen_fs`, `YW4_SCREEN_PASSES`). Every program does the game's
operations in the game's order (its fused multiply-adds, reciprocals, F16 constants, odd steps such as
`(v + 1) - 1`), so the results can be bit-exact; names and comments say what each step means.

| Game program | Ours | What |
|---|---|---|
| `95ea1b` | `depth_copy.frag` | colour and depth copy, shrunk (half and third size; `f_80d270`, `f_8050d0`, `main+0x80f988`) |
| `6b4575` | `depth_only_copy.frag` | depth-only copy |
| `d2aaa3` | `vertex_colour.frag` | fill with the quad's colour |
| `2571d0` | `clamp_copy.frag` | copy, negatives to 0 |
| `2d68c8` | `tinted_copy.frag` | copy times the quad's colour |
| `790774` | `lighting_inputs.frag` | the lighting inputs (`f_7f4c90`): shadow mask and two factors, normals in -1..1 |
| `42759b` | `lamp_light.frag` | lamp lights: point-light volumes at a third of the size |
| `3c94bd` | `edge_upsample.frag` | edge-aware upsample of a small image |
| `627287` | `sky_fog.frag` | sky and aerial perspective (Rayleigh and Mie scattering, height fog) |
| `22d015` | `tonemap.frag` | tone mapping (extended Reinhard with eye adaptation) |
| `3f9fc9` | `game_fxaa.frag` | the game's own FXAA (the console FXAA 3) |

The vertex programs stay the game's for now (pass-through quads and the lamps' volumes).

## Checking

A same-frame A/B per draw, with no hook: `YW4_AB_PASS=screen` with `YW4_AB_FS=<program>` (and `YW4_AB_DRAW=<n>`
for the frame's n-th such draw) makes the executor put the A/B markers (gpu_ab.c) right around that draw, so it
runs with ours, then again from the same images with the game's program, and the targets are compared texel by
texel. `YW4_AB_FS=all` compares the frame's (frame % 32 + 1)-th screen draw, so 32 frames in a row cover each.

Result: on the town save (frames 2500 and 2600, each draw of each program) 0 texels differ, colour and depth, for
all eleven. On all 13 test saves (`YW4_AB_FS=all`, frames 2500-2531: 420 compares) 418 are exact. The two that
are not, checked again over 32 frames: the sky and fog on the save `save_base_lag`, 3-6 of 1.44 million texels a
frame, and the lamp lights on `save_base_yokaiworld`, 1 texel in 3 of 32 frames. Each is the lowest bit of one
channel of the packed R11G11B10 colour (format 122), e.g. 0x6918d329 against 0x6918db29: the same driver-level
difference as the shadow mask's (0044), where the same operations in the same order still compile a little
differently. Accepted as there: one step of one channel at a few scattered pixels is not visible.

## Lamp lights, faster (2026-11-18)

`lamp_light.frag` departs from the game's program where the result can only be 0: a light whose colour is 0 reads
nothing (in daylight every lamp is), and a pixel past the light's reach (falloff 0, most of a volume's pixels) skips
the normals. Both write the (0, 0, 0, 1) the full sum gives there. The reads now take gradients worked out before any
pixel stops (`textureGrad`), not `texture()`'s own from its neighbours, which may have stopped (AMD, issue #8). At 4K
with full-size effects, the owner's settings, the third-size pass (shrink-copy + lamp lights): busy street 1.09 →
0.50 ms, the owner's progress save 1.22 → 0.49, schoolyard 0.49 → 0.18. The pass reads 4K images at a third of the
size, so each read saved counts. Same-frame screenshots: the lamp pools differ between two runs of the unchanged game
as much as against this one (rain, wet road). Tried and left out: lighting half the pixels in a checkerboard (no
saving: the GPU shades 2x2 blocks).

```

`docs/decisions/0047-versioning.md`:

```md
# 0047 — Versioning: one number for the project, one for the launcher
<!-- decision
state: accepted
date: 2026-11-03
replaces: none
code: VERSION, recomp/build.py, runtime/src/version.h
-->

Status: accepted (2026-11-03). The project's number is in place (0.7.0); the launcher doesn't exist yet.

## Context

Shipping to other players (option A: a launcher builds the game on the player's PC) means bug reports from
builds we never saw. Until now a build had no name: the only clue was the log's date. We need to know which
code a report came from, and the launcher needs to know whether the game it built is current.

There are two programs with their own lives: the **game** (runtime + recompiler + tools in this repo, built on the
player's PC) and the **launcher** (the setup and play window). A launcher fix shouldn't force a rebuild of the
game, and a game fix shouldn't need a new launcher. The game version is separate again: always 2.2.0
(`target.toml`, rule 3).

## Decision

- **The project:** `VERSION` at the repo root holds `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`, starting at `0.7.0`, counting the
  milestones so far: 0.1 first run, 0.2 playable town, 0.3 own renderer passes, 0.4 4K and ultrawide, 0.5 high
  frame rates, FSR, DLSS and frame generation, 0.6 mods and controls, 0.7 contact shadows, screen passes,
  performance, XCI. 0.x while the game isn't playable end to end. MINOR for new features or anything that needs a rebuild of the game; PATCH for
  fixes. A release is a git tag `vX.Y.Z` on the commit that changes `VERSION`.
- **Which code exactly:** every build writes `<work_dir>/build/version.c` (`recomp/build.py`, `version_source`):
  the number, the git commit (`+dirty` when tracked files had uncommitted changes) and the build day (UTC). A
  release archive has no git, so the build reads a `COMMIT` file there instead (the release packaging writes it);
  with neither, `unknown`. It is its own object file and rewritten only when it changes, so a new commit
  recompiles one small file, not the game.
- **Where it shows** (`runtime/src/version.h`): the log's first lines (`yw4: YW4 Recomp 0.7.0 (commit a8b8184,
  built 2026-11-03)`), the window title, and `yw4 --version` (one line on stdout, without starting the game), which
  the launcher reads and a player can paste into a bug report.
- **The launcher** gets its own `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`, kept in its own folder when it's written, shown in its status
  bar next to the game's. It rebuilds the game when the project version it would build differs from the one
  `yw4 --version` reports.

## 1.0.0 (2026-11-13)

The first public release: game 1.0.0 and launcher 1.0.0 (owner's choice: the plain number, "beta" only in the
release's title and the README). The launcher reads only `N.N.N` and skips GitHub's pre-releases (decision 0054),
so a `1.0.0-beta` tag or a pre-release would never be offered as an update. Bumped in the same places as before:
`VERSION`, `launcher/VERSION`, `launcher/package.json`, `launcher/src-tauri/Cargo.toml`, `Cargo.lock`,
`tauri.conf.json`, and the launcher's What's new (`NEWS` in `launcher/ui/app.js`).

## Consequences

- Every log names its build: a report with a log is enough to find the code.
- Bumping `VERSION` is a manual step at release time; between releases the commit identifies the build.
- `+dirty` builds (the owner's day-to-day ones) are marked as such, so a report from one is easy to spot.

```

`docs/decisions/0048-home-folder-and-icon.md`:

```md
# 0048 — The exe finds its own files from anywhere; the game's icon from the user's files
<!-- decision
state: accepted
date: 2026-11-03
replaces: none
code: tools/yw4/icon.py, recomp/build.py
-->

Status: accepted (2026-11-03). Both checked: the game started from an unrelated folder finds its shaders, mods
and DLC and draws the town; the exe and its window carry the 4++ icon made from the owner's update NSP.

## Context

`yw4.exe` is given its game files (`yw4 <exefs work folder> <romfs folder> <save folder>`), but finds its own
files by paths starting `work/`: the translated and our shaders (`work/shaders/glsl`, `work/build/shaders`),
mods (`work/mods`), logs, perf files, screenshots and input recordings. Those are relative to the folder it is
started from, so it only worked when started from the repo (as `play_from_save.bat` does with `cd`). A
double-click, a shortcut or a launcher starting it from elsewhere would find no shaders. (`settings.ini` and the
DLLs were already found next to the exe.)

Players also expect the game's own icon on the exe and its window. The icon is game data (rule 1): it can't be
in the repo, only made on the player's PC from their own files.

## Decision

**Home folder.** At start-up, before the log opens, the game makes the three paths it was given absolute and
then changes to its home folder: `YW4_HOME` if set, else the folder above `work/` when the exe sits in
`<home>/work/build/` (what `recomp.build` makes: the owner's repo, and an install the launcher builds the same
way), else it stays where it was started. Every existing `work/...` path then works unchanged; the log names the
folder (`yw4: home ...`). Chosen over renaming every path to exe-relative folders: one place, no change to the
layout tools and docs rely on.

**Icon.** `python -m tools.yw4.icon` (and `tools.yw4.extract` at the end of an extraction) takes the icon from
the user's own NSP or XCI:

- it lives in the Control NCA (with `control.nacp`), which extracted ExeFS/RomFS folders don't have: those users
  get no icon, nothing else changes;
- only NCAs under 64 MB are unpacked (the Control one is under 1 MB); hactool names the Control one; the
  update's is preferred (the 4++ icon);
- the 256x256 JPEG (`icon_AmericanEnglish.dat`, else another language) is drawn as PNGs at 256, 48, 32 and 16
  pixels by Windows' own System.Drawing (through PowerShell) and packed into `<work_dir>/icon/yw4.ico`: no new
  Python dependency;
- `recomp.build` compiles it as resource 1 (`llvm-windres`, from the same llvm-mingw as clang) into `yw4.exe`
  when the file exists; the window takes resource 1 (`SDL_HINT_WINDOWS_INTRESOURCE_ICON`).

## Consequences

- The game can be started from anywhere; relative paths in environment variables (`YW4_REPLAY=work/...`) are
  now relative to the home folder, which is where they pointed before for every existing use.
- The icon stays in `work/` (gitignored) and in the built exe, which is never shared.
- Linux (2026-11-15): the original JPEG is also the launcher's picture (`icon.jpg`: the Ready screen's icon, and its
  banner until there is a screenshot). It was copied after the `.ico` was made, and the `.ico` needs Windows, so on
  Linux the error came first and the launcher showed no icon and no banner (a Linux tester). `icon.make` now writes
  `icon.jpg` first and makes the `.ico` on Windows only; `tools/yw4/build_install.py` counts a Linux install's icon as
  done with the JPEG alone (`tests/test_icon.py`).

```

`docs/decisions/0049-dlc-on-boot.md`:

```md
# 0049 — DLC: the game finds and checks the owner's add-ons on boot
<!-- decision
state: accepted
date: 2026-11-03
replaces: none
code: target.toml, recomp/build.py, runtime/src/svc_misc.c
-->

Status: accepted (2026-11-03). The owner's 11 add-ons are found; an empty file named like an add-on unlocks
nothing; a real add-on renamed to another's title ID counts as what it is.

## Context

The game asks `aoc:u` once at start which add-ons are owned. Until now Python worked that out from the title IDs
in the file names of `[input] dlc_dir` and passed the indices in `YW4_AOC`: only `recomp.build --run` did it
(fixed for `tools.dev.run` in a8b8184), the exe couldn't run without a launcher handing it the list, and a renamed
empty file would unlock paid DLC.

What an add-on NSP of this game holds (the owner's 11, measured): a content NCA (112 KiB), a meta `.cnmt.nca`
(3.5 KiB), a ticket (`.tik`, 704 B) and a certificate. A content file's name is the first half of its own
SHA-256 (Nintendo's content IDs), so it is the same file for every owner; a ticket can carry console- or
account-specific data, so the NSP as a whole is not.

## Decision

- `target.toml` `[dlc]`: index (title ID − application ID − 0x1000) = SHA-256 of that add-on's content NCA.
  Hashes only (rule 1); the latest versions of each add-on (4 of them have updates: v65536 to v262144).
- `recomp.build` writes them into `<work_dir>/build/dlc_known.c` (rewritten only when the table changes), as it
  writes `version.c` (decision 0047).
- On boot (`runtime/src/svc_misc.c`) the game reads every `.nsp` in `YW4_DLC_DIR` (default `work/dlc`; the dev
  tools and `recomp.build --run` set it to `[input] dlc_dir`), hashes each content NCA under 16 MiB and owns the
  add-on whose hash it is. Files that match nothing are named in the log and left out (the base game and update
  NSPs, when they share the folder, are among them). Hashing 11 × 112 KiB costs nothing noticeable.
- `YW4_AOC` (indices) still replaces the scan, for tests.

## Consequences

- The exe needs no launcher for DLC: drop the NSPs in its DLC folder. The launcher only shows what the game will
  find.
- An owner with an older version of an updated add-on isn't recognised for that add-on until its hash is added.
- Adding DLC support for another dump format (an XCI of add-ons, NSZ) means reading that container here too.

## Update 2026-11-12: the hash leaves out the NCA header

A tester's add-ons (issue #3) were all left out although 12 of them hold the same content as the owner's. They had been
run through a ticket-removal tool: it rewrites bytes 0x200–0x33F of each content NCA's header (rights ID and key
area) and can rename the file (the 4++ Upgrade Pack's was `bcca0183….nca`), so neither the whole-file hash nor the
name prefix matched.

- `[dlc]` now holds the SHA-256 of each content NCA from byte 0xC00 to the end: the body, past the main header and
  the four section headers. It is the same with or without a ticket.
- The name prefix filter is gone: every content NCA up to 256 MiB is hashed (the game's and update's program NCAs are
  GiBs and still skipped; their small control/manual NCAs cost nothing). The runtime's cache is now `aoc-body.cache`;
  the old `aoc.cache` held whole-file hashes and is not read.
- Same rule in `tools/yw4/extract.py` (add-on RomFS) and the launcher's check (`launcher/src-tauri/src/check.rs`).
  The launcher's DLC tab now lists every file it left out, with a reason: not an `.nsp`, can't be read, the game or
  an update, or not a known copy.
- Add-ons 1 and 9 stay unknown. The only copies found (a widely shared "15 DLC Pack") have blank header signatures,
  SDK 0.12.17.0 and key generation 0: built by a homebrew tool, not dumped. Their `aoc.cfg.bin` names slots that do
  exist in the game's `add_content_config.cfg.bin` (33 slots), but nothing shows they were ever sold. Files nobody can
  own are not added to the table.

```

`docs/decisions/0050-launcher-and-install-layout.md`:

```md
# 0050 — The launcher (Tauri) and the install folder
<!-- decision
state: accepted
date: 2026-11-03
replaces: none
code: launcher
-->

Status: accepted (2026-11-03) and built: the launcher in `launcher/`, all five screens, tested end to end from an
installed download (2026-11-05). The install layout below is the plan; as built, the game is in `work\build\` and
the build tools in `builder\` (decision 0052). The screens were designed first as
a clickable mockup (Home, game files, check, check failed, options, building, ready to play).

## Context

Other players get the game by option A (2026-11-03): no game code is shipped; a launcher takes the player's own
dump, checks it, builds the game on their PC (about 6 minutes, once) and starts it. It must be one download that
needs nothing else installed, and the game it builds must not depend on it afterwards.

## Decision

**One app, two jobs.** Setup and build on the first run; after that a play screen (Play, mods, DLC, downloads,
rebuild). The game itself runs without the launcher: `yw4.exe` reads `game.ini` next to it (the folders below,
as paths relative to it) when started with no arguments, finds mods and DLC on boot (decisions 0043, 0049) and
its own files from its home folder (0048). The launcher is only needed to build, update or change downloads.

**Tauri** (MIT/Apache-2.0): the screens are HTML/CSS/JS ported from the mockup, shown in Windows' own WebView2;
Rust handles files, processes, the GPU check and starting the game (with `YW4_HOME`). The build steps stay the
Python tools of this repo, run by a small embedded Python the launcher brings; nothing that works is rewritten.
Its code goes in `launcher/`. Chosen over pywebview (one language, but the owner prefers Tauri), Qt (large, LGPL,
restyling) and plain C + SDL (the look by hand).

**Install folder** (default `C:\Games\YW4 Recomp`, the player can change it; not under Program Files, which the
game can't write to):

```
<install>\
  YW4 Recomp.exe     the launcher
  game\              yw4.exe, its DLLs, game.ini, shaders\
  data\              exefs\, romfs\, dlc\: from the player's dump, checked
  mods\  screenshots\  logs\
  tools\             compiler, Python, glslang, hactool, FSR/DLSS SDKs (~1.5 GB): only for builds
  build\             generated C and objects (~0.7 GB): kept so updates rebuild faster
```

- **Game files are always copied** (or extracted) into `data\`, never moved or hard-linked: the install owns its
  files, whatever happens to the player's originals. NSP/XCI are extracted; DLC is checked, then copied; keys are
  used during extraction only and never copied. The copied RomFS is checked against one fingerprint of the clean
  2.2.0 RomFS (a hash, kept in `target.toml`).
- **Deleting the originals** is offered once after a successful build, with a confirmation popup listing the
  files and sizes; never the keys.
- **Saves and settings**: the player's choice, in the install folder (default: portable, one folder) or in
  `%AppData%\YW4 Recomp` (survives deleting the install). Changing it moves them, after a confirmation.
- **Free up space**: a button deletes `tools\` and `build\` (~2.2 GB); an option does it after every build. The
  next update then downloads and rebuilds everything.
- Confirmations are popups.

## Consequences

- Install size: ~11.3 GB with the RomFS copy and DLC; ~9.3 GB after freeing up space (~2.0 GB reclaimed, measured
  2026-11-10; see [docs/disk-usage.md](../disk-usage.md)). Peak disk space during building is 11.4 GB (folders) or
  ~20.7 GB (NSP extraction).
- The order of work: `game.ini` in `yw4.exe`; progress lines in the build steps; the launcher screens with real
  logic, one at a time; packaging, tested on a clean PC.

```

`docs/decisions/0051-function-starts-without-ghidra.md`:

```md
# 0051 — Function starts without Ghidra: 597 addresses in the repo
<!-- decision
state: accepted
date: 2026-11-03
replaces: none
code: recomp/main_extra_functions.txt, recomp/translate.py
-->

Status: accepted (2026-11-03). `recomp.translate` gives byte-identical output (all 152 generated files) with the
file as it did with Ghidra's export.

## Context

`recomp.translate` finds `main`'s functions from the player's own file: `.eh_frame` starts, address-taken code
pointers, exported symbols and BL targets (39,631 functions), plus Ghidra's function list
(`<work_dir>/ghidra/main.functions.json`, `python -m tools.yw4.ghidra`). The launcher builds the game on players'
PCs (decision 0050), where there is no Ghidra (a Java install, a Switch loader, a long analysis): its first real
build stopped at the translate step for want of that file.

Ghidra's list has 597 starts the rules miss: 74 reached only by a tail call (B), 328 only by a conditional
branch, 202 by no direct branch at all (jump tables, pointers in data). No single rule finds them; leaving them
out would fold them into neighbouring functions and trap if the game ever jumps to one indirectly.

## Decision

`recomp/main_extra_functions.txt`: those 597 offsets, one per line with a header saying what they are. The
translator reads it instead of the Ghidra export. It is numbers only (where functions begin in 2.2.0, as
`target.toml` holds hashes and sizes): no game code and no recompiled output (rule 1). Only the starts the
translator can't find from the player's file are kept; the other ~39,600 still come from that file.

## Consequences

- Building needs no Ghidra; Ghidra stays a research tool (`docs/ghidra.md`).
- When the translator's own rules improve, the file can shrink; it must be regenerated (from a Ghidra export)
  only if the target build ever changed, which rule 3 rules out.

```

`docs/decisions/0052-launcher-packaging.md`:

```md
# 0052 — Packaging the launcher: what the download holds and what it fetches
<!-- decision
state: accepted
date: 2026-11-04
replaces: none
code: launcher/src-tauri/src/buildrun.rs
-->

Status: **accepted** (2026-11-04, the owner's answers below) and built 2026-11-05: `launcher/package.py` makes the
installer and portable zip, the compiler comes on the first build, from this repo's `deps-mirror` release first (the
owner's choice) and the official address after. Decision 0054 later moves the game's build code into its own
download. Follows decision 0050 (one
download, nothing else to install, the build stays this repo's Python tools run by an embedded Python).

## Context

Today the launcher borrows everything from the repo it was built in (`buildrun.rs`): `python` from the PATH, the
repo's `tools/`, `recomp/` and `runtime/`, and the compiler, `glslang` and `hactool` paths from the owner's
`config.local.toml`. On another PC none of that exists. Measured on the owner's PC (2026-11-04):

| Needed by the build | Size | Licence | Used for |
|---|---|---|---|
| Python 3.11+ (3.13 here) | embeddable zip ~10 MB | PSF | every build step |
| this repo's `tools/`, `recomp/`, `runtime/` | ~3 MB | MIT (ours) | the steps themselves |
| llvm-mingw (clang, lld, mingw-w64) | 737 MB unpacked; the x86-64 parts only (bin, include, lib, x86_64-w64-mingw32) ~480 MB | Apache-2.0 with LLVM exception; mingw-w64 permissive | compiling the game |
| glslang (`glslang.exe` only) | 4.9 MB | BSD-3 / MIT / Apache-2.0 mix | the shaders |
| hactool | 1.6 MB | ISC | unpacking NSP/XCI (not for extracted folders) |
| SDL3, FSR, DLSS, Streamline | ~565 MB download (`tools/yw4/deps.py`, already pinned by SHA-256) | zlib, MIT, NVIDIA RTX SDK | already fetched by the build |

The build path uses only Python's standard library (`numpy` and `PIL` appear only in dev tools: `capview.py`,
`gaiji.py`).

## Proposal

**The installer carries the small things; the build fetches the big one.**

1. **In the download** (Tauri's NSIS installer, about 25 MB): the launcher, the embeddable Python (unpacked next
   to it, never on the PATH), the repo's `tools/`, `recomp/`, `runtime/` at the release tag, `glslang.exe`,
   `hactool.exe`, and the licence files of each. The launcher runs `<install>\builder\python\python.exe` with
   the builder folder as the working directory instead of the repo.
2. **Fetched on the first build**, as `deps.py` already does for SDL/FSR/DLSS: llvm-mingw's official release zip
   at a pinned version and SHA-256, unpacked into `<install>\builder\toolchain\`. The Build screen already shows
   a download line ("About 565 MB"), which grows by the toolchain's size. **Decided (owner):** the player can
   delete it afterwards to save space: "Free up space" (the Ready screen's popup and the Options row "Free up
   space after building") also deletes `builder\toolchain\`, and says so; the next build (an update, Build
   again) downloads it again, checked against the same pinned hash. The game never needs it to run.
3. **`config.toml` for the install** (`write_config`) names the bundled tools instead of the repo's `[tools]`.
4. **Version lock stays as it is**: the main NSO hash check refuses any other game version (rule 3).

Why fetch the compiler instead of bundling it: it is 20 times the rest together, and its official zip is already
pinned and checked the same way as the other downloads, so nothing new is trusted. Why bundle Python and the
two small tools: without them the launcher can't even start the download step, and they are small.

## Alternatives

- **Bundle everything** (~250-300 MB installer): works offline, but every launcher update re-downloads the
  compiler, and the download page carries an LLVM toolchain.
- **Prune llvm-mingw to x86-64** (~480 MB → maybe ~250 MB after dropping unused tools from `bin`): smaller, but
  a hand-made subset is fragile across llvm-mingw releases. Only worth it if the download size matters.
- **No Python: port the build steps to Rust**: rejected in 0050 (rewrites working, tested code).

## Open questions for the owner

1. ~~Fetch the compiler on first build or bundle it?~~ Fetch on the first build, deletable after (owner, 2026-11-04).
2. ~~NSIS installer or a plain zip?~~ **Both** (owner): Tauri's NSIS installer (Start menu entry, uninstaller) and a
   portable zip of the same files, side by side on each release.
3. ~~Where releases live, update check?~~ **GitHub Releases on this repo, and the launcher checks for a newer
   version** (owner) and offers it; the check reads the repo's latest release (GitHub's API, no account needed) and
   is the launcher's only network call besides the build's pinned downloads.
4. Pin llvm-mingw at the version used here (20261006, ucrt, x86_64) so every player builds with the compiler the
   owner tested.

## Then

Implement, then the clean-PC (VM) test from the shipping plan: a fresh Windows with nothing installed, the
installer, the owner's own files, Build, Play.

```

`docs/decisions/0053-in-game-overlay.md`:

```md
# 0053 — The in-game overlay: the game's own pause, a side panel drawn on the CPU from its design
<!-- decision
state: accepted
date: 2026-11-05
replaces: none
code: runtime/src/pause.c, runtime/src/ui.c, runtime/src/gamemenu.c, runtime/src/gamelogo.c, third_party/fonts, third_party/nanosvg
-->

Status: **accepted** (2026-11-05; the owner chose the buttons, the fonts and that it must match the design 1:1).

## Context

The owner wanted a Steam-like overlay inside the game: a side panel with Resume, Settings, Controls, Performance,
Take screenshot and Exit game, usable with a controller, in the launcher's purple and gold, with the game paused
behind it. Its look was settled first as a design (the overlay canvas, `Main.dc.html`, 1600 × 900). Three questions:
how to pause the game, how to draw a see-through, rounded, font-rich panel when the window only copies overlays
onto the picture, and which buttons open it.

## Decision

**Pausing: the game's own pause, its screen hidden** (`runtime/src/pause.c`). The game's main loop is a state
machine (`f_846d20`); Plus in the field switches it to `yw::MenuState`, whose Enter (`f_866540`) opens a
`SceneMenu` with the menus `gameover_menu` + `pause_menu` (the "Paused" screen), and whose Exit (`f_866cc0`) runs
once Continue has closed it. The overlay presses Plus for the player, keeps the picture of that moment and shows
it while paused, so the pause screen underneath never shows; resuming presses A on Continue until the Exit hook
says the game has left its pause. Rejected:

- *Losing focus* (FocusStateChanged, as the Home button): the game asks not to be suspended and ignores it.
- *MenuState without the pause screen* (the scene-open hook handing back "no scene"): the player and camera stop,
  but people and Yo-kai on the map keep moving and Whisper comes out; the pause scene is what freezes the world.
- *Guessing from the picture* when the screen opened or closed (the first version): failed at 30 frames/s.

**Drawing: on the CPU, in the design's units** (`runtime/src/ui.c`, `gamemenu.c`). The window copies overlays with
`vkCmdBlitImage`, without blending. While paused the picture doesn't change, so the kept picture is read back once,
and the overlay is put together on the CPU: the picture scaled to the window, the design's tint, then the panel
drawn over it, uploaded as one image only when what it shows changes. The design's numbers (CSS pixels) are used
as they are, scaled by the picture's height / 900, so it matches the design at any window size. Rounded boxes are
drawn by coverage (a signed distance per pixel), text with stb_truetype, the design's line icons with nanosvg.
A GPU pipeline with blending would also work, but needs shaders and a render pass for something that changes only
on a key press.

The design's fonts (M PLUS Rounded 1c, Zen Kaku Gothic New; SIL OFL 1.1) are built into the exe with `#embed`,
cut down to Latin (about 190 KB in all, `third_party/fonts`); nanosvg (zlib) draws the icons (`third_party/nanosvg`).
The header's logo is the game's own icon, read back from the exe's icon resource (`gamelogo.c`): it is game data,
put in by the build from the player's files (decision 0048), never in the repo.

**Pages use the real data**: Settings shows the player's settings by section (`settings_player_rows`,
`settings_change`), Controls the bindings with their own selection and key capture (`bindings.h`), Performance the
HUD's form (off, compact, detailed), corner and parts, saved with the settings and previewed with the HUD itself. The HUD is a see-through rounded card drawn with `ui.c` (`hud_style.c`) and blended by the GPU in `window.c`; its layout and the frame generation rule (big number = frames on screen with DLSS or FSR, the game's FPS small, the colour following the game's FPS) are the owner's pick from a design canvas, 2026-11-06.

**Buttons** (the owner's choice): Escape on the keyboard (no longer the keyboard's second B); the touchpad on
PlayStation pads, the button SDL calls MISC1 on the others (Share on Xbox Series, Capture on Switch Pro), and Back +
Start on any pad (Xbox One and older have no Share). On a DualSense MISC1 is the mic button, which toggles the HUD.
Home / PS is left alone: Steam opens Big Picture on it. In the overlay W/S choose, D enters a page, A leaves it,
Q/E or LB/RB jump between sections, Left/Right change a value.

Later the same day (the owner): the performance HUD's page is called **Overlay** ("Performance" read like a
picture setting), **Take screenshot** became **Report a bug** (a stub for now; F12 takes screenshots), the hints under
each setting are sentences with **Switch default** / **Recommended** tags instead of the F1 panel's capitals, the
Controls icon is a fuller pad, and the exit popup follows the launcher's popups.

## Consequences

- Once drawn, the overlay costs one image copy per frame; a change (a key press) redraws it on the CPU (not timed
  yet).
- Where the game can't pause (cutscenes), the overlay still opens, over the picture of that moment, while the game
  runs on behind it.
- If a setting changes the picture's size while paused, the overlay keeps the earlier picture behind it until the
  game resumes.
- The F1/F2 panel stays as it was (its developer page is only there); keyboard players can use either.

```

`docs/decisions/0054-game-and-launcher-updates.md`:

```md
# 0054 — Game updates and launcher updates, each on its own
<!-- decision
state: accepted
date: 2026-11-05
replaces: 0052 (part)
code: launcher/VERSION, launcher/package.py, launcher/src-tauri/src/buildrun.rs, launcher/src-tauri/src/update.rs, tools/yw4/build_install.py
-->

Status: **accepted** (2026-11-05, the owner's answers below). **Built** (2026-11-05, tested end to end with a fake
0.7.1 game update and a fake launcher 0.6.0 on a test install): the launcher's own number, the build steps in the
game code with the old game kept during an update (`tools/yw4/build_install.py`), the game zip (`package.py game`),
the update check (`update.rs`). The Play screen band became a popup with the release's change log (owner). Not yet:
a real public release (game v0.8.0 and launcher-v0.6.0; the owner's call). Changes decision
0052 (the game's build code no longer lives only inside the launcher's installer) and carries out decision 0047's
"the launcher has its own number".

## Context

Since decision 0052 the installer carries two things: the launcher (the window, its Rust side, the bundled Python,
`glslang`, `hactool`) and the game's build code (`builder\src`: the recompiler, the runtime and `tools/yw4`, about
3 MB, from `git archive`). So today:

- a game fix (most of our changes: the renderer is still moving fast) needs a whole new installer, and
- a launcher fix (a button) changes the number players see and would tell them to rebuild for nothing.

Decision 0047 already wanted the two apart: "A launcher fix shouldn't force a rebuild of the game, and a game fix
shouldn't need a new launcher." On 2026-11-05 the status bar was made to read the repo's `VERSION` file to fix a
stale "0.1.0"; that tied them together again and is undone here.

The build code is different from the downloads we already fetch (compiler, SDL, FSR, DLSS): those are fixed files
pinned by hash in the code. A game update is new code by definition, so it can't be pinned in advance. It is
compiled and run on the player's PC, so it needs a way to prove it came from us.

## Proposal

### Two numbers, two kinds of release

| | Game | Launcher |
|---|---|---|
| Number | `VERSION` (0.7.0 now), as in 0047 | `launcher/VERSION`, its own, starting at 0.5.0 (1.0 once every page is done) |
| GitHub release tag | `vX.Y.Z` | `launcher-vA.B.C` |
| Release files | `yw4recomp-game-X.Y.Z.zip` (the build code) | the installer and the portable zip |
| What a player does | the launcher downloads it (~3 MB), checks it, then offers a rebuild | the launcher says a new one is out; the player installs it over the old one |
| Needs a rebuild | yes (~5 min, not measured yet) | no |

The installer still carries the game code of its day, so a first install needs no extra download.

### Where the game code lives on the player's PC

`<install>\builder\game\X.Y.Z\` for each downloaded version, next to the compiler (`builder\toolchain\`). For a
build the launcher picks the newest of: the version it carries itself, and the downloaded ones. It keeps the
previous one too. Free up space deletes everything but
the one in use.

### The build steps move into the game code

Today the list of steps (extract, ingest, translate, shaders, build) is written into the launcher's Rust code
(`buildrun.rs`). A game update that adds or changes a step would then need a new launcher, which defeats the
point. So the game code gets one entry point, `python -m tools.yw4.build_install`, that runs every step itself.
At the start it prints the steps it will run (`@steps <id> <label> <seconds> ...`), then the usual `@progress`
lines. The launcher only runs it and draws what it reports, so its build screen works with any game version.

Each game release also says which launcher it needs, in a small `release.toml` inside the zip
(`version`, `min_launcher`, `python`). If the player's launcher is too old, it says "Update the launcher to get game
update X" instead of downloading code it can't run.

### Checking a game update: GitHub's hash, no signing key for now

Each download is checked against the SHA-256 GitHub reports for that release file (its API's `digest`), which
catches broken and partial downloads. That trusts the owner's GitHub account, as the installer download already
does; the account should have two-factor sign-in.

**Not done for now (owner, 2026-11-05): signing with a private key.** It would also stop someone who took over the
GitHub account from shipping code to players, at the price of a key to look after (lost key: no game updates
until players install a launcher with a new public key). It can be added later with one launcher update: the
launcher would then refuse unsigned game zips. Worth it if other people get publish rights or the project grows.

### If an update's build fails, the old game stays playable

Before a rebuild the launcher moves the working game aside (`work\build`'s `yw4.exe`, its DLLs, `shaders\` and
`game.ini`, about 200 MB) and puts it back if the build fails, so Play still starts the old version and the player
can try the update again later. It is deleted once the new build has finished.

### When the launcher looks, and what the player sees

- **On start**, one request to GitHub's list of releases (no account, no token), at most once an hour. If GitHub
  can't be reached, nothing is shown and nothing breaks. A launcher built from the repo (`cargo build`) never
  looks: it builds the repo's own code.
- The newest release of each kind counts; pre-releases (such as `deps-mirror`) never do.
- On the Play screen, one band at most:
  1. **Game update:** "Game update 0.8.0 · What's new · Update": download, check its hash, then the build
     screen (the player can wait and do it later).
  2. **Launcher update:** "Launcher 1.1.0 is out · Download": opens the release page in the browser.
  3. Both: the game band, unless the game update needs the newer launcher; then the launcher band, which says why.

### Releasing (the owner)

- `python launcher/package.py game`: bumps nothing by itself. Makes the game zip from the commit and prints the files and the `vX.Y.Z` tag to publish.
- `python launcher/package.py launcher`: makes the installer and zip as today, with the newest game code inside.
- Publishing stays by hand at first (`gh release create`). A GitHub Actions job can do it later.

## Alternatives

- **Keep one installer for everything** (today): simplest, but every game fix is a full reinstall, and launcher
  fixes look like game updates.
- **Sign game updates with a private key:** also stops a stolen GitHub login from shipping code; left for later
  (above).
- **Tauri's own updater for the launcher too:** one click, but it needs its own signing key and setup. Worth it
  later, once releases come regularly.

## The owner's answers (2026-11-05)

1. Signing: not now (GitHub's hash, two-factor sign-in on the account; signing can come later).
2. The launcher's number: 0.5.0; 1.0 when every page is done.
3. The build steps move into the game code: yes.
4. No new dependencies needed without signing.
5. A failed update build keeps the previous game playable: yes.

## Later: the launcher installs its own update (2026-11-12)

The owner asked that the launcher update itself when the player presses Update, written here (not taken from a
fork's). It uses no new dependency and no signing key, the same trust as a game update: GitHub's SHA-256 of the
release file.

- `check_updates` also reads, from a `launcher-vA.B.C` release, the asset `YW4-Recomp-Launcher-A.B.C-setup.exe`
  (package.py's name) and its digest. A release without it, or without a digest, is offered as before: its page.
- Update: `download_launcher_update` takes only that version's file from this repo's release downloads, into the temp
  folder, and checks it; not while a build runs. `run_launcher_update` starts only the file it checked, with Tauri's
  NSIS flags `/P` (passive: a progress window, no questions), `/UPDATE` (over the installed launcher) and `/R` (the
  new launcher started afterwards, as the user), then quits. If the launcher is still open when the installer
  looks, the installer closes it itself (Restart Manager). The flags were read in the installer template of
  `@tauri-apps/cli` 2.12.4, the version this repo pins.
- Works from the first launcher that has it: players on an older one still get the page.

## Later: a first build takes the newest game code (2026-11-13)

After 1.0.1, a new player's first build still made the game code the installer carries (1.0.0), and only the Play
screen then offered 1.0.1, so they built twice. Now a first build asks GitHub first (`check_updates`) and downloads a
newer game update (`download_game_update`) before it starts; the build takes the newest code it finds, as for any
update. The status line under the bar says so for those seconds, with no step of its own in the list (the owner's
pick). No GitHub or a failed download: the build goes on with the code the launcher carries, and a log line says
why. Cancel is hidden for those seconds, as stopping there wouldn't stop the build that follows. Reaches players
with the next launcher release.

## Then

Build in this order: the launcher's own number; `tools.yw4.build_install` with the launcher using it; the game zip in
`package.py`; setting the old game aside during a rebuild; the update check and the band; then a full test (an old install updated to a newer
game version, and a launcher update with no rebuild).

## 1.0.0: one release, the launcher's (2026-11-13)

The first public release is the launcher's alone (`launcher-v1.0.0`). Its installer already carries the 1.0.0
game code (`builder/src`), and its "What's new" text ships inside it, so a `v1.0.0` game-code release would add
nothing but a second entry on the Releases page with a 3.7 MB zip a player can't run (owner: people would get
confused). `v1.0.0` is a plain git tag, which the Releases page doesn't show and the update check doesn't read.

The first game-code release comes with the first game update (1.0.1), which is what the two kinds exist for:
players get it inside the launcher and never download the launcher again for a game change. Then: a title that
says the launcher downloads it, and not "the latest release", so the launcher's stays the one GitHub shows first.

```

`docs/decisions/0055-overlay-themes.md`:

```md
# 0055 — Overlay and HUD themes: the launcher's theme files, read when the game starts
<!-- decision
state: accepted
date: 2026-11-06
replaces: none
code: runtime/src/theme.c, runtime/src/theme.h, runtime/src/gamemenu.c, runtime/src/hud_style.c, runtime/src/settings.c, launcher/src-tauri/src/ready.rs
-->

Status: **accepted** (2026-11-07: the owner OK'd it, "push all", and asked for the sync below). The owner asked for themes for the in-game overlay and the HUD, switched live
from the overlay's Settings. The question of reading the files at run time or building them in was put to the
owner, who went to bed and left the job to finish; run time was picked as below.

## Context

The launcher already has themes: one CSS file per theme in `launcher/ui/themes/<id>.css` (a `name:` comment, then a
`:root` block of colour tokens with the names at the top of `launcher/ui/style.css`). Anyone can drop a new file in
that folder. The overlay and the HUD had their colours fixed in the code (the overlay design's).

## Decision

- **One set of themes for both.** The game reads the same files, when it starts. A theme added to the folder
  shows up in the launcher and in the game, with no build.
- **Built in: the design's colours** ("YW4 Recomp", id `recomp`, no file). Any token a theme leaves out falls back
  to it, so a theme can't break the overlay, and a missing folder only means one theme.
- **Roles, not colours.** `theme.h` lists what each colour does (body text, the dark, headings, the focus ring,
  fills, hover, the HUD's card...), and each role takes one launcher token: `--ink`, `--violet-deep`, `--violet`,
  `--lilac-0..3`, `--gold` for gold fills, `--select` for the focus ring (the launcher's "selected" outline: some
  themes' gold is too pale for a ring), `--bar-ink` for soft text on the dark, `--danger`. The HUD's traffic-light
  colours (good, slow, bad) stay the same in every theme: they mean something.
- **Colours in the files:** `#rgb`, `#rrggbb`, `rgb()`, `oklch()` are read; anything else (a `var(...)`) keeps the
  built-in colour.
- **Where the folder is:** `YW4_THEMES_DIR`, else `themes` next to yw4.exe, else the repo's
  `launcher/ui/themes` (a build in `work/build`). An installed game is in `<install>\work\build`, so the launcher
  passes `YW4_THEMES_DIR` (its own themes folder) when it starts the game.
- **The choice:** the overlay's Settings > Look > Theme (Left / Right step through them, as any row; Preview shows
  them on the bar), saved as `YW4_THEME=<id>` in settings.ini.
- **Synced with the launcher** (owner, 2026-11-07): on Play the launcher passes its theme (`YW4_THEME`, which wins
  over settings.ini) and its themes folder (`YW4_THEMES_DIR`); when the game closes, the launcher reads the game's
  settings.ini line back and takes that theme (`launcher/src-tauri/src/ready.rs` game_theme, the `game-theme`
  event). A theme picked in either place is the other's too.

## Why not build them in

Built in, a new theme needs a rebuild of the game, and the two lists drift apart. Reading about ten small files at
start costs nothing measurable.

## Open

- The old F1 panel stays in its own colours (its pixel font and look are separate).

`docs/decisions/0056-dlc-content.md`:

```md
# 0056 — DLC content: extracting add-on RomFS files and serving them on `fsp-srv` 202
<!-- decision
state: accepted
date: 2026-11-07
replaces: none
code: target.toml, runtime/src/svc_misc.c, runtime/src/svc_fs.c, runtime/src/romfs.c, tools/yw4/extract.py, tools/yw4/build_install.py, launcher/src-tauri/src/check.rs, launcher/src-tauri/src/buildrun.rs
-->

Status: accepted (2026-11-07). Recognises add-ons 2 (`010086C00AF7D002`) and 100 (`010086C00AF7D064`, the 4++ Upgrade
Pack), extracts add-on RomFS sections to `<romfs_dir>/../dlc-romfs/<index>/`, and serves them through `fsp-srv`
command 202 (`OpenDataStorageByDataId`).

## Context

Decision 0049 taught `aoc:u` to recognise the 11 small item/pass add-ons (112 KiB content NCAs) on boot by hashing each
NSP's content NCA against `target.toml` `[dlc]`. Those small add-ons only need `aoc:u` to report their indices as owned;
the game never opens their RomFS (`aoc.cfg.bin`, 320 B).

Two more add-ons exist for the game:
- Index **2** (`010086C00AF7D002` v0): another 112 KiB ticket-encrypted PublicData NCA (`aoc.cfg.bin`, 320 B).
- Index **100** (`010086C00AF7D064` v196608, the 4 → 4++ Upgrade Pack): a 222 MiB NSP with no ticket (standard crypto,
  decrypted with `prod.keys` alone). Its PublicData NCA holds a RomFS section with `yw4_evop_0002.usm` (232,239,040 B).

When `aoc:u` reports index 100 as owned, the game calls `fsp-srv` command **202** (`OpenDataStorageByDataId`, storage id
+ 64-bit data id `0x010086C00AF7D064`) to mount the pack's RomFS. Without command 202 implemented, the runtime stops on
the unimplemented IPC command.

## Decision

- **`target.toml` `[dlc]`**: add `"2"` and `"100"` with their content NCA SHA-256 hashes.
- **Boot & launcher check (`runtime/src/svc_misc.c`, `launcher/src-tauri/src/check.rs`)**:
  - Raise the content NCA size cap from 16 MiB to 256 MiB and stream SHA-256 in chunks (`yw4_sha256_init` /
    `update` / `final_hex` in `runtime/src/sha256.c`; `std::io::copy` in `check.rs`) instead of allocating the whole
    NCA in memory. Use `_wfindfirst64` / `_wfopen` on Windows so NSPs with Japanese filenames open regardless of the
    active ANSI code page.
  - NCAs over 256 MiB are skipped without reading, so multi-GB base and update NCAs sharing the folder cost nothing.
    (Until 2026-11-12 the filter was the file name; see decision 0049's update: the hash now leaves out the header.)
  - Software SHA-256 on the 222 MiB pack takes ~1028 ms on the first boot; once an NCA over 1 MiB passes its full
    SHA-256 check, `svc_misc.c` records `(name, size, first-4-KiB SHA-256) -> body SHA-256` in `aoc-body.cache` next to
    `yw4.exe`, bringing subsequent boot scans of all 15 NSPs down to ~11–13 ms.
- **Extracting add-on RomFS (`tools/yw4/extract.py`, `tools/yw4/build_install.py`, `launcher/src-tauri/src/buildrun.rs`,
  `launcher/src-tauri/src/ready.rs`)**:
  - Reuse the existing `hactool` + `write_temp_keys` pipeline in `tools/yw4/extract.py` (`extract_dlc(cfg)`): scan
    `[input] dlc_dir` for recognised add-ons in `target.toml` `[dlc]`, unpack any whose `<romfs_dir>/../dlc-romfs/<index>/`
    folder is not yet populated, and extract its RomFS section there. Add-ons that have no ticket (such as the 4++
    Upgrade Pack) need only `prod.keys`; ticket-encrypted add-ons whose title key is absent from `title.keys` are
    skipped with a note (the game never opens the small add-ons' RomFS).
  - Run `extract_dlc` during `python -m tools.yw4.extract`, during the launcher's DLC step (`copy_dlc` in `buildrun.rs`,
    after copying checked NSPs into `data/dlc`), and in `ready.rs` (`install_info` and `play`) whenever the 4++ Upgrade
    Pack NSP is in `data/dlc` without `data/dlc-romfs/100/` unpacked yet. If `data/dlc-romfs/100/` is still missing
    (for instance after an "Extracted folders" setup with no `prod.keys`), the Ready screen's DLC tab shows a
    **Choose prod.keys…** banner (`set_dlc_keys` in `ready.rs`, `save_keys_dir` in `buildrun.rs`) that saves `keys_dir`
    to `config.toml` and unpacks the pack on the spot.
  - `game.ini` (`tools/yw4/build_install.py`) and `cfg.dlc_env()` (`tools/yw4/config.py`) set `YW4_DLCROMFS_DIR` to
    `<romfs_dir>/../dlc-romfs` (`../../data/dlc-romfs` in an install).
- **Serving add-on RomFS at run time (`runtime/src/romfs.c`, `runtime/src/svc_fs.c`)**:
  - Factor `romfs.c`'s virtual RomFS builder into `RomfsImage` so additional RomFS images (`romfs_image_open`,
    `romfs_image_size`, `romfs_image_read`) can be built in memory from `<YW4_DLCROMFS_DIR>/<index>/` without copying
    the files on disk.
  - Implement `fsp-srv` command **202** (`OpenDataStorageByDataId`): read `storage_id` (u8 at +0) and `data_id` (u64 at
    +8), check that `data_id - 0x010086C00AF7D000` is an owned add-on index (`aoc_owned`) and open its `RomfsImage` from
    `YW4_DLCROMFS_DIR/<index>/` (default `work/dlc-romfs/<index>`), returning an `IStorage` backed by `romfs_storage`.
    If the add-on is not owned or its folder is missing, return `FS_TARGET_NOT_FOUND` (`0x7D402`) instead of stopping.

## Consequences

- Owning the 4++ Upgrade Pack (index 100) no longer aborts on `fsp-srv` 202; the game mounts its RomFS and reads its
  files on demand.
- Players who add DLC NSPs after building get their RomFS extracted automatically on the next launch from the launcher
  (or via `python -m tools.yw4.extract --dlc-only`).
- The runtime still links no encryption or NCA code: decryption stays in `hactool` with the owner's keys.

`docs/decisions/0057-mouse-menu-lists.md`:

```md
# 0057 — Mouse support in Yo-kai Pad pages and scrolling lists
<!-- decision
state: accepted
date: 2026-11-08
replaces: none
code: runtime/src/mousemenu.c, runtime/src/mousemenu.h, runtime/src/window.c, docs/debugging.md
-->

Status: accepted (2026-11-08). Extends the Yo-kai Pad mouse prototype in `runtime/src/mousemenu.c` to the pages opened
from the Pad (item lists and "Use on who?" Yo-kai selection list, quest lists, scrolling menus, Ukiukipedia categories and entry list,
Organize Members Watcher card, 3x2 party grid, and "What will you do?" character action popup, Watch skills character selection,
Treasure photos, Soulmate, and Settings left/right arrow clicks) and adds mouse wheel scrolling in lists and page cycling on the
Yo-kai Pad main screen.

## Context

Commits `abdbb2f` and `359c251` added mouse support to the Yo-kai Pad (`yw::CMainMenu`, vtable `main+0x14c0a88`, grid
control hash `0x6098c54d`): while the Pad is in front, hovering an icon steps the focus there with D-pad presses, a left
click goes there and presses A, and a right click presses B.

When the player opens a page from the Pad, the Pad's layers close and a child `yw::CMenu*` object opens on top. Most of
these pages are vertical lists or fixed-row menus that derive from `yw::CMenuCursor`:

- **Scrolling lists backed by `lives::CMenuListView` (`vt = main+0x14b8520`)**:
  - **Inventory** (`yw::CMenuStopWatchItem`, `vt = main+0x14c0838`, `lv_hash = 0x17001a6a`, item control `0x50937ef4`, 8 visible rows)
  - **Inventory "Use on who?" Yo-kai Selection List** (`yw::CMenuStopWatchItem`, shares `vt = main+0x14c0838`, `lv_hash = 0x802b98b6`, item control `0x4e925801`, 6 visible rows for party members to receive the item)
  - **Quests / Story / Cases** (`yw::CMenuQuestOrder`, shares `vt = main+0x14c0838`, `lv_hash = 0xaab2a496`, item control `0xb4eb3a55`, 8 visible rows)
  - **Info / Play Record** (`yw::CMenuRecord`, `vt = main+0x14c4558`, `lv_hash = 0x04f7643f`, item control `0xa17f69cc`, 8 visible rows)
  - **Settings** (`yw::CMenuSetting`, `vt = main+0x14c60f8`, `lv_hash = 0xc3a04661`, item control `0x857cd4fe`, 7 visible rows)
  - **Help** (`yw::CMenuHelp`, `vt = main+0x14c00f8`, `lv_hash = 0x9ee9efdf`, item control `0x0142cd83`, 8 visible rows)
  - **Yo-kai Trophies** (`yw::CMenuTrophyObj`, `vt = main+0x14c9658`, `lv_hash = 0xffb21636`, item control `0xb3f13b48`, 8 visible rows)
  - **Treasure Photos** (`yw::CMenuTreasure`, `vt = main+0x14c9488`, `lv_hash = 0xafdaecc2`, item control `0x14cc3aa3`, 4 visible rows)
  - **Soulmate** (`yw::CMenuKonkatsuList`, `vt = main+0x14c0498`, `lv_hash = 0x596edf43`, item control `0x933f4e58`, 8 visible rows)
  - **Ukiukipedia Entry List** (`yw::CMenuDictionaryTop`, shares `vt = main+0x14befd8`, `lv_hash = 0xb5ac8c55`, item control `0xca481af3`, 8 visible rows)
  - **Members — Full List** (`yw::CMemberMenu`, `vt = main+0x14c1948`, `lv_hash = 0x252cc057`, item control `0xceb4579b`, 8 visible rows)
  - On these screens, `f_9f3e90(menu, lv_hash, 0) + 0x118` holds the `lives::CMenuListView*` (`lv`). The item control's
    `+0x138` (`u16`) is the ring-buffer slot count (typically `rows + 2`, with `s32` at `lv + 0xb0 = 1` top buffer row)
    and `+0x13c` (`u16`) is the ring-buffer slot index (`0 .. slot_count - 1`), which wraps modulo `slot_count` as the
    list scrolls. The `CMenuListView` stores the absolute selected item index at `lv + 0x11c` (`s32`), the total item
    count at `lv + 0x128` (`s32`), and the scroll base at `lv + 0x114` (`s32`, initialized to `-ld32(lv + 0xb0)` at the
    top of the list, as seen in `f_9d31a0`, `f_9d4480`, `f_9d5530`, and `f_9d6550`). Thus the first visible item index
    is `top = ld32(lv + 0x114) + ld32(lv + 0xb0)` and the focused visible row on screen (`0 .. rows - 1`) is
    `ld32(lv + 0x11c) - top`.
- **Fixed-row menus and sub-grids (no `CMenuListView`, `lv_hash = 0`)**:
  - **Pad — Members sub-popup** (`yw::CMainMenu`, `vt = main+0x14c0a88`, hash `0x48a3835c`, 2x1 icons: *Main Members* / *Full List* on
    the Pad itself).
  - **Ukiukipedia Categories** (`yw::CMenuDictionaryTop`, `vt = main+0x14befd8`, hash `0x4c41ffe9`, 1x4 rows).
  - **Members — Watcher card** (`yw::CMemberMenu`, `vt = main+0x14c1948`, hash `0x180cb413`, 1x1 top card).
  - **Members — Main Members** (`yw::CMemberMenu`, `vt = main+0x14c1948`, hash `0x634fbf8d`, 3x2 party card grid).
  - **Members — "What will you do?" popup** (`yw::CMenuSubWindow`, `vt = main+0x14c7b78`, hash `0xb2869aec`, 1x6 action choices:
    Switch, Switch Moves, Set Leader, Remove, Change Name, Reset Name).
  - **Watch skills** (`yw::CMenuGeneralWindow`, `vt = main+0x14bfa78`, hash `0x1405a5f7`, 6x1 character card row).

## Decision

- Replace the single-screen Pad state in `runtime/src/mousemenu.c` with an 18-entry `screens[]` table describing each
  known screen's `vtable`, `hash`, optional `lv_hash`, grid/list dimensions (`cols`, `rows`), and measured
  1280 x 720 slot geometry (`x0`, `y0`, `dx`, `dy`, `hw`, `hh`).
- Support bidirectional navigation between sibling controls on the same menu:
  - In Organize Members (`yw::CMemberMenu`), the Watcher card (`members_watcher`, hash `0x180cb413`) and the 3x2 party
    grid (`members_grid`, hash `0x634fbf8d`) are separate child controls of the same menu. When the Watcher card is
    focused, hovering or clicking a grid card sends `BTN_DOWN` to transition focus to the grid; when a grid card is
    focused, hovering or clicking the Watcher card sends `BTN_UP` to return focus to the Watcher card.
  - During `CMemberMenu` initialization, both `members_watcher` and `members_grid` receive focus calls; `yw4_hook_menu_focus`
    ignores `members_grid` while `layers_open == 0` and the previous screen was `members_watcher`, preserving initial
    Watcher focus so the two sibling controls do not fight during menu open.
- Support value-change arrows on Settings (`yw::CMenuSetting`, `vt = main+0x14c60f8`):
  - When the user clicks the left arrow area (`x in [470, 530]` in 1280x720 menu space), send `BTN_LEFT`.
  - When the user clicks the right arrow area (`x in [730, 798.5]`), send `BTN_RIGHT`.
  - Avoid setting `step_from` on arrow clicks since row focus does not change.
- Prevent relative mouse capture during menu interaction:
  - In `runtime/src/window.c`, guard the SDL relative mouse capture on left click with `!mousemenu_open()` so clicking
    on menu items does not capture or hide the mouse cursor.
- Track the active screen (`active_idx`, `active_menu`) in `yw4_hook_menu_focus`, `yw4_hook_menu_layer_opened`, and
  `yw4_hook_menu_layer_closed`:
  - When a non-Pad screen receives focus, switch `active_idx` to that screen and reset pending D-pad/click state (preserving
    state across sibling transitions between `members_watcher` and `members_grid`).
  - When a child popup layer closes (e.g. `item_action` or `pad_members`), restore the underlying parent menu screen.
- For `CMenuListView`-backed screens (`lv_hash != 0`), read `top = ld32(lv + 0x114) + ld32(lv + 0xb0)` and
  `sel = ld32(lv + 0x11c)` so hover and click map visible rows `0 .. rows - 1` even after scrolling past the first page,
  and clamp hit-testing to `top + row < ld32(lv + 0x128)`.
- Forward `SDL_EVENT_MOUSE_WHEEL` in `runtime/src/window.c` to `mousemenu_wheel(dir)` before gameplay wheel bindings:
  when a list screen (`cols == 1`) is in front, queue one `BTN_UP` (`dir > 0`) or `BTN_DOWN` (`dir < 0`) step per wheel
  notch; when the Yo-kai Pad grid (`pad`, `cols > 1`) is in front, alternate `BTN_R` and `BTN_L` (`pad_page ^= 1`,
  reset when the Pad closes) so scrolling in either direction cycles between Page 1 and Page 2 (since `L1` and `R1`
  clamp at Page 1 and Page 2 in `yw::CMainMenu`); cancel any in-flight hover target.
- Extend `YW4_MOUSE_SCRIPT` to accept an optional 5th column `<wheel>` (`<ms> <x> <y> <buttons> [<wheel>]`) and add
  `YW4_MOUSE_LOG=1` for menu focus and state logging.

## Consequences

- The Yo-kai Pad and the main pages opened from it (Inventory, Quests, Info/Record, Settings, Help, Trophies,
  Ukiukipedia, and Organize Members) respond to mouse hover, left-click selection, right-click back, mouse wheel
  scrolling in lists, and mouse wheel page cycling on the Yo-kai Pad main screen.
- Gameplay mouse wheel bindings (`window.c`) remain untouched when no supported menu is in front.

### Open issues (owner playtest, 2026-11-08)
The rest of the Yo-kai Pad pages are assumed working; remaining issues to fix:
- **Watch skills**: still broken (character cards cannot be clicked).
- **Soulmate**: page is buggy.
- **Slimey marks (Trophies)**: page not working.
- **Treasure photos**: only Y axis working.
- **Organize Members → Switch moves**: not working.

### Open issues: test results (2026-11-16)
Full screen map with the vtables, hashes and screenshots: [docs/mouse-menu-map.md](../mouse-menu-map.md).
- **Watch skills**: partly. The first character (Cole) opens her skill tree by click. The game moves the character
  highlight with LEFT and RIGHT but does not report it through OnChangeFocus, so the mouse keeps its own count
  (`wsk_index` in mousemenu.c). Built; not yet proven by a scripted-mouse run (see map).
- **Soulmate**: partly. The 2 x 2 tile menu (Pad page 1) is now in `screens[]`, so Soul List opens by click.
- **Slimey marks (Trophies)**: partly. The Slimey Mark list (its own class, not the Yo-kai Trophies class) is in
  `screens[]`. Its row click is sent, not yet shown to open a sub-page. Yo-kai Trophies (page 2) gained SCR_CLICK.
- **Treasure photos**: fixed. It is a 5 x 3 grid, not a 1 x 4 list; hover and click work.
- **Organize Members -> Switch moves**: partly. Switch Moves opens by click; its moves and equipment page is not in
  `screens[]`.
- Found on the way: "isn't available right now" message boxes (Diary, Lambert Mail, Ark Swap) take all clicks until A
  is pressed, and a right click does not close them.

`docs/decisions/0058-controller-rumble.md`:

```md
# 0058 — Controller rumble and haptic feedback

<!-- decision
state: accepted
date: 2026-11-09
replaces: none
code: runtime/src/svc_hid.c, runtime/src/window.c, runtime/src/window.h, runtime/src/bindings.c, docs/debugging.md
-->

Status: accepted (2026-11-09). Translates guest Switch HD Rumble IPC commands to the host controller via SDL3.

## Context

On Nintendo Switch, games send vibration data through `nn::hid` IPC calls (`SendVibrationValues` cmd 206, and
`SendVibrationValue` cmd 201). Since the start of the port (decision 0014, commit `d47c8b3`), vibration was stubbed out
as `{206, SIMPLE_OK, 0, "SendVibrationValues(aruid, X: handles, X: values): dropped"}`: vibration requests were accepted
with success so the game wouldn't fail, but the vibration data was dropped and never forwarded to the connected host controller.

## Findings

- **IPC buffers**:
  `SendVibrationValues` provides two buffers:
  - `X[0]`: array of 4-byte `VibrationDeviceHandle` integers (specifying the target controller npad ID and left vs. right actuator).
  - `X[1]`: array of 16-byte `VibrationValue` structs:
    `{ float amp_low; float freq_low; float amp_high; float freq_high; }`.
- **Downmix to host dual-motor controllers**:
  Standard PC controllers (Xbox, DualShock/DualSense in standard rumble mode, Switch Pro over SDL) provide dual ERM motors:
  a heavy low-frequency motor and a lighter high-frequency motor, controlled by `SDL_RumbleGamepad(pad, low, high, duration_ms)`.
  The low-frequency band (`amp_low`) maps to the heavy motor, and the high-frequency band (`amp_high`) maps to the light motor.
  When multiple actuators are targeted for Player 1 (e.g. stereo left/right Joy-Con actuators), the maximum intensity across the
  actuators is computed for each motor:
  `low_u16 = (uint16_t)(max_low * 65535.0f)`, `high_u16 = (uint16_t)(max_high * 65535.0f)`.
- **Duration and cancellation**:
  While active, the game streams updates periodically; a 1000 ms duration maintains active rumble across update intervals.
  When vibration ceases, the game transmits a zero-amplitude update, which cancels rumble immediately (`duration = 0`). If
  updates stop abruptly without a zero packet, rumble automatically expires after 1000 ms.
- **Thread safety**:
  `SDL_RumbleGamepad` is documented by SDL3 as thread-safe to call from any thread. Access to the active `SDL_Gamepad*` pointer
  is synchronized using the existing `input_lock` in `runtime/src/window.c`.

## Decision

1. **`window_rumble`**:
   `runtime/src/window.c` implements `window_rumble(uint16_t low, uint16_t high, uint32_t duration_ms)`. If `gamepad` is active,
   it calls `SDL_RumbleGamepad`.
   - `YW4_RUMBLE=0` disables rumble.
   - `YW4_RUMBLE_GAIN=<float>` scales vibration strength (default 1.0).
2. **`svc_hid.c` dispatch**:
   `runtime/src/svc_hid.c` handles commands 201 and 206, parses the `VibrationValue` entries for Player 1, and routes them to
   `window_rumble`.
3. **Controls overlay toggle**:
   `runtime/src/bindings.c` adds a "Controller vibration" toggle row on the Controls page right under the mouse
   sensitivity rows (with the battle/explore set toggle positioned beneath it so it directly heads the key bindings
   table). In `runtime/src/gamemenu.c`, the toggle renders as a full coloured pill when active (`On`) and a border-only
   pill when inactive (`Off`). Toggling vibration on triggers a 1-second rumble burst (`window_rumble_test`), which is
   protected in `runtime/src/window.c` against premature cancellation by the guest engine's 60 Hz zero-amplitude idle
   vibration updates. Choices are saved to `settings.ini` (`YW4_RUMBLE=1` / `0`).

## Shaping for PC pads (2026-11-10)

Played as the game sends it, the rumble was weak on a DualSense: most effects are too faint to start a spinning
motor. Gemini proposed a minimum speed with a curve, a split of the low band by frequency, and the Xbox trigger
motors. Measured first (late-game save, `YW4_RUMBLE_LOG=1`, a few minutes of play):

- Effects are smooth swells of about 0.4 s (rise ~10 frames, fall ~13), often back to back. Amplitudes are mostly faint:
  median 0.04 (low band) and 0.07 (high band), peaks 0.12 and 0.6.
- **The frequencies carry no pitch.** The game scales all four values of a `VibrationValue` with the swell's envelope:
  frequency / amplitude stays constant through a swell (e.g. 12 Hz at 0.024 up to 150 Hz at 0.12, high band). The
  split by frequency was dropped.
- A minimum speed with a curve made it stronger, but the motors never stopped between swells (owner: "BUZZZ BUZZZ
  BUZZZ": strong, not sharp).

What `window_vibration` (`runtime/src/window.c`) does now, per motor (low band to the heavy motor, high band to the
light one), as force-feedback drivers do with such motors:

1. Below 0.04: off. This drops the faint texture and leaves a gap between back-to-back swells.
2. A swell's start: a 50 ms kick at 70% speed, so the motor spins up at once. This is the sharp edge.
3. While it holds: 0.10 + 0.90 × a^0.75.
4. While it falls: 55% of that, so the motor stops before the next swell.
5. Xbox One / Series pads also get the high band's kicks on their trigger motors (45%).

In the run after the change the motors stopped 46 times between swells and 54 swells got the kick. Owner
(DualSense): "better, good enough", more tuning after 1.0. Switches: `YW4_RUMBLE_SHAPE=0` (as sent, linear),
`YW4_RUMBLE_TRIGGERS=0`, `YW4_RUMBLE_LOG=1`.

Open: the kick is the same for every swell (its peak isn't known when it starts); a weak swell may feel as punchy as
a strong one. Xbox trigger motors are untested (no Xbox pad here). The DualSense's own haptics (audio-driven, USB
only) are not used: SDL's rumble emulation drives them as two motors.

```

`docs/decisions/0059-amd-depth-format-fallback.md`:

```md
# 0059 — AMD Vulkan depth format fallback (D24S8 to D32S8)

<!-- decision
state: accepted
date: 2026-11-10
replaces: none
code: runtime/src/gpu.c, runtime/src/gpu_ab.c, docs/debugging.md
-->

Status: accepted (2026-11-10). Falls back to `VK_FORMAT_D32_SFLOAT_S8_UINT` when `VK_FORMAT_D24_UNORM_S8_UINT` is not supported as a depth/stencil attachment.

## Context

On clean installations running on AMD GPUs (e.g. AMD Ryzen integrated Radeon graphics and discrete Radeon GPUs),
the 3D game world failed to render, blowing out to a blinding white screen, and character models appeared inverted
with their facial features and mouth interiors rendered across the backs of their heads.

The opening prologue scene in Nate's room exhibited:
1. Missing walls, tatami floor, and furniture, entirely overwritten by pure white.
2. Whisper's mouth and eyes drawn directly on the back of his body mesh.
3. Jibanyan's mouth interior and skull geometry drawn over his front facial features.

## Findings

- **AMD 24-bit depth support**:
  NVN format `0x35` (`NVN_FORMAT_DEPTH24_STENCIL8`) was mapped to `VK_FORMAT_D24_UNORM_S8_UINT`. On AMD's Vulkan
  driver, `VK_FORMAT_D24_UNORM_S8_UINT` does not support `VK_FORMAT_FEATURE_DEPTH_STENCIL_ATTACHMENT_BIT`.
- **Attachment bit dropped**:
  In `runtime/src/gpu.c:1404-1406`, format properties are queried from the physical device:
  ```c
  if (fp.optimalTilingFeatures & VK_FORMAT_FEATURE_DEPTH_STENCIL_ATTACHMENT_BIT)
      usage |= VK_IMAGE_USAGE_DEPTH_STENCIL_ATTACHMENT_BIT;
  ```
  Because the driver lacks attachment support for D24S8, the primary scene depth buffer (`0x7269ff3000`) was
  allocated without `VK_IMAGE_USAGE_DEPTH_STENCIL_ATTACHMENT_BIT`, disabling depth testing and depth writes.
- **Why symptoms appeared**:
  - Without depth testing, rendering defaults to order-of-submission (painter's algorithm). Character details
    (facial decals, mouth interiors) drawn after base body meshes overwrote front faces and back heads alike.
  - The scene geometry is drawn in the G-buffer pass. Later, `sky_fog.frag` draws a full-screen quad at far-plane
    depth (`1.0`) with `LESS_OR_EQUAL` depth comparison. With depth comparison non-functional, the quad overwrote
    the entire room geometry with white sky/fog.

## Decision

1. **Dynamic format fallback**:
   In `runtime/src/gpu.c`, format `0x35` queries physical device capabilities via `d24s8_format()`. If
   `VK_FORMAT_D24_UNORM_S8_UINT` supports depth attachment and sampled image operations, it is preserved. If not
   (as on AMD Radeon), it dynamically falls back to `VK_FORMAT_D32_SFLOAT_S8_UINT`.
2. **Test override**:
   `YW4_FORCE_D32S8=1` forces the D32S8 mapping on any GPU (including NVIDIA) for verification.
3. **A/B comparison support**:
   `runtime/src/gpu_ab.c` recognises `VK_FORMAT_D32_SFLOAT_S8_UINT` alongside `VK_FORMAT_D32_SFLOAT` for floating-point
   depth comparisons.

## Tested

- 2026-11-10 (owner): an ASUS Zenbook with a Ryzen 5 7530U (integrated Radeon graphics), clean install through the
  launcher: the picture is right, about 40 frames/s at native resolution, where the Eden emulator gets 25-30.
- On NVIDIA (RTX 4070 laptop), `YW4_FORCE_D32S8=1` runs the fallback without problems; the D24S8 path is unchanged.

```

`docs/decisions/0060-launcher-icon.md`:

```md
# 0060 — The launcher's icon: the owner's own Whisper silhouette
<!-- decision
state: accepted
date: 2026-11-10
replaces: none
code: launcher/icon-source.png, launcher/src-tauri/icons
-->

Status: accepted (2026-11-10). The owner's choice: the repo's icon now shows a character from the game.

## Context

The launcher and its installer need an icon before setup has run, so it can't come from the player's files the
way `yw4.exe`'s does (decision 0048). Until now it was our own placeholder: "YW4" in a gold ring on a purple
rounded square, with no Nintendo or LEVEL-5 art.

The owner wanted an icon fans recognise at a glance. Logo ideas built from the official 4++ logo were tried
first and dropped: the AI drafts garbled the lettering.

## Decision

The icon is the owner's own artwork: a white silhouette of Whisper, made by the owner, inside the old gold ring
on the old purple rounded square (base `#45297a`, ring `#e6bc50`). `launcher/icon-source.png` (1024 px) is the
source; the icons Tauri uses (`32x32`, `128x128`, `128x128@2x`, `icon.png`, `icon.ico`) were made from it with
`npx tauri icon icon-source.png -o src-tauri/icons` in `launcher/`.

## Consequences

- The repo now ships one piece of fan art of a game character. It is not game data (rule 1 covers dumps,
  extracted files, binaries and recompiled code), but it is a trademark and copyright risk the owner accepts. If
  LEVEL-5 or Nintendo object, the old "YW4" icon is in git history (`launcher/icon-source.png` before this
  record) and goes back in one commit.
- `yw4.exe` still gets the game's own icon from the player's files (0048); only the launcher and installer use
  this one.
- Windows caches taskbar icons: after a swap the old one can show until Explorer restarts.

```

`docs/decisions/0061-time-change-check.md`:

```md
# 0061 — The game's "time was changed" check is answered "not changed"
<!-- decision
state: accepted
date: 2026-11-11
replaces: none
code: runtime/src/svc_time.c, recomp/overrides.toml
-->

Status: accepted (2026-11-11). The owner saw "The time on the console has been changed. Changing the time
repeatedly will give you penalties such as not being able to crank the Crank-a-Kai!" on every load, without
having changed anything.

## What we found

The check is the game's function at `main+0x3bd260`. It makes a clock snapshot of now
(`nn::time::ClockSnapshot::CreateWithStandardSystemClock`), takes the snapshot kept in the save (its object
`+0x160`; `main+0x3bd6b0` stores a new one there) and answers "changed" when any of three things holds:

1. `nn::time::CalculateStandardUserSystemClockDifferenceByUser(now, saved)` is not 0. On a Switch this is how
   far the user moved the clock by hand in the settings: 0 when time merely passed.
2. The two snapshots' time zone names (`GetLocationName`) differ.
3. A CRC-32 of the console's pseudo device id (`nn::oe::GetPseudoDeviceId`, printed as a UUID string) differs
   from the one in the save (`+0x230`).

Two of them fired here through no doing of the player:

- Our time service (command 500) answered 1 with the time between the two snapshots, the real time since the
  save. Coming back the next day looked like pushing the clock forward a day.
- A save made on a Switch or in an emulator holds that device's time zone name and id. The late-game test save
  holds "Asia/Bangkok"; our service calls the zone "LOCAL" (logged by the hook).

## Decision

- Command 500 answers 0: a PC has no console clock for the user to set.
- A hook on `main+0x3bd260` (`yw4_hook_time_changed`) answers the whole check with "not changed" instead of
  running it, so a save brought over from a Switch or an emulator gives no warning and no penalty count for 2
  and 3 either. Its first call logs the save's time zone name and device id CRC.

The game still gets the real date and time (the snapshots' times, `StandardUserSystemClock::GetCurrentTime`),
so the time of day and daily resets follow the PC's clock. Changing the PC's clock is no longer noticed.

## How it was checked

The owner loaded the late-game save: with command 500 alone fixed the warning still showed (the time zone);
with the hook it is gone.

## Not done yet

- Whether a penalty is already counted in saves that saw the warning before, and where the game keeps it.

```
