```md
# 0062 — First start: graphics picked for the GPU, two levels
<!-- decision
state: accepted
date: 2026-11-11
replaces: none
code: runtime/src/settings.c, runtime/src/window.c
-->

Status: accepted (2026-11-11). Tested on the owner's RTX 4070 laptop with the level forced; not yet on an
integrated GPU.

## Context

A new install has no `settings.ini`, so every setting starts at its default, and the defaults are the high ones
the owner plays with: a 4096 shadow map, soft shadows x2 (decision 0025), contact shadows (0045) and full-size
effects. On integrated graphics the game crawled. The owner asked for a first-run check.

## Decision

**Two levels, not three.** The owner (2026-11-11): a dedicated GPU with 4-8 GB runs the shadows at their highest
fine; what costs most there is resolution and aspect ratio, which stay as the player sets them. So:

- **Lighter:** an integrated GPU (Vulkan's device type is not "discrete"), or under 4 GB of video memory (the
  largest device-local heap). Shadow map 1024, soft shadows off, contact shadows off, effects resolution half:
  the Switch's values. Nothing else changes.
- **High:** everything else. The defaults stay.

**Once, in the game.** `settings_load` notes that a settings file is in use but doesn't exist yet, or has no
`YW4_SHADOW_RES` line (2026-11-16, below). Right after
the Vulkan device is made (`vk_init`), the window sorts the GPU and `settings_first_run` steps the four settings
the way the panel would, then writes the file, so it never runs again and never overrides the player's choices.
The game does it, not the launcher, because it knows the GPU it actually draws on, and a double-clicked
`yw4.exe` gets it too. A variable set in the environment is left alone.

**"Not picked yet", not "no file" (2026-11-16, issue #14).** This first said "the launcher never makes
`settings.ini`", but since 1.0.0 its "Full screen at start" switch writes `YW4_WINDOW` there, and since 1.2.0 its
Cheats card writes the cheat lines, creating the file if needed. A player who flipped one before the first start
had a one-line file, so the game skipped this and ran the high defaults on any GPU: on an Intel HD 520 (Linux,
Mesa) the GPU was lost in the first cutscene. The game's own save writes every setting, so a file without
`YW4_SHADOW_RES` was started by someone else and the graphics were never picked: that now counts as a first start
too. The lines already there are kept (they are loaded first, and the save writes them back). The log says
"(graphics not picked yet)" after the settings count. Test runs (`YW4_SETTINGS_FILE=none`) never trigger it.

**A notice that fades.** A corner toast at the bottom left of the picture (the owner's pick of four mockups,
2026-11-11: the first, one long line at the top, was hard to read): a tile with a gauge, **gold** for lighter
graphics and **green** for high, then a bold title ("Lighter graphics for this PC" / "High graphics for this PC")
over a softer line with the GPU's name and "Change them in Settings", on the theme's deep violet with a soft
shadow. It fades in over 0.4 s, stays 6 s and fades out over 1.2 s. It is drawn with the HUD's blend pipeline
from its own small image, over the game and under the overlay.

**A second card for the controls, at every start (2026-11-13).** The owner wanted new players told where the
controls are, in the same way. Of three mockups he picked the one-line card: "Press F2 to see the keys" over
"Keyboard and mouse · Change them in Controls", with a keyboard on a lilac tile (lilac so it doesn't read as a
graphics level). It only points at the F2 card, which already shows every key, so it can never be out of date.

- **Controllers:** "Hold View to see the buttons" (Create on PlayStation, Minus on Switch), with a controller
  on the tile. The card follows the device while it shows: a connected controller counts until a key or the
  mouse is used, and the first touch of the other device rewrites the card.
- **Every start, with a switch:** unlike the graphics card it shows at each start, because it costs nothing and
  a player may come back after months. The launcher's Settings turns it off ("Controls hint", under "In the
  game": it starts the game with `YW4_KEYS_NOTICE=0`, kept in `launcher.json` like "Show log"). It was first a
  row in the game's Advanced settings; the owner couldn't find it there and chose the launcher, where there was
  room. A game started without the launcher always shows it unless that variable is set. Test runs (no settings
  file) don't show it, so their pictures stay the game's alone. Not with LEGACY MENUS on: there is no quick
  look to point at.
- **One at a time:** on a first start it waits for the graphics card to fade, then takes the same corner.
- **No shadow** under either card (owner, 2026-11-13).

## Consequences

- `YW4_FIRST_RUN_LEVEL=low|high` forces the level in tests (with `YW4_SETTINGS_FILE` pointing at a file that
  doesn't exist); screenshots include the notice.
- Existing installs are untouched when the game has saved its settings once (every line is written then). Those
  with only the launcher's lines get the first start on their next start after the 2026-11-16 fix.
- Not done: a "reset to recommended" row (the owner didn't ask for it); checking the levels on a real
  integrated GPU and an AMD card (the clean-PC test).

```

`docs/decisions/0063-pipeline-cache.md`:

```md
# 0063 — Pipeline cache and journal on disk, and when they are thrown away
<!-- decision
state: accepted
date: 2026-11-12
replaces: none
code: runtime/src/gpu_pcache.c, runtime/src/gpu_draw.c
-->

Status: accepted (2026-11-12). The code is from Quandiy's fork (Quandiy/YW4Recomp, commits 69bf471 and 58b448c)
with the changes below. The numbers are Quandiy's, on a Radeon RX 6650 XT; the owner has no AMD card and the
merged code has not run on a real GPU yet.

## Context

Every graphics pipeline was built from nothing in every run, on the GPU thread, the first time a draw needed it,
and every translated shader was loaded from its files the same way. On the owner's NVIDIA card the driver's own
disk cache hides this ([baseline.md](../baseline.md): no stalls). On the Radeon it did not: 40 to 300 ms per
pipeline, 117 at once when the town appears, 35 hitches in four minutes; shader loads of 5 to 10 ms each.

## Decision

Taken from the fork:

- **A `VkPipelineCache` kept in `work/pipelines.cache`** (`gpu_pcache.c`), passed to every pipeline build, saved
  every 10 s when something was built and at exit (temporary file, then rename).
- **A journal, `work/pipelines.journal`:** each pipeline the game builds, as its shader keys and state. At start,
  background threads build the journal's pipelines into the cache while the game boots, so the game's own builds
  are cache hits. The shadow-mask prebuild (decision 0025's pipeline, `prebuild_thread`) goes through the same
  cache.
- **Every translated shader loaded on background threads at start** (`YW4_SHADER_PRELOAD=0`: off).
- `load_shader` splits its interface file by hand. `strtok` keeps its place in one hidden variable, and
  `prebuild_thread` already called `load_shader` beside the GPU thread: a bug before the fork's change too.

Changed from the fork:

- **Background builds that skip the draw are off** (`YW4_ASYNC_PIPELINES=1` turns them on). The owner: an object
  missing for a few frames is worse than a hitch that happens once.
- **The prewarm and preload threads run at low priority** (as `prebuild_thread`, 232829c).
- **The files are thrown away when what they were made with changes.** `work/pipelines.cache.stamp` holds one
  line: the GPU's `vendorID`, `deviceID` and `pipelineCacheUUID`, and a number for the shaders. A different line,
  or no stamp, deletes the cache and the journal before either is read. The cache's own header (the same three
  values) is also compared before the data goes to the driver; Vulkan's specification leaves that to the
  application.

**Why the shader number is a directory listing.** It is a sum over the names, sizes and modification times of the
`*.spv` and `*.iface` files in the two shader folders (`YW4_SHADER_DIR`, `YW4_NATIVE_SHADER_DIR`). The other
choices were worse:

- *The folder's own time*: it changes when a file is added or removed, not when one is written again in place,
  which is what the shader build does.
- *A hash of the files' contents*: exact, but it reads thousands of files at every start; the start-up work of
  8013a94 was about not doing that.
- *A stamp written by the build*: two programs would have to agree, and a shader rebuilt by hand
  (`python -m recomp.shader`) would be missed.

The listing costs one directory read per folder (on Windows the listing carries sizes and times; a time over
20 ms is logged). Its weakness: a shader rebuilt to the same bytes has a new time, so the files go although
they were still good. That costs one run of first-time builds, after a game update.

## Consequences

- Three small files in `work/`, next to the other run-time files; the cache is replaced in place and its stale
  entries go whenever it is thrown away. `YW4_PIPELINE_CACHE` and `YW4_PIPELINE_JOURNAL` move them or turn them
  off (`none`).
- Done in [decision 0070](0070-pipeline-cache-kept-on-shader-change.md): when only the shaders change, the cache
  and the journal are kept and the journal's pipelines are built again at start.
- Not taken from the fork: FSR 3.1 as the default on Radeons without RDNA 4 (it belongs with decision 0062, whose
  first start only writes settings the panel has). The same fork commit's refresh-aligned pacing for 30 and 60
  frames/s is in as an option, to be measured: decision 0064.
- To check on a real GPU: the files appear in `work/`; a second run logs `pipelines to prewarm` and fewer
  `stall:` lines than the first; and the same on an AMD card.

```

`docs/decisions/0064-pacing-tick-or-refresh.md`:

```md
# 0064 — Holding 30 and 60 frames/s: the vsync tick, or the display's refresh
<!-- decision
state: accepted
date: 2026-11-12
replaces: none
code: runtime/src/framerate.c, runtime/src/vi.c, runtime/src/perf.c
-->

Status: accepted (2026-11-12): measured the same day (below); the display's refresh is the default at 30, the
tick at 60. The sections up to "The measurement" are the plan as it was written before measuring.

## Context

At FRAME RATE 30 and 60 the present waits so that frames come at an even pace. There are now two ways to wait:

- **Tick (ours, the default).** A thread counts an emulated 60 Hz vsync (`vi.c`); the present waits for the next
  tick, or every second one at 30. The same tick drives the game's vsync event and the input update. Since 232829c
  that thread runs at the highest priority, so that it is not woken late.
- **Refresh (`YW4_PACE=refresh`, from Quandiy's fork, commit 58b448c).** The presenting thread keeps its own
  deadline. Its period is a whole number of the display's refreshes when the cap divides the refresh rate within
  1% (two refreshes of 8.33 ms on a 120 Hz screen), else 1/cap. It sleeps to 1 ms before the deadline and spins
  the rest. A frame more than half a period late starts the deadline again from now.

Quandiy measured the tick wait on a Radeon RX 6650 XT at 120 Hz, before 232829c: about 1 frame in 400 was shown
for 33 ms with 6 ms of work, because a tick was lost. In the fork the refresh way was the default.

What differs, besides who keeps time:

| | Tick | Refresh |
|---|---|---|
| Period | 16.667 ms, whatever the display | Matched to the display when the cap divides its refresh |
| A 59.94 Hz display | Drifts against it: a frame repeats or drops about every 17 s | Follows it (60 is within 1%) |
| Frame and game's vsync event / input | Same clock | Two clocks: their phase can wander |
| A late frame | Waits for the next tick: one late frame costs a whole tick | Starts again from now |
| Cost | A sleeping thread | Up to 1 ms of spinning per frame on the presenting thread |

## Decision

Keep the tick as the default until the two are measured on the same machine, then make refresh the default **if
it has clearly fewer long frames and brings no new problem**; else keep the tick and leave refresh as an option
(or remove it, if it is never better).

## The measurement

What to run (the same replay each time, as for [baseline.md](../baseline.md): `python -m tools.dev.run` with the
town walk, `work/testsaves/save_base_walk` and `work/inputs/walk.txt`, 135 s):

| Run | FRAME RATE | `YW4_PACE` | Frame generation |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1, 2 | 60 | unset, then `refresh` | off |
| 3, 4 | 30 | unset, then `refresh` | off |
| 5, 6 | 60 | unset, then `refresh` | on (FSR; DLSS if the GPU has it) |

- On a 60 Hz display, and on a 120 Hz one if there is one. Each pair twice, alternating, so that one odd run
  doesn't decide it (`python -m tools.dev.perf_compare` alternates two settings).
- Settings at which the GPU has room (the cap must be what limits the frame rate, not the GPU): for example
  1080p or upscaling on. At the baseline's 4K settings the game runs near 50 and neither way is doing the pacing.
- Check the log's first lines: `yw4: pacing: tick ...` or `yw4: pacing: refresh, period ... ms at ... Hz`.

What to read, from each run's performance summary (`work/perf/perf_<time>.txt`, also in the log every 600 frames):

- `pacing <way> at <cap> frames/s: N frames over 25 ms = x%, standard deviation y ms`: frames longer than one and
  a half of the cap's frame time (25 ms at 60, 50 ms at 30), and the spread of the frame times.
- The line above it: the 99th percentile and the longest frame.
- By eye: the menus' scrolling background and a slow camera pan (uneven pacing shows there first); input feel.

With frame generation the swapchain presents without waiting and the generated frames are paced by their own
thread (`gpu_fg.c`), so runs 5 and 6 show whether the game's frames still arrive evenly enough for it.

New problems to look for with refresh: judder that comes and goes over tens of seconds (the two clocks' phase),
input that feels later, a higher CPU use of the presenting thread, and the replay ending in another place.

## First results (2026-11-12, runs 1 to 4 only)

The owner's PC: NVIDIA (DLSS frame generation capable), a 120 Hz display, 900p (no settings file, so the GPU has
room), the town walk, each pair twice alternating (`perf_compare --pairs 2`). Frame generation (runs 5, 6) and a
60 Hz display are not measured yet.

| Cap | Way | Frames over 1.5 frame times, whole run | Standard deviation | Process CPU (% of one core) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 30 | tick | 80, 71 (1.09%, 0.97%) | 4.74, 4.02 ms | 62, 63 |
| 30 | refresh | 7, 10 (0.10%, 0.14%) | 3.62, 3.36 ms | 67, 65 |
| 60 | tick | 223, 223 (3.04%) | 5.32, 6.13 ms | 114, 113 |
| 60 | refresh | 220, 217 (3.00%, 2.96%) | 4.36, 4.23 ms | 122, 127 |

Read by the 600-frame windows of the log, not only the whole run:

- In steady play both ways are near perfect: 0 or 1 long frames per window, a spread of about 0.25 ms (tick)
  against 0.01 ms (refresh). Neither is visible.
- The difference is in the heavy stretch when the town appears, where frames run late. At 30 the tick turned 66
  of them into 50 ms frames (a late frame waits for the next 60 Hz tick: 16.7 ms more), refresh 1 (on a 120 Hz
  display a late frame waits one refresh, 8.3 ms). At 60 that stretch is GPU-bound in both ways (188 long frames
  each), so neither can help there.
- Refresh costs CPU: 3 to 5 points of one core at 30, 8 to 14 at 60 (the spin before each deadline).

Runs 5 and 6, the same day and display, cap 60 with frame generation (both really generating: FSR's log says 600
of 600 frames had a generated one before them; DLSS's says on):

| Frame generation | Way | Frames over 25 ms, whole run | Steady-play spread | Process CPU | Game work p95 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| FSR (`YW4_AA=4 YW4_FG=1`) | tick | 221, 222 | 0.26 ms | 141 | 7.95 ms |
| FSR | refresh | 111, 218 | 0.01 ms | 161 | 9.05 ms |
| DLSS (`YW4_AA=5 YW4_FG=2`) | tick | 225, 221 | 0.25 ms | 125 | 7.85 ms |
| DLSS | refresh | 220, 223 | 0.01 ms | 127 | 7.65 ms |

The long frames are again the town's arrival, GPU-bound, the same in both ways (the 111 was one run of two). No
gain with frame generation; with FSR's, refresh used 20 points more CPU.

The same display switched to 60 Hz (it reports exactly 60.00 Hz, so the drift against a 59.94 Hz display could
not be tried), the same walk, no frame generation:

| Cap | Way | Frames over 1.5 frame times, whole run | Steady-play spread | Process CPU |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 30 | tick | 57, 33 | 0.25 ms | 62 |
| 30 | refresh | 6, 7 | 0.01 ms | 65.5 |
| 60 | tick | 223 | 0.26 ms | 117 |
| 60 | refresh | 218 | 0.01 ms | 120 |

(At 60 only one pair is whole: the second pair's runs were cut short, most likely by another session building
and starting the game in the same minutes: the exe was rebuilt at 22:33 by none of these runs.) So the gain at 30 does not come from the display's faster refresh:
it is the late-frame rule. A tick wait that misses its tick waits a whole tick more; refresh starts its deadline
again from the late frame.

Result: refresh is clearly better at 30 on both displays (about one long frame for every eight with the tick),
the same at 60 with or without frame generation, and costs CPU at 60. The owner chose (2026-11-12): **refresh is
the default at 30, the tick stays at 60** (`framerate_pacing` in `framerate.c`; `YW4_PACE=refresh` or `tick` forces
one way at both).

## Consequences

- One more variable to test with (`YW4_PACE`, [debugging.md](../debugging.md)); the summary line is there for
  both ways at caps of 30 and 60.
- If refresh wins, the default flips in `framerate_pacing` and this record is updated with the numbers.

```

`docs/decisions/0065-linux-upload-events.md`:

```md
# 0065 — Linux: textures and geometry follow the game's events, not page tracking

<!-- decision
state: accepted
date: 2026-11-13
replaces: none
code: runtime/src/gpu.c, runtime/src/nvn_objects.c, runtime/src/gpu.h, docs/debugging.md
-->

Status: accepted (2026-11-13).

## Context

The game's memory pools are its own memory, imported into Vulkan as they are (decision 0021). A texture is uploaded
again, and a vertex or index range copied again into video memory (decision 0028), when the CPU has written one of
its pages since. On Windows the host says which pages were written (`GetWriteWatch`). On Linux `host_written_pages`
had no implementation, so every pool counted as "untracked": every CPU-visible texture was uploaded again every
frame, and geometry was read across PCIe from system memory.

A Linux tester (issue #3) measured 20-28 fps in town on an RX 6600 XT and an Intel UHD 730, with the GPU fans idle.
His log showed "378 texture uploads" every few frames. In WSL the title screen alone re-uploaded 1,768 times in about
500 frames, and only 129 of those were real changes (the movie).

## Why not page tracking on Linux

The obvious way is Linux's equivalent of write-watch: `PAGEMAP_SCAN` (kernel 6.7+), soft-dirty bits, or
write-protect + `SIGSEGV`. All of them watch the page tables, and the pools are host memory shared with the GPU
driver. In the kernel 6.12 source, amdgpu calls `hmm_range_fault` with write access over every userptr buffer on
**every submission** (`amdgpu_cs_parser_bos`), and its MMU notifier waits on the buffer's fences. i915 pins the
pages again with `FOLL_WRITE` after any invalidation, and a write-protect is one. So every page would look written
every frame, plus the cost of the faults. WSL could not have shown this: it renders with llvmpipe, which has no
such driver path.

## Decision

On a host that can't track writes, uploads follow the events the game gives:

- **Textures** are uploaded again when
  - a newer registration (`nvnTexturePoolRegisterTexture`) of the same memory is drawn with. Draws use the
    registration's copy, so loading a new texture into old memory always goes through one.
  - our own code wrote its pages (`WriteTexels`: `gpu_note_written`).
  - it is a movie plane (one level of R8, 2D) and a sample of its content (every 64th word) changed.
- **Geometry** copies are stale when the game flushed one of their pages since the copy (`nvnBufferFlushMappedRange`,
  `nvnMemoryPoolFlushMappedRange`: `gpu_note_flushed`), checked at every use.

## Evidence (Windows, where page tracking works, `YW4_REUPLOAD_LOG=1`)

- **Textures, 7 scenes** (town walk, busy spot, slow street, late game, Yo-kai World, forest cutscene, schoolyard):
  apart from the title movie's Y/U/V planes, no texture's content ever changed after its first upload without a
  new registration. 0 `untracked rule MISSED` lines. The movie planes are not flushed, hence their own check.
- **Geometry, 2 scenes**: all 31,522 copies made again whose content had changed were of ranges the game had
  flushed since. The 32 unflushed ones were unchanged.
- **`YW4_UNTRACKED=1`** (the Linux rules on Windows), busy spot / slow street, uncapped: 118 / 93 fps, against
  120 / 105 with page tracking. The old Linux behaviour, faked with `YW4_GPU_REUPLOAD=1 YW4_VRAM_GEOMETRY=0`: 24 / 17
  fps, with 449 / 683 stall lines.
- **Screenshots**, Linux rules against normal, at the same frames of frame-locked replays: they differ only where
  two normal runs also differ (characters' idle animation, an NPC, wind on bushes, minimap dots).

- **The owner's own play session** (late-game save, a battle, Yo-kai Pad screens, 16,385 frames, page tracking on,
  `YW4_REUPLOAD_LOG=1`): 0 `untracked rule MISSED` for textures and for geometry. All 186,787 geometry copies whose
  content had changed had been flushed; the 78 unflushed ones were unchanged. Menu icons (64x64, 32x32, 256x16) had
  their pages written with the same content. A second session on another map (22,206 frames): 0 `MISSED` again;
  the map's textures loaded into memory older ones had used (1024x1024 and 512x512 maps, icons) all came with a new
  registration, and all 651,337 changed geometry copies had been flushed.

The `MISSED` check only means something with page tracking on: with `YW4_UNTRACKED=1` the rules decide the uploads,
so a texture they miss is never uploaded and never logged.

## Not covered

The slow street's 12% gap to page tracking is not looked into. Not measured on a real Linux GPU yet.

```

`docs/decisions/0066-typed-names-half-width.md`:

```md
# 0066 — Typed names keep their plain letters

<!-- decision
state: accepted
date: 2026-11-14
replaces: none
code: runtime/src/swkbd.c, recomp/overrides.toml
-->

Status: accepted. Owner-tested 2026-11-14 (a rename to "Summer" is accepted and reads normally).

## Context

A name typed in our keyboard (new game, or a rename) showed spread out on the game's name plates: "N a t e",
"H a m". The body text and other speakers' names were fine, and names typed on the owner's Switch read normally.

## Findings

- Our keyboard answers plain UTF-8, as the game asks (`utf8` in its KeyboardConfig), the same form the Switch's
  keyboard gives (a result code, then the text; Switchbrew, Ryujinx).
- After an OK answer the game's keyboard function (`f_959be0`) copies the text (`strcpy`) into a buffer at
  `[main+0x56b8288]`, then its handler `f_8aa550` runs it through `f_9997e0(dst, src)`: each character through a
  156-entry table at `main+0x12be9d0` (u16 from, u16 to). The table maps every ASCII character to its full-width
  form (A to Ａ, space to U+3000) and half-width katakana to normal katakana. The script then reads the buffer and
  stores the name (`f_268140`), as Ｎａｔｅ, which the name plate draws a full-width cell per letter.
- Found with the write watch (`YW4_WATCHW`) on the stored name and then on that buffer, during a rename.
- The game's name check (the text-check callback, `f_959ee0`) runs the same conversion and then allows
  full-width letters only: skipping the conversion there makes every English name "cannot be used".
- Not explained: why Switch-typed names stayed plain (the owner played only this version). The conversion above
  runs for every OK answer, so something on the console differs; it doesn't change the fix.

## Decision

A hook on `f_9997e0` (`yw4_hook_kbd_fullwidth`): for the call that converts the answer the game keeps
(`f_8aa550`, return address `main+0x8aa5f8`) it does the same conversion with the game's own table, except that
ASCII stays as typed. Katakana are still made full-size, so Japanese names are as before. Every other call,
including the name check's, runs the game's conversion unchanged.

## Rejected

- Converting the stored name back afterwards: the name is copied to several places (save record, text
  buffers, message strings) before we could see it.
- Skipping the conversion for every caller: the name check then rejects English names.

```

`docs/decisions/0067-mods-merge-cpk-list.md`:

```md
# 0067 — Several mods' cpk_list files are merged

<!-- decision
state: accepted
date: 2026-11-14
replaces: none
code: runtime/src/romfs.c, launcher/src-tauri/src/ready.rs
-->

Status: accepted. Tested 2026-11-14 with the English translation and four gameplay mods together (see Checks).

## Context

`data/cpk_list.cfg.bin` names every file in the game and the `.cpk` archive it is in. The game reads a listed file
from its archive and a file with no archive (the value 0xFFFFFFFF or an empty string) from the folder. A mod that
ships loose files "frees" them by clearing their archive, in its own copy of the whole list (4.7 MB, 65,836 entries).

With mods laid over each other in name order (decision 0043), only the last mod's list is used. Measured on the
owner's downloads (2026-11-14):

- the English translation frees 2,984 files (5,157 entries: 8,504 paths are listed more than once, the same file
  in several archives, and a mod frees every entry of a file);
- Crank-a-kai Overhaul, Unrestricted Crank, Free Tag Battles, Uncapped Training and Unshackled Equipment each start
  from the original game's list and free only their own 1-7 files.

So a gameplay mod sorted after the translation sent ~2,980 translated files back to the Japanese archives, and one
sorted before it ("Tags") had its own files ignored. On a modded Switch the player merges the lists by hand.

Several of these mods also ship only the romfs contents (`<mod>/data/...`, no `romfs/` folder), which the loader
did not find.

## Decision

- After laying the mods over the tree, if two or more mods ship a `cpk_list`, the one used is the **last mod's list
  with every file any mod freed also freed** (archive set to an empty string, as the mods free files, in place: the
  offset of a NUL already in the string table). "Freed"
  is measured against the game's own list, per path (a path is loose only if all its entries are). Anything else a
  later mod changed in its list stays as it was. The result lives in memory (`File.mem`); no file is written.
- If any list can't be read as a cfg.bin, the old behaviour (last one wins) stays and the log says why.
- **Sizes** (found 2026-11-14): a file's entry also holds its size, and the game reads a loose file by that size.
  A mod that frees a file writes its own copy's size (the English patch: 2,168 of its 2,984 files). The merged list
  first kept the last mod's sizes, so with Unshackled Equipment's list last the translation's item text (177,072
  bytes) was read as 324,736 (the game's): every item name blank; with a merged item list (decision 0068) the
  menu was empty. Now, after all the laying over and merging, every loose entry gets the size of the file the game
  will read at that path (4,344 entries with the owner's six mods). Found by replaying the owner's own route into
  Items and Quests with one mod set after another (the cause looked like a mod incompatibility until a test with
  one hand-made list showed the merge was it).
- A mod folder with `data/` directly is a mod too (runtime `check_add_mod`, launcher `mod_roots`), and a folder that
  isn't a mod is looked into one level more: downloads wrap the mod in a folder of their own
  (`free_tag_battles/Tags/romfs`, found 2026-11-14 when it didn't load from `contents/<title id>/`).
- Two mods replacing the same file still can't both apply: the later one wins, as before (e.g. three of these mods
  ship `item_config_0.13.66.cfg.bin`).

## Rejected

- Writing the merged list to disk: needs a writable place that matches both the dev tree and launcher installs,
  and a stale copy could be read after a mod is removed.
- Building the list from the game's own and only the mods' freed entries: would drop any other change a mod made to
  its list (none of the measured mods made one, but nothing stops one from doing it).

## Checks

- Log with the translation + Overhaul + Tags + Uncapped Training + Unshackled Equipment: `cpk_list: 5 mods' lists
  merged, 5185 entries freed by an earlier mod kept loose`, the same count as an independent Python reader of the
  same files.
- Late-game save: text stays English (location banner, hints); the trace shows the item file read from Unshackled
  Equipment and the shop file from Crank-a-kai Overhaul, two different mods.

```

`docs/decisions/0068-mods-merge-data-files.md`:

```md
# 0068 — Mods' copies of one data file are merged entry by entry

<!-- decision
state: accepted
date: 2026-11-14
replaces: none
code: runtime/src/modmerge.c, runtime/src/romfs.c, runtime/src/main.c, launcher/src-tauri/src/ready.rs, launcher/ui/app.js
-->

Status: accepted. Tested 2026-11-14 with the owner's six mods (see Checks).

## Context

Mods lay files over the game's (decision 0043). When two mods ship the same file, the later one's copy replaces
the earlier one's, so the earlier mod's change does nothing. Decision 0067 merged `cpk_list`; the launcher's Mods
tab then warned about every other shared file.

Measured on the owner's downloads: Crank-a-kai Overhaul, Free Tag Battles and Unshackled Equipment all ship
`data/common/gamedata/item/item_config_0.13.66.cfg.bin` (1,566 entries in 2.2.0). Overhaul adds 1 item and raises a
count (2 entries), Tags edits 6, Unshackled edits 201, and **no entry is changed by two of them**. They only clash
because the file is replaced whole.

Level-5's `.cfg.bin` data files are flat lists of entries (a name crc and a few int, float or string values), so
two copies can be compared entry by entry.

## Decision

- **Merge** (`modmerge.c`): for each `.cfg.bin` that two or more mods replace (not `cpk_list`, 0067), each mod's
  copy is compared with the game's own copy (Myers diff over whole entries, after the common start and end), and
  the result takes every changed run of entries from the mod that changed it. Two mods' runs that share base
  entries, or two inserts at one place, are a clash: then nothing is merged, the later mod's copy is used as before,
  and the log names both. A copy that adds new kinds of entries (a different name table at the end) isn't merged.
- **The game's copy** is its loose file when it has one, else read from the archive the game's own `cpk_list` names,
  with our own CPK reader and CRILAYLA decompressor (ported from `tools/yw4/cpk.py`).
- **Writing**: entries, `0xFF` padding to 4 and 16, the strings once each in first-use order, the name table copied.
  Checked: writing back any of the four item files above gives the same bytes.
- The merged file is kept in memory (`File.mem`, as 0067), so nothing is written and removing a mod undoes it.
- **The launcher asks the game** (`yw4 --mod-clashes`, folders from game.ini): every pair of mods (on or off) that
  can't both have their way with a file, one `clash` line each. The Mods tab groups those by file, so it warns only
  about real clashes and the launcher and the game can't disagree. Games before 1.1.1 don't know the flag (an old
  build takes it for a start and writes a log, which would push aside the log a bug report sends), so for them the
  launcher keeps comparing file names.

## Rejected

- Merging without the game's copy (by majority of the mods' copies): can't tell which of two mods changed an entry.
- Merging a clash entry by entry ("later mod wins per entry"): a mod's entries depend on each other (Overhaul's
  count goes with its new item); mixing two mods' versions of one run could break both.
- Treating identical changes from two mods as agreement: two mods each adding an item would both raise a count to the
  same number, and the merge would keep one count for two new items.

## Checks

- Real files: the archive read matches `tools/yw4/cpk.py` byte for byte; the merge of the three item files equals an
  independent Python merge of the same changes (1,567 entries, all 209 changed entries kept).
- `yw4 --mod-clashes` with the six mods (1.5 s): only Overhaul + Unrestricted Crank (capsule prizes: the same entries)
  and the translation + Overhaul (item text, hidden by the launcher's known-harmless rule).
- Game start with all six: `item_config_0.13.66.cfg.bin: merged from 3 mods`, the game reads the merged size and plays.
- Tests: `RomfsTest.test_mods_data_files_merged` (a merge, a clash, `--mod-clashes`), launcher `test_clashes_from`.
- Not checked in play: each mod's feature (the new item in the Crank-a-kai, a tag battle, unrestricted equipment).

```

`docs/decisions/0069-motion-least-time.md`:

```md
# 0069 — Above 30 frames/s a motion's time counts at least 1/30 s for its least time

<!-- decision
state: accepted
date: 2026-11-14
replaces: none
code: runtime/src/framerate.c, recomp/overrides.toml, runtime/src/kernel.c, runtime/src/dispatch.c
-->

Status: accepted. Measured 2026-11-14 at 30, 60 and 120 frames/s (see Checks); not yet confirmed by the reporter.

## Context

Issue #9: at high frame rates a jump made while running is a small hop; standing still, or on the Switch, it is a
full jump. The game measures its time step every frame and scales its work by it (framerate.c), so most of it runs
right at any rate. This did not.

Measured with a replay whose clock steps a chosen rate (`YW4_REPLAY_HZ`, below) and the player's records dumped
every frame (`YW4_PROBE_DUMP`):

| | Peak above the ground | Rising part |
|---|---|---|
| 30 frames/s | +1.39 | about 0.23 s |
| 60 frames/s | +1.38 | about 0.23 s |
| 120 frames/s | +0.62 | 0.1 s |

The chain, from the jump's height back to its cause:

- The physics record's target height (`+0xb2c`) is copied every frame from the action parameters (`+0x94`), which
  the action state machine (`main+0x1bcd70`) fills from the current motion's data (`motion+0xbc`). At 120 it was
  1.4 for one frame, then 0.8.
- 0.8 is the take-off's own height. At 30 and 60 the player leaves the take-off (state 0x11) for the air (state
  0x10) one frame after it starts. At 120 it never left.
- Leaving needs "may leave" (`action+0xb1e`). `main+0x1c6170(action, dt)` adds dt to the time in the motion
  (`action+0xafc`) and sets it once that reaches the motion's least time (`motion+0xb8`, when bit 0 of
  `motion+0xc1` is set). The take-off's least time is about one 60 Hz frame. One 120 Hz step (1/120 s) falls short;
  while the flag is unset the state machine (`main+0x1c2aa0`) asks for the take-off again, which restarts it and
  sets its time back to 0. So the time never grows past one step.

## Decision

A hook on `main+0x1c6170` (`yw4_hook_motion_time`) runs the game's update, then, if the time step is under 1/30 s
and "may leave" is still unset: a motion whose least time is 1/30 s or less, and whose time is still under 1/30 s,
may be left. That is what the Switch does, where every frame counts 1/30 s: such a motion can always be left after
its first frame.

Why this and not the alternatives:

- **Not stopping the restart.** Asking for the same state again is how the state machine waits; changing it touches
  every state, not only motions with a least time.
- **Not adding to the motion's time.** `action+0xafc` is read elsewhere; only the one comparison changes here.
- **1/30 s, not 1/60 s.** The game was made for 30 frames/s. 1/60 s would fix 120 but leave least times between
  1/60 and 1/30 s stuck the same way at 60.
- Longer least times are counted as before, and at 30 frames/s (dt = 1/30) nothing changes. `YW4_MOTION_TIME_FIX=0`
  turns it off to compare.

## Checks

- Running jump, same replay and save: 30 +1.39 / 0.63 s in the air, 60 +1.38 / 0.65 s, 120 +1.38 / 0.68 s (was
  +0.62). Screenshots 0.1 s apart look the same at 60 and 120.
- Standing jump: the same at 30, 60 and 120 (see Standing jump).
- Town walk at 60 frames/s with the fix on and off: it ends in the same place; the pictures at frames 5000 and
  7300 differ by a frame or so of timing (camera and running pose a little apart). Expected: at 60 a motion whose
  least time lies between 1/60 and 1/30 s can now be left after one frame, as on the Switch, instead of two. With
  60 frames/s a real frame's step also jitters around 1/60 s, so a least time of one 60 Hz frame could be missed at
  60 too; counting 1/30 covers that.

## Standing jump

A first measurement suggested the standing jump fell faster at 60 and 120 than at 30. Measured again on its own
(walk a moment, stop, wait, jump): peak +1.37 to +1.39 about 0.5 s after take-off and back on the ground at about
0.9 s at 30, 60 and 120, within one 30 Hz frame of each other (at 30 gravity starts one bigger step later). The
first reading came from a jump taken right after a run toward a building; nothing to fix.

## Test tools added for this

- `YW4_REPLAY_HZ=<rate>` with `YW4_REPLAY_HZ_AT=<frame>` (kernel.c): during a frame-clock replay, each frame moves
  the game's clock 1/rate s instead of 1/60 from that frame on, so a route can load at 60 and then play as at
  another frame rate. `YW4_DT_LOG=1` shows the step the game got.
- `YW4_PROBE` lines now show s0 to s2 and the presented frame; `YW4_PROBE_X0=<hex>` keeps one object's calls;
  `YW4_PROBE_DUMP=<bytes>` prints that many bytes at x0 (or at the pointer chain `YW4_PROBE_DUMP_PTR=<off>[,<off>]`)
  as floats on each call (dispatch.c).

```

`docs/decisions/0070-pipeline-cache-kept-on-shader-change.md`:

```md
# 0070 — The pipeline cache and journal are kept when only the shaders change

<!-- decision
state: accepted
date: 2026-11-14
replaces: none
code: runtime/src/gpu_pcache.c
-->

Status: accepted. Measured 2026-11-14 on the owner's RTX 4070 laptop (see Checks). Changes one rule of
[decision 0063](0063-pipeline-cache.md); the rest of 0063 stands.

## Context

Decision 0063 threw the pipeline cache and the journal away whenever the stamp changed: another GPU, another
driver or another set of translated shaders. Every game update rebuilds the shaders, so every update started
from nothing. On NVIDIA that went unnoticed, because the driver keeps its own cache keyed by each shader's bytes,
and updates rarely changed those bytes.

The shader fix of 2026-11-14 (c386b89, the vertex outputs within 128 components) changes the bytes of every
vertex and geometry shader. Measured on the town walk with the old rule:

| | Pipelines built in play | Build time | Worst frame |
|---|---|---|---|
| A normal update (driver cache warm) | 136 | 0.56 s | 0.25 s as the town appears |
| Shaders changed, driver cache empty | 170 | 4.0 s | **2.9 s** as the town appears |
| Our cache kept, driver cache empty | 138 | 0.33 s | only at start-up |

Our own cache alone was enough; the freeze came from throwing it away. 0063 already listed keeping the journal
as an open point.

## Decision

The stamp's two parts are compared on their own:

- **Another GPU or driver** (vendor, device, `pipelineCacheUUID`), or no stamp: both files go, as before. Data
  from another driver is never handed to it.
- **Only the shaders changed:** both files stay and the stamp is updated. The log says so.
  - The cache's entries are keyed by the shaders' bytes: those of changed shaders just don't match any more,
    those of unchanged ones still do. Vulkan lets a cache hold entries that are never used.
  - The journal's records name the shaders by the game's keys and hold the pipeline state, which a shader
    rebuild doesn't change. At start the prewarm threads build them again from the new files, in the background,
    before the game asks for them. Records whose shader files are gone are skipped (as before).
  - A cache file over 64 MiB is emptied then (the journal fills it again), so stale entries can't pile up over
    many updates. It was 5 to 8 MiB after a full town walk.

## Checks

The update simulated: shaders translated as in 1.2.2, the town walk played once (cache and journal filled), then
the new shaders and NVIDIA's driver cache set aside (the worst case), then the walk again:

- 261 pipelines prewarmed in 0.66 s in the background, done before the first frame.
- In play: 130 pipelines asked for, 18 ms in all (cache hits); nothing when the town appears (was 2.9 s).
- The first frame takes about 1 s, as in every start-up.

```

`docs/decisions/0071-linux-launcher.md`:

```md
# 0071 — The launcher on Linux: one source, the distribution's tools, an AppImage

<!-- decision
state: accepted
date: 2026-11-14
replaces: none
code: launcher/src-tauri/src/platform.rs, launcher/src-tauri/tauri.linux.conf.json, launcher/package.py, launcher/ui/app.js, tools/yw4/system.py, tools/yw4/build_install.py, recomp/build.py
-->

Status: accepted. Built and checked in WSL (Ubuntu 24.04, software rendering); since then players use the AppImage on
their own Linux desktops (owner, 2026-11-17).

## Context

The launcher (decision 0050) was Windows only, though nothing in Tauri is: built in WSL as it was, it compiled, its
tests passed and its screens drew, with no change. What did not work was around it: about 40 places named a Windows
program or folder (`explorer`, `powershell`, `taskkill`, `tasklist`, `%APPDATA%`, `System32\curl.exe` and `tar.exe`,
`yw4.exe`, `python`), and the download (decision 0052) ships Windows programs: an embeddable Python, glslang,
hactool and the llvm-mingw compiler it fetches.

## Decision

**One source, the differences in one file.** `launcher/src-tauri/src/platform.rs` holds every Windows / Linux
difference; the rest of the launcher calls it and names no system program itself. On Windows each function does
what the launcher did before, so the Windows launcher behaves the same.

| | Windows | Linux |
|---|---|---|
| The launcher's records, "appdata" saves | `%APPDATA%\YW4 Recomp` | `$XDG_DATA_HOME/YW4Recomp` (`~/.local/share/YW4Recomp`), the game's own default |
| Links, folders | `explorer` | `xdg-open` |
| Cancel a build | `taskkill /T` | the step's own process group, killed |
| Graphics card names | `Win32_VideoController` | `vulkaninfo --summary`, else `lspci` |
| Shortcuts | `.lnk` on the desktop and in the Start menu | `.desktop` in the desktop folder and `~/.local/share/applications` |
| Free space | `GetDiskFreeSpaceExW` | `df` |
| Unpack a game update | `tar.exe` (bsdtar) | Python's `zipfile` (GNU tar reads no zip) |
| A newer launcher | its installer, run | its release page, as for the portable zip |

**The distribution's build tools, checked first.** On Linux the download ships no Python and no compiler. A build
uses the system's Python 3.11+, Clang 19+ (or GCC 15+), glslang and pkg-config, as README.md's "Building on Linux"
already asks. `tools/yw4/system.py` runs as the build's first step ("Checking the build tools"). It picks the newest
compiler that has `#embed` and stops with one message naming everything missing and the install line for Arch,
Fedora and Debian/Ubuntu. That check is in the game's code, not the launcher's, so a game update can change it.

Why not ship them: a compiler or Python built for one distribution's C library breaks on others, and every
distribution packages these four. The Windows reason for shipping them (decision 0052: nothing to install) is met
on Linux by one package-manager line.

**Shipped anyway: hactool and SDL3.** hactool has no Linux release, so `package.py` builds it from its pinned
1.4.0 source (it links only libc). SDL3 is missing from Ubuntu 24.04, the most used distribution. The download
carries an SDL3 build that loads its X11, Wayland and audio parts at run time, so one build works across
distributions, the way Steam ships it. The build uses the system's SDL3 when there is one; `recomp/build.py` copies
an SDL3 from outside the system folders next to `yw4` and links with run path `$ORIGIN`.

**An AppImage.** One file that runs on any distribution with WebKitGTK's libraries bundled. Tauri builds it
(`tauri.linux.conf.json`). That file also turns the window's see-through Mica backdrop off, which only Windows has.
`package.py` on Linux builds with cargo's Tauri CLI into a target folder of its own, never the repo's `target/` or
`node_modules`, which hold the Windows build's files.

**The screens.** The page sees Linux in WebKitGTK's user agent. It leaves out what only Windows has (the FSR and
DLSS options, their mentions, the DLSS slide), says "App menu entry" and "In your home folder", and suggests
`~/Games/YW4 Recomp`. Since [decision 0073](0073-dlss-fsr-on-linux.md) the DLSS and FSR options are back on Linux,
as upscaling only; only frame generation is left out.

## Found on the way

The launcher's "Find it" (an existing install) wrote `%APPDATA%/YW4 Recomp/save` into a new `game.ini` for
"appdata" saves. The game expands no `%APPDATA%` (`runtime/src/game_ini.c`), so it read a folder literally named
`%APPDATA%`. It now writes the real folder, on both systems.

## Issue #13: the AppImage's environment reached the build (2026-11-15)

A player on AOSC OS built the launcher. Two problems, one after the other:

1. **Bundling:** `cargo tauri build` stopped with only "failed to run linuxdeploy". Their `cargo tauri` was 2.10.1,
   older than the 2.12.4 we use (pinned in `package.json` for Windows; for Linux only a docstring said so). With 2.12.4
   it bundled. `package.py` now checks `cargo tauri --version` against `package.json`'s pin before it starts, and stops
   with the `cargo install tauri-cli --version 2.12.4 --locked` line instead.
2. **Running:** in the AppImage, BUILD failed at 0%: the system's `python3` stopped with "No module named 'encodings'",
   `PYTHONHOME` and `PYTHONPATH` pointing into the AppImage's mount. The binary run on its own worked. The AppImage's
   AppRun (AppImageKit's, which Tauri bundles) sets those for the launcher, with PATH, LD_LIBRARY_PATH, XDG_DATA_DIRS
   and the GTK / GStreamer / Qt module paths, and every program the launcher started inherited them: Python first, but
   also the compiler, the game, curl and xdg-open (the player's browser), which could load the AppImage's libraries.

   Fix: `platform::command`, used for every program the launcher starts (no `Command::new` left elsewhere). Inside an
   AppImage (APPDIR set) it gives the child the launcher's environment with every entry inside the mount left out of
   its variable's `:` list, the variable removed when nothing else is left, and AppRun's `PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE`
   removed. The launcher keeps its own (its web view needs it). Nothing the builder starts needed the AppImage's
   libraries: hactool links only libc, and SDL3 is found next to the game through its run path. A Rust test feeds it
   the variables from the player's log.

   Never caught before: the AppImage was built in WSL but never started (Not done, below).

## Not done

- Tried only in WSL with software rendering: no real GPU, desktop, file manager or controller.
- hactool and SDL3 are built against the packager's glibc (Ubuntu 24.04: 2.39); distributions older than that would
  need them built on an older system.
- A Linux release (publishing the AppImage) is the owner's call.

```

`docs/decisions/0072-occlusion-queries.md`:

```md
# 0072 — The game's occlusion queries on Vulkan, and its draws skipped on the GPU

<!-- decision
state: accepted
date: 2026-11-14
replaces: none
code: runtime/src/gpu_query.c, runtime/src/gpu.c, runtime/src/gpu_draw.c, runtime/src/nvn_cmdbuf.c, runtime/src/shadow.c, runtime/src/gpu_shadow.c, runtime/src/window.c
-->

Status: accepted. Measured 2026-11-14 on the owner's RTX 4070 laptop, saves `lategame` and `lag` (evening town).
Not yet seen on AMD, Intel or Linux.

## Context

`ReportCounter(SAMPLES_PASSED)` wrote 0 since decision 0017 (headless first), and `SetRenderEnable` /
`SetRenderEnableConditional` were recorded but never done. Answering "visible" instead changed nothing on screen,
which made the queries look unused.

Measured with `YW4_COUNTER_LOG`: before each shadow cascade and before the main view, `f_9ab8c0` draws one 36-vertex
box per object into the 240×135 depth target, each between two reports 16 bytes apart. The model renderer
(`f_a45890`, at `a4a18c`) then wraps that object's draws in `SetRenderEnableConditional(RENDER_IF_NOT_EQUAL, first
address)`: the GPU skips the draws of an object whose box had no visible sample. The CPU never reads the counts.
Answering "visible" changed nothing because the condition itself was ignored. Evening town: 270 pairs, 920
conditions, 878 conditional draws a frame, 498 of them hidden.

## Decision

`runtime/src/gpu_query.c`:

- A pair of reports is one Vulkan occlusion query (precise where the GPU has `occlusionQueryPrecise`) around the
  draws between them. The first value is written as 0, the second is the query's count, copied into the game's own
  memory on the GPU (`vkCmdCopyQueryPoolResults` into the imported pool, decision 0021). No wait, no read-back.
- The conditional draws use `VK_EXT_conditional_rendering` on the second value, begun and ended around each single
  draw. Nothing of ours (our passes, copies, upscaling) can fall under a condition by accident.
- Our own draws that stand in for a game draw take the game's condition along: the shadow casters (decision 0024),
  and the G-buffer, material and takeover draws that run in place.
- The NVN mode order (`RENDER_IF_EQUAL` = 0, `RENDER_IF_NOT_EQUAL` = 1) is from memory of the NVN headers, not
  checked against one. The check is the picture: with the order inverted, the ~380 visible objects of the town
  would vanish and the 498 hidden ones would be drawn. The town looks the same with and without culling.

Fallbacks, none of which fired in the tests: without the extension, or for an address no pair of ours wrote, the
draws are made as before; a pair that spans two render passes with draws in both answers "visible".

## Why not answer on the CPU

The CPU could read the counts a frame late and skip the draws while recording. But the game asks within the same
frame, on the GPU, so a CPU answer would be one frame stale: objects would pop in a frame late when they come out of
hiding. Conditional rendering is what the Switch's GPU does here.

## Checks

- Counts are real and varied, 0 to 64800, in both scenes.
- `YW4_OCCLUSION=0` (all conditional draws made) against the default, same frame numbers across runs: 0.6%
  (`lategame`) and 1.6% (`lag`) of pixels differ, from idle-animating characters and a passing car.
- Vulkan validation: no error from this code.
- Frame rate: unchanged within the noise. The town is CPU-bound, so skipping draws buys no speed here; it is on by
  default because it is what the game asks for. `YW4_OCCLUSION=0` turns it off.

## Cost at 4K (2026-11-18)

With the owner's settings (4K, DLSS) the box pass costs ~1.2-1.3 ms in the busy town spot, most of it the ~250
separate queries rather than the boxes. Resetting queries 512 at a time instead of 64 (each reset ends and restarts
the render pass behind a barrier) cut the pass's restarts from 7.9 to 4.5 a frame and its time from 1.28 to 1.15 ms;
nothing else changes. Ordinary instead of precise queries: no difference (1.15 / 1.16 ms), so they stay precise.
`YW4_OCCLUSION=off` (no queries, every conditional draw made) was 0.15-0.3 ms faster in total, about the run-to-run
noise: the queries stay on.

## Not done

- `SetRenderEnable(false)`: not done, logged once if it ever happens (not seen).
- Whether any game code also reads the counts on the CPU was not checked.

```

`docs/decisions/0073-dlss-fsr-on-linux.md`:

```md
# 0073 — DLSS and FSR upscaling on Linux

<!-- decision
state: accepted
date: 2026-11-14
replaces: none
code: tools/yw4/fsr_linux.py, third_party/fsr3-linux, tools/yw4/deps.py, recomp/build.py, runtime/src/gpu_fsr.c, runtime/src/gpu_fg.c, runtime/src/gpu_dlss.c, runtime/src/settings.c, runtime/src/window.c, runtime/src/host.c, runtime/src/c11_keywords.h, launcher/ui/app.js
-->

Status: accepted, experimental on Linux. FSR upscaling checked in WSL on Lavapipe (software Vulkan) against AMD's own Windows library; FSR
frame generation checked there too (added later on 2026-11-14, below); DLSS only builds and links. None has run on a
real Linux GPU yet.

## Context

Upscaling and frame generation were Windows only (decisions 0039-0041): the build fetched AMD's signed Windows DLLs
and NVIDIA's Windows libraries. The owner asked for both upscalers on Linux.

## DLSS

NVIDIA's DLSS SDK at our pinned 310.9.16 already has Linux files: the static `libnvsdk_ngx.a` (built with GCC) and
`libnvidia-ngx-dlss.so.310.9.16`. `tools/yw4/deps.py` fetches them on Linux (pinned by SHA-256, NVIDIA's own address
only, as on Windows); `recomp/build.py` links the static library with the C++ runtime and `dlopen`, and copies the
DLSS library next to `yw4`. `gpu_dlss.c` names yw4's folder to NGX as the place to find it (NGX's default is the
application folder too). `msvc_shim.c` is Windows only: it stands in for the MSVC runtime the Windows library expects.

No DLSS frame generation or Reflex: they come through Streamline, which is Windows only.

## FSR

AMD ships no Linux build, and SDK 2.x has no Vulkan backend at all. SDK v1.1.4 (FSR 3.1.4) is the last with a Vulkan
backend and GLSL shaders. Building it on Linux needs AMD's shader compiler (Windows only) ported, and fixes to the
backend. A search found several projects doing this; the one we use is
**[xplane-fsr3](https://github.com/JonathanOrr/xplane-fsr3)** (MIT), whose `fsr3-linux/` holds exactly those parts.
It is a new project with no other users, so the owner asked for it to be checked before use, and it was:

- Its patches were read against AMD's source: the shader compiler changes are Windows file and text calls only;
  the four backend fixes are real (one is an AMD bug, `poolSizeCount` 5 for 6 pool sizes).
- Its smaller descriptor pool (16 per type per set) was checked against the generated shaders: at most 9 sampled
  images, 7 storage images, 2 constant buffers, 1 sampler.
- Its self-test reproduced its published numbers on Lavapipe: FSR 16.62 dB against bilinear 13.81 (panning), and
  13.11 with the motion vectors flipped (so the motion is used).
- In the game (late-game save, Mystic Grove, frame 2650, 1067x600 to 1600x900): our Linux build against AMD's own
  Windows library 3.1.6 on the RTX laptop, 31.7 dB on the 3D (mean difference 3.9 of 255, 0.6% of pixels more than
  30 apart: a software rasteriser against NVIDIA's); for scale, FSR against TAA is 18.5 dB.

The owner chose to use it with credit (option 1 of the two offered: theirs credited, or ours rewritten).

What is built (`tools/yw4/fsr_linux.py`, on the player's PC, about a minute):

1. AMD's SDK v1.1.4 source archive, pinned by SHA-256 (~200 MB; our deps-mirror first, GitHub after), its `sdk/` and
   `ffx-api/` folders.
2. xplane-fsr3's two patches (`git apply`, else `patch`), then ours, `third_party/fsr3-linux/patches/yw4_ffx_api_linux.py`:
   the SDK's `ffx-api` (the five functions the game calls) on Linux with only the FSR 3 provider, no DX12 driver hook,
   case-correct includes, standard integer literals, and headers usable from C.
3. AMD's shader compiler (xplane-fsr3's port) built with the system's C++ compiler; the upscaler's shader permutations
   generated with it and glslang.
4. `libamd_fidelityfx_vk.so`: the upscaler, AMD's Vulkan backend, the ffx-api layer, xplane-fsr3's host shim and our
   `yw4FfxHostSet`, with its C++ runtime inside (it needs only the C library). It exports exactly the five ffx-api
   functions and `yw4FfxHostSet`.

`gpu_fsr.c` opens it with `dlopen` (Windows: `LoadLibrary`) and calls `yw4FfxHostSet` with the device's extensions
and its 16-bit and synchronization2 features first: AMD's backend picks fp16, wave64 and other paths from what the GPU
*supports*, and the shim limits it to what the game *enabled*. It compiles against v1.1.4's headers on Linux, never
2.4.0's: the two use different values for the Vulkan backend's description type.

If the FSR build fails on a player's PC (an unusual compiler), the game is built without it and says why: FSR is an
optional extra, and TAA takes its place.

## FSR frame generation (added 2026-11-14)

First the Linux build was the upscaler only. Frame generation is now in the same library:

- `tools/yw4/fsr_linux.py` also builds AMD's frame interpolation, optical flow and frame generation provider, with the
  sources and shader options AMD's own CMake files give them. Which ones they are follows
  **[NX2navi](https://github.com/tangerineturtle1/NX2navi)**'s pull request #455 (MIT), which builds on the same
  xplane-fsr3 port; its `%s` to `%ls` fix in AMD's provider is in our patch, credited in
  `third_party/fsr3-linux/README.md`. No file of theirs is copied.
- Our ffx-api patch now takes in the frame generation provider and leaves out FSR 2 and AMD's frame generation
  swapchain: the game presents and paces frames itself, as on Windows (decision 0041).
- `gpu_fsr.c` opens the library once for both (`gpu_ffx_library()`); `gpu_fg.c` finds the functions with `dlsym`.
  v1.1.4 has no `PrepareV2`: Linux sends `Prepare` with a chained `PrepareCameraInfo`, and has no reset field (unused
  in v1.1.4). Its backend description has the three Vulkan fields flat, not in a `VkDeviceContext`.
- Linux thread stacks now get at least 8 MiB (glibc's default; was 1 MiB, `host.c`). AMD's frame interpolation puts
  a 142 KiB frame on the GPU worker's stack, which overflowed at the first generated frame (signal 11).
- The settings lock only what comes through Streamline on Linux: DLSS frame generation and Reflex.

Checked in WSL on Lavapipe (late-game save, frame 2600): a generated frame against the real one next to it, mean
difference 1 of 255, no pixel more than 64 apart, no holes or speckles; only soft edges differ. An earlier run had
black holes on characters and white speckles; they were gone after fixes in the same session, and which change fixed
them was not recorded. Not compared against Windows frame generation, no speed numbers.

## Issue #12: FSR built unpatched inside a clone; C11 keywords in C++ (2026-11-15)

A Linux player (GCC and Clang, AOSC) reported FSR failing to build with both compilers:
`sizeof(FfxFsr3UpscalerContext) >= sizeof(FfxFsr3UpscalerContext_Private)`, 524288 >= 837848. 524288 bytes is AMD's
default context size, `(1024 * 128)` uint32s, so our `-DFFX_SDK_DEFAULT_CONTEXT_SIZE=(1024 * 256)` never took effect:
stock `ffx_types.h` defines it without `#ifndef`, and only xplane-fsr3's Linux patch makes it overridable (wchar_t is 4
bytes on Linux, so the private contexts are larger).

The patches had not been applied at all. `apply_patches` ran `git apply` in the unpacked sources. Outside a git
repository that works like `patch`. Inside one, git reads the patch's paths from the repository's top, finds them outside
the folder it runs in, and skips them, printing nothing and exiting 0. The default work folder is `<clone>/work`, inside
the player's clone of this repository. Ours in WSL (`~/yw4linux/work`) is not, which is why it built here: reproduced in
WSL with the work folder inside a fresh `git init`, the same error with the same numbers, with Clang 19 which had just
built it fine outside one.

Fix (`tools/yw4/fsr_linux.py`): `git apply` runs with `GIT_CEILING_DIRECTORIES` set to the folder above the sources,
so it never looks for a repository there, and its errors are shown. After the patches, a line the Linux patch adds
(`#ifndef FFX_SDK_DEFAULT_CONTEXT_SIZE` in `ffx_types.h`) must be in the sources, or the build stops with that reason:
a skipped patch can't pass quietly again, whichever tool applied it. Checked in WSL with the work folder inside a
repository: GCC 13 and Clang 19 both build the library.

The same report: g++ stopped on `_Noreturn` in `host.h`, which `gpu_dlssg.cpp` (C++) includes. `runtime/src/c11_keywords.h`
gives `YW4_NORETURN` (`[[noreturn]]` in C++, `_Noreturn` in C), used by every runtime header that had `_Noreturn` (host.h,
kernel.h, hle.h, nvn.h, gpu_internal.h). In C++ only, it also defines `_Noreturn` and `_Thread_local` as the C++ words,
for the headers that keep the C11 spelling: `runtime/include/yw4rt.h` (the generated code's header; a change there makes
every player's build recompile all the generated code) and the thread-locals in nvn.h and gpu_internal.h, which g++
stopped on next. A test compiles those five headers as C++ with each compiler at hand, clang++ with
`-Werror=c11-extensions` (it otherwise takes C11 keywords as extensions): `tests/test_runtime.py`, CxxHeadersTest.
`recomp.ci` compiles all 131 runtime files with Clang 19 and with GCC 13 except `ui.c` (`#embed`: GCC 15 or newer, as
the setup page says).

## The launcher

Its Linux screens (decision 0071) now offer DLSS (RTX cards, upscaling only, about 60 MB) and FSR (upscaling and
frame generation, about 200 MB). The frame generation slide and chip show on Linux too.

## Not done

- No real Linux GPU yet: AMD, Intel or NVIDIA. No speed numbers.
- FSR frame generation on Linux not compared against the same shot on Windows.
- FSR's wave64 and 16-bit shader variants are built but only used where the game enabled the features they need.
- The SDK archive is not on our deps-mirror yet (uploading is the owner's): until then GitHub's generated archive is
  the only source, and GitHub has changed such archives' bytes before.

```

`docs/decisions/0074-cheats.md`:

```md
# 0074 — Cheats: a page in the overlay, and unlimited Crank-a-kai

<!-- decision
state: accepted
date: 2026-11-15
replaces: none
code: runtime/src/cheats.c, runtime/src/cheats.h, runtime/src/settings.c, runtime/src/gamemenu.c, recomp/overrides.toml, launcher/ui/app.js, launcher/ui/index.html, launcher/src-tauri/src/ready.rs
-->

Status: accepted. The crank cheat was checked in the owner's play (late-game save, 2026-11-15): the count stayed at
30 while coins went down. The overlay page and the launcher switch build; not yet seen on screen or tried from the
launcher.

## Context

The owner wanted unlimited Crank-a-kai cranks per day, with each crank still costing a coin. The game allows 30 a
day on the owner's save (an older copy of it had 3). The prize table (`capsule_config.cfg.bin`) has no limit, and
the community mod that changes it only blanks prize conditions, so the limit had to be found in the running game.

## How the count was found

- Memory searches for 2-byte and 4-byte numbers going 30, 29, 28 found nothing that held: the count is **one
  byte**.
- The game autosaves after each crank. Copying the autosave after each one and comparing the copies showed one byte
  stepping down by one per crank (`AUTOSAVE/data.bin` offset `0x822`), with the day's limit (30) in the next byte.
- A byte-pattern search (`YW4_FINDBYTES`, `runtime/src/memscan.c`, a test tool) found the same bytes in memory, and
  a write watch on them caught one write per crank.

## The command that writes it

The write comes from `main+0x296560`, a script command (registered as `0xd0c06ed4` by the startup function at
`main+0xe7b0`) that the Crank-a-kai menu's script calls: "save one byte by ID". It looks the ID up in a sorted table
of (ID, slot) pairs and stores the value at `[save data + slot + 0x288]`. No game code calls it directly.

A hook just before its store (`main+0x2966a8`: x9 the ID, x20 the value) logged every change in a play session
(`YW4_TRACE_SAVEBYTE=1`). Only the Crank-a-kai's three IDs changed anything:

| ID | Slot | What |
|---|---|---|
| `a45a65ec` | 11 | Cranks left today: set to the limit at the day's reset, one down per crank |
| `9076e662` | 12 | The day's limit, set at the reset |
| `2f508d80` | 13 | A byte set at the reset (seen 8, 15, 3, 5) |

## The cheat

Unlimited Crank-a-kai (`YW4_CHEAT_CRANK`): when a store to `a45a65ec` would lower it, the hook puts the old value in
x20, so the count stays. The day's reset (a raise) still happens, and coins are spent as usual: they are an item
count elsewhere in the save. The hook reads the switch at every store, so it changes while the game runs.

Turned on with no cranks left (0, or 255, -1 as a byte), the count is set to 1 so the next crank can happen; it then
stays there (owner, 2026-11-15). The byte is found as the command finds it, through the ID table.

## Unlimited coins

Added 2026-11-17 for issue #17, where a player asked for coins that don't run out (`YW4_CHEAT_COINS`). Each crank
spends one coin through the game's "remove items" function (`main+0x4f2e90`: an inventory handle and how many). A
trace (`YW4_TRACE_ITEMREMOVE=1`) of the owner's play, cranking with a Crank-a-Coin, a One-Star Coin and an Old Coin,
showed one call per crank (count 1), all on the same path. At `main+0x4f3038` the item's ID is in w21 and the count
to take off is in w19. The store at `main+0x4f32c4` writes the count minus w19 (at least 0); a count left at 0
removes the item.

The cheat sets w19 to 0 there for the ten coins (the item config's `ITEM_CONSUME_INFO` entries in categories 107,
Crank-a-kai coins, and 111, Oni coins: Crank-a-Coin, One-Star, Five-Star, Special, Old, Y, Ark, Oni, Super Oni,
Ultra Oni). The count stays the same and the crank still counts as paid.

Not the script command the Crank-a-kai calls (`0x195e1fd9`, `main+0x293760`, "remove 1 of this item"): about 20
other scripts call it too (events, the battle item menu, the skill tree reset, equipment making), so the coins are
picked out by item ID instead. Spending a coin any other way, such as selling it, also keeps it while the cheat is
on.

Tested in the owner's play, 2026-11-17: with the cheat on, two cranks (Crank-a-Coin, One-Star) took 0 coins; after
it was turned off, the next crank took one. The switch is read at every call, so it changes while the game runs.

## Where the switch is

The owner chose option B of the design canvas (<https://claude.ai/artifact/XcwzdE1gju4aNQJgxgE2e5>): a **Cheats**
page in the overlay's side menu, between Overlay and Report a bug, with the cheats as rows like the Settings page's.
The choice is saved in the settings file like any setting.

The launcher's Settings has a **Cheats** card of its own (under Playing) with a **Cheats page** switch (on by
default). Off, the game starts with `YW4_CHEATS=0`: the page is hidden, the keys pass over its place, and no cheat
acts whatever the settings file says.

The card's **Manage** button opens **Manage cheats** (owner, 2026-11-15): "Toggleable in game" lists the cheats the
game's page also switches, read from and written to the game's settings.ini (the same `YW4_CHEAT_CRANK` line, so the
last change wins; `ready.rs` `game_cheats` / `set_game_cheat`, which write only the known cheat lines); "Launcher
only (needs game restart)" is for cheats that can't change while playing (none yet). While any `yw4` runs, its
switches are locked (the game rewrites the file as it plays); the page looks every 2 s, so a game started from a
shortcut locks it too.

## Not done

- The launcher's switches have been seen (screenshots) but not used end to end: a launcher change picked up by the
  game, or the Cheats page switch off from the launcher.
- Report a bug moved one place down the side menu: a recording that reaches it with Down from Resume now lands on
  Cheats.

```

`docs/decisions/0075-shortcut-wheel.md`:

```md
# 0075 — The shortcut wheel: hold L's key, point with the mouse

<!-- decision
state: accepted
date: 2026-11-15
replaces: none
code: runtime/src/shortcutwheel.c, runtime/src/shortcutwheel.h, runtime/src/window.c, runtime/src/bindings.c, runtime/src/gamemenu.c, recomp/overrides.toml, tools/yw4/wheel_icons.py, tools/yw4/bc7.py, recomp/build.py, recomp/ci.py, tools/yw4/build_install.py
-->

Status: accepted. Built and tried in scripted runs (`YW4_WHEEL_TEST`, 2026-11-15): shortcuts 1-4 work (Auto-Navi,
Diary, Bike on and off, Naviwoof Guide), the hold-L four through Mirapo (its list opens), with the green "on"
state, locked and "not usable here" slots. Not yet played by the owner with a real mouse.

## Context

The game has eight field shortcuts on the D-pad: four on their own (Auto-Navi, Diary, Bike, Naviwoof Guide) and four
while L is held (Change Watchers, Mirapo, Change Yo-kai Companion, Change moves and Equipment). With the starting
keys the D-pad is the arrow keys and L is 1: a long reach from WASD. The owner wanted the mouse to pick them instead.
Ideas tried on paper first (work/mockups/shortcut-wheel): WASD as the D-pad while 1 is held, blind mouse flicks,
two hold keys, then a wheel with all eight. The owner chose a wheel, then Steam's radial menu as the model, then the
"Searchlight" look out of six styles (Watch Mode's teal lens finds the pick, the rest dims, the name in the middle).

## What it does

- **Exploring only.** It opens when a key bound to L in the exploring set is pressed (1 to start) and the game has
  the mouse, outside battles, the game's menus (the Yo-kai Pad, conversations, the map, the Stopwatching menu), the
  overlay and its pause. Elsewhere the key is plain L, as before.
- **While it is open** the game still gets L (2026-11-16, the owner's hand test: with L held back the cross never
  turned its page and 1 + an arrow key did nothing), and the mouse's movement goes to the wheel instead of the
  camera. A pointer collects the movement (at most 140 mouse pixels from the middle); past 100 (first 40: the owner
  wanted to come closer to a slot) it points at one of eight sectors of 45 degrees.
- **Letting go of the key** uses the slot pointed at: the D-pad direction for 6 reads of the game's input (slots 1-4),
  or L and the direction (slots 5-8). The game takes the hold-L four only once its HUD has turned to their page,
  about a second after L goes down (3 and 12 reads of L did nothing, 60 opened Mirapo's list). L has been held since
  the wheel opened, so on letting go only the rest of the 60 reads is waited. A D-pad slot lets L go 8 reads first
  (the cross back on its page), then presses the direction. Let go in the middle: nothing.
- **The old way still works:** an arrow key (any D-pad press) while the key is held closes the wheel and lets L
  through until the key is let go (owner's answer, 2026-11-15).
- **When it doesn't open** the log says why ("key down, not opened: map"). Found that way in the owner's test: after
  Mirapo's list (the map's menu class) was backed out of, the field's HUD menu never focused again, so the map
  counted as open for good; the cross's next update now ends it (mousemenu_field_hud_seen). Mirapo's "warp here?"
  Yes / No box turned the Stopwatching menu's flag on outside a battle (a Yes / No box now counts only over that
  menu). And after a game menu the mouse wasn't always taken back: the wheel opens if the window has the keyboard,
  and takes the mouse itself.
- **On / Off** on the Controls page (Mouse shortcut wheel), saved as `YW4_SHORTCUT_WHEEL` in settings.ini (owner's
  requirement). Off: nothing of it runs.

Why the ring order: the four D-pad shortcuts on the straight lines where the D-pad points, the hold-L set on the
diagonals. A player who knows the pad finds the first four where they expect them.

## How it is drawn

As F2's quick look is (decision 0053's overlay canvas, `menu_draw` in window.c): drawn on the CPU with ui.c into a
see-through canvas and blended over the running game, only its square, in the overlay's 1600 x 900 design units.
The look is style A "Refined" of the second styling round (work/mockups/shortcut-wheel/styles3.html, the owner's
pick): a cone of light from the middle to the pick, a scope lens with an inner glow and corner marks, the rim lit
where it points, faint plates under the icons. The soft light is drawn per pixel, only over the box it covers.
Animations: opening grows from 85 % and fades in (120 ms) with the icons arriving 15 ms apart; the lens glides to a
new pick (80 ms); using one flashes the lens and fades (100 + 80 ms); cancelling shrinks to 90 % and fades
(100 ms). The picture is redrawn every frame only while something moves, else only when the pick changes.
After the owner's hand test (2026-11-16): the middle circle is the pointer (it follows the mouse, full size, and
hides once a slot is picked); the other icons aren't dimmed (the pick is already larger); a long name goes on two
lines (it ran into the side slots).

## What the wheel reads from the game

The field HUD's shortcut cross (read with Ghidra, `work/ghidra/hud_guide*.c`, game code never in the repo):
- **Its object**, kept by a hook at the cross's update (main+0x755ea0, x0). The wheel opens only once it exists (so
  not before the first load). A first try, "the field HUD had the last menu focus", blocked it in the late-game save.
- **Locked** (not unlocked in the story): D-pad up / right / down / left = object bytes +0x5ea / +0x5eb / +0x5ed /
  +0x5ec; the hold-L four +0x600..0x603, only when +0x5ff says the game has the hold-L page at all (an early save
  has none: its cross shows no "Hold"). Drawn as a dashed outline and a lock; letting go there uses nothing.
- **Not usable here** (the cross's grey-out, main+0x758e20): +0x604 + page * 4 + direction. Set for the D-pad four
  inside Mystic Grove, where the game blocks them. Drawn in grey, with "not usable here" under the name.
- **On** (the HUD's green disc): the state the game gives each button through main+0x756520 (hooked: x1 the button,
  w2 on): 0xe Auto-Navi, 0x11 Bike (0xf Diary and 0x10 Naviwoof are buttons too, never "on"). The ids are the
  cross's places, shared by the hold-L four: while the game has L (and 8 reads after) its reports are theirs
  (Change Watchers set Auto-Navi "on", opening the wheel turned both off), so they are ignored then.

## The game's icons

The icons are the field HUD's own (its "guide" sheet, `rpg00_01.g4tx` in menu.cpk, a BC7 texture). They are game
data, so they follow decision 0048's icon: `tools.yw4.wheel_icons` takes them from the player's RomFS at build time
into `<work_dir>/wheel/icons.bin`, and recomp.build writes them into a generated `wheel_icons.c`. The launcher's
build runs it before compiling. Without the file the wheel draws D-pad arrows.

Players' builds have no Pillow, so `tools/yw4/bc7.py` decodes BC7 in plain Python, only the blocks the icons cover
(tests/test_bc7.py checks it against Pillow on random blocks of every mode; the real icons match byte for byte).

## Not done yet

- All eight used by hand in the late-game save (2026-11-16); not with a controller (the wheel is the mouse's).
- The names are the English patch's words in the code; a Japanese game shows them in English.
- The HUD object could be stale for a moment after an area change (a new HUD is built; the hook then updates it).

## Test hooks

`YW4_WHEEL_TEST=<read>:<slot>[,...]` holds the key for 40 input reads from each read and points at the slot (0: the
middle), and takes a screenshot of the open wheel (or at `YW4_WHEEL_SHOTS=<reads>,...` after each start: past 40
the use or cancel animation); `YW4_WHEEL_LOG=1` logs what it does, the HUD's bytes and its button states. Input
reads come about twice per drawn frame, so `--shots` frames can't aim at it. Replays (`s` lines) give buttons in
hex. In save_base_busy rain starts a few seconds in and takes the player off the bike.
```
